questions.prompt:
With reference to the history of ancient India, which
of the following statements is/are correct?
1. Mitakshara was the civil law for upper castes and
Dayabhaga was the civil law for lower castes.
2. In the Mitakshara system, the sons can claim right to
the property during the lifetime of the father, whereas
in the Dayabhaga system, it is only after the death of
the father that the sons can claim right to the property.
3. The Mitakshara system deals with the matters related
to the property held by male members only of a family,
whereas the Dayabhaga system deals with the matters
related to the property held by both male and female
members of a family.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Mitakshara is a vivarti on the Yajnavalkya smriti, written
by Vijnanesvara. Dayabhaga is a Hindu law treatise written
by Jimutavahana. These treatises deal with the laws of
inheritance. Hence statement (1) is wrong. In Mitakshara
system, the sons can claim right to the property during the
lifetime of the father, whereas in Dayabhaga system, it is only
after the death of the father that the sons can claim right to
the property. Hence statement (2) is right. Mitakshara system
deals with matters related to the property held by both male
and female members of a family. While Dayabhaga only deals
with matters related to the property held by male members
of a family. So, statement (3) is also wrong.

questions.prompt: Who was the fi rst ruler of the Slave Dynasty?

The fi rst ruler of the Slave Dynasty was Qutbuddin Aybak
who ruled from 1206 A.D. to 1210 A.D. He established his
capital at Lahore. Qutbuddin Aibak was born in Turkistan.
Though he was ugly in appearance, he was intelligent and
impressive in behaviour. He was taken as a prisoner and
sold to the Qazi of Nishapur named Fakhruddin as a slave in
his childhood. He was taken care and pro vided with proper
education and military training by the kind-hearted Qazi
but soon after the death of the Qazi, his sons sold Aybak to
Muhammad Ghori. He was well-versed in Islamic theology,
horse riding and swordsmanship. Owing to his skill and
qualities, he soon attracted the attention of his master and
was appointed commander of a troop. Shortly after battles;
he was promoted to the post of Amir-i- Akhur, the master
of the royal stable. When Ghori invaded India, Aybak came
with his master and provided him with active support during
battles. The successes of his master by and large depended
on his military skill. Ghori was immensely pleased with him,
and he appointed him his governor of the Indian empire. In
1206 A.D., on his way to Ghazni, Ghori died. His empire
was inherited by his slaves, as he had no son to succeed him.
Aybak, who was a viceroy of his Indian Empire was invited
by the Amirs of Lahore to assume the powers. He bestowed
the title of Malik and Sipahasalaar on himself. Muhammad
Ghori had no male successor to inherit his empire; hence his
nephew, Ghiyasuddin Mahmud ascended the throne of Ghori
after his death in 1206 A.D.

questions.prompt: The capital of Qutbuddin Aybak was
questions.explanation:
After the death of Muhammad Ghori in 1206 A.D., his
General Qutbuddin Aybak, who was in charge of Lahore and
north-Indian possessions, was invited by Amirs of Lahore
to assume the powers of Ghori. The capital of Qutbuddin
Aybak was Lahore. Taj-ud-Din Yalduz, Governor of Kirman
ascended the throne of Ghazni. It seems that it was the
desire of Muhammad Ghori that Qutbuddin Aybak should
succeed him in India. In his brief reign of four years (1206-10
A.D.), he moved his capital to Lahore to frustrate Yalduz’s
ambition of annexing Punjab. He strengthened his position
by matrimonial alliances with infl uential rival Turkish Chiefs.
Nasiruddin Qabacha of Multan refused to accept Qutbuddin
as the ruler of Delhi Sultanate. Due to this, Aybak always
stayed in Lahore and never got the chance to move to Delhi.

Bazaar. He was the founder of the Slave Dynasty in India.

questions.prompt: Who was the fi rst Muslim ruler of Delhi?
questions.explanation:
Iltutmish was the fi rst Sultan of Delhi who received the
investiture from Caliph. In 1229 A.D., the Caliph of Baghdad,
Al-Muntasir Billah, bestowed on Iltutmish the title of
“Sultan-i- Azam” or the Sultan The Great. Thus, in this way,
he was the fi rst legally independent Sultan of Delhi. He was
successful in keeping the throne of Delhi safe from the danger
of Mongol invasion as well as from the attacks of both Taj
ud-din Yalduz and Qabacha. He broke up the Rajput powers
in the north and established his supremacy over them. He
made his rule hereditary, issued coins with his name and made
Delhi a beautiful capital. He is said to have introduced fi rst
Arabic silver (175gm) and copper currency which were two
basic coins of the Sultanate period. Iltutmish belonged to the
tribe of ‘Ilbari’ in the Eurasian Steppe of Turkestan. Iltutmish
was fi rst appointed governor of Badaun in recognition of
his services during the campaign of Muhammad of Ghur
against the Khokhars in 1205-06 A.D. Amirali Ismail invited
Iltutmish for the coronation in Delhi with the approval of
Turkish nobles after the death of Aybak. Iltutmish declared
himself Sultan in 1211 A.D.

Khan reached the Indus in pursuit of the fugitive
Khwarezm prince.

that Taimur occupied Multan and crossed the

questions.prompt: The full name of Sultan of Delhi Balban was?
questions.explanation:
The full name of Balban was Ghiyasuddin Balban. He was the
ninth Sultan of the Mamluk dynasty of Delhi. Ghiyasuddin
was the Wazeer and heir of the last Shamsi Sultan, Nasiruddin
Mahmud. He reduced the power of the treacherous nobility
and heightened the stature of the Sultan. In spite of having
only a few military achievements, he was the most powerful
ruler of the Sultanate between Shamsuddin Iltutmish and
Alauddin Khalji. He reached on the post of Amir-i-Shikar
during Raziyya period. Like Iltutmish, he also was an Ilbari
Turk. Balban married his daughter to Sultan Nasiruddin, on
this occasion was given the title of Ulugh Khan and the post
of Nayab-i- Mamlikat. Balban sat on the throne of Delhi in
1266 A.D.

questions.prompt: The kingdom of Vijayanagara was founded by-
questions.explanation:
The Vijayanagara empire was founded by Harihara and Bukka
in 1336. This dynasty is known as Sangama Dynasty after their
father’s name. Harihara and Bukka were the feudatories of the
Kakatiyas of Warangal. After the fall of Warangal at the hands
of Delhi Sultan, they shifted to Kampili and became ministers.
Muhammad Tughluq invaded Kampili and arrested Harihara
and Bukka. Both were forced to convert to Islam. Later, both
were sent to the south to suppress a rebellion. They could not
succeed, but under the infl uence of Saint Vidyaranya, they again
reverted to Hinduism to establish the Vijayanagara Dynasty.
They were inspired by their spiritual teacher Vidyaranya and
Sayan, a noted commentator of Vedas. Four Dynasties ruled
under this empire.
(i) Sangama dynasty (1336-1485 A.D.). (ii) Saluva dynasty
(1485-1505 A.D.), (iii) Tuluva dynasty (1505-1570 A.D.)
and (vi) Aravidu dynasty (1570-1672 A.D.). These dynasties
ruled over three hundred years. The capitals of Vijayanagara
were Anegundi, Vijayanagara, Penukonda and Chandragiri
respectively.

What was the chief characteristic of the fi nancial

questions.explanation:

various sources like land revenue, wealth tax, trade tax,
commercial tax, tax on industry, social and community tax
and fi nes charged on crime. The main source of income
was from land revenue, which was fi xed after the land was
measured and categorized. The tax, namely ‘Shist’ (Rai-
Rekha) was the main source of income to the state. The
revenue department was known as ‘Athavane.’

divided into four categories for purposes of assessment,

rate varied depending upon the quality of land, crop, soil,
method of irrigation, etc. Thus, statement (1) is correct. The
private owners of the workshop had to pay industry tax. Thus,
statement (2) is also correct.

questions.prompt:
Which one of the following is NOT the characteristic
of 'Iqta System'?

options.text: Iqta was a revenue collection system

Siyasatnama was the source of information for Iqta
system

Revenue from Iqta was directly deposited in Sultan's
account

Muqti was supported to maintain troops out of the
revenue collected from Iqta

questions.explanation:
Iqta system in India was introduced by Iltutmish during
Sultanate period. According to this system, the owner of
Iqta (Iqtadar or Muqti) was given the responsibility of
collecting revenue and taxes in his area. Revenue from Iqta
was not directly deposited in Sultan's account, whereas it was
used by the Muqti to meet his administrative and military
expenditures. Muqti had to maintain troops out of this revenue
collected from Iqta for the service of Sultan. Siyasatnama
authored by Abu Ali Hasan Ibn Ali Tusi (Nizam-ul-Mulk) is
the source of information for primary Iqta system.

the control of the State.

questions.explanation:

standard division of territories is accepted as Khalisa and
Jagirs (Iqta). Therefore, Assertion (A) is correct.

questions.prompt:
With reference to medieval India, which one of the
following is the correct sequence in ascending order
in terms of size?
questions.explanation:
With reference to medieval India, entire empire was divided
into Suba (province). 'Subedar' was head of administration
of Suba. For better administration, every Suba was divided
into smaller units called Sarkar whose head was 'Fauzdar'.
Every Sarkar was further divided into 'Pargana' or 'Mahal'.
Shiqdar was head of this unit. There were villages under
Pargana, which were called 'Mavada' or 'Deeha'. 'Nagla' were
small colonies under Mavada. During the reign of Shahjahan
another unit was formed between Pargana and Sarkar called
'Chakla' under which a few Parganas came. Hence with
reference to medieval India, the correct sequence in ascending
order in terms of size is – Pargana-Sarkar-Suba.

questions.explanation:
(i) Al-Biruni : Al-Biruni was a resident of Khiva (ancient
Khwarizm). He was in the court of the last emperor
of Khiva dynasty as a scholar and diplomat before
Mahmud Ghazni’s victory over India. He came to India
with Mahmud Ghazni during his invasion of India.
(ii) Ibn Battuta (1333-1342 A.D. ) : He was Moroccan
traveller. He came to India during the Sultanate
period in the regime of Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq
(1325-1351A.D.). Muhammad Tughluq appointed
him as ‘Qazi’ of Delhi. Later, he sent him to China as
an ambassador in 1342. He composed his travelling
experiences in his book “Rihla.”
(iii) Jean-Baptiste Tavernier (17th century A.D.) : A French
gem merchant and traveller began his voyage the period
of Shahjahan. He made six voyages to the East. He wrote
his travel accounts in his book "The Six Voyages of John
Baptista Tavernier".
(iv) Niccolao Manucci (1653-1708 A.D.) : He was an Italian
traveller. He reached India from his hometown Venice
while travelling to Turkiye and Asia. He had given his
services to Prince Dara Shukoh as a cannoneer. Later, he
opted for the medical profession. Manucci is famous for
his work. "Storia do Mogor or Mogul India, 1653-1708".

that Dr. Harishchandra Verma, in his book ‘Madhyakalin

questions.prompt: The city of Jaunpur was founded in the memory of :

Bahlul Lodi defeated its last emperor Hussain Shah and was
able to reconquer Jaunpur in 1479.

questions.prompt: Who were Polygars of South India?
questions.explanation:
Palaiyakkarar or Polygar was the feudal title of a class of
administrative and Military governors appointed by the
Nayaka rulers of South India during 16th to 18th centuries.

questions.prompt: The Bhakti movement was started by –
questions.explanation:
The Bhakti Movement is a Hindu religious movement in
which the main spiritual practise is loving devotion among
the Shaiva Nayanars and the Vaishnava Alvars. Devotional
worship had a long history of almost a thousand years across
the sub-continent. The early medieval Bhakti movement
originated in Dravida region and began to spread to the north
during the late medieval ages (during 13th-14th centuries
onwards) when North India was under Islamic rule. The
Bhakti movement was started in the 8th century by the great
philosopher Adi Shankaracharya.

questions.prompt: The Bhakti culture was reborn in India during-
questions.explanation:
The Bhakti Movement started with the great philosopher Adi
Shankaracharya propounding the philosophy of Advaitavada
to eliminate the infl uence of Buddhism during the 8th century.
The Bhakti movement was reborn in the 15th-16th century
when Kabir, Tulsi, Nanak, Sur, Mirabai etc. encouraged the
movement.

questions.prompt:
The common belief of life of both Buddha and Mirabai
was–

that the world is full of sorrow. 'Sorrow is fi rst among the
Four Arya Truths of Buddhism'.

questions.prompt: A common feature of all Bhakti Saints was that they –

options.text:

their followers
Rejected the authority of the priestly class
Encouraged women to go to the temples

questions.explanation:
The conduct of Bhakti saints was of a very high standard.
Many of them visited the country and met many people
having different views. They also contributed to the
advancement of Hindi, Kannada, Punjabi, Bengali, Telugu,
Tamil and other languages. The Saints of Bhakti Movement
gave their verses in regional and local languages so that their
followers could easily understand them. This was the main
reason behind the development of local languages.

questions.prompt:
With reference to the religious history of medieval
India, the Sufi mystics were known to pursue which
of the following practices?
1.
Meditation and control of breath.
2.
Severe ascetic exercises in a lonely place.
3.
Recitation of holy songs to arouse a state of ecstasy
in their audience.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
questions.explanation:
The emergence of Sufi saints in medieval India helped to
promote communal harmony in the society. They promoted
activities like meditation and practised spiritual disciplines
such as remembrance and devotional practices like 'Sama'
and sometimes breath-focused remembrance. They took the
help of holy songs and music to spread unity and harmony
in society and to arouse a state of spiritual ecstasy in their
audience.

opposed both rituals and idolatry. They were known as

questions.prompt: Ramanujacharya is related to –
questions.explanation:
Ramanujacharya was the earliest propagator of the Bhakti
Movement. The philosophy of Sri Ramanujacharya is known
in Sanskrit as Vishishtadvaita. This term literally means
“non-duality of reality as characterized by attributes. The
central idea of Vishishtadvaita is this: ‘there exists an ultimate
principle, an absolute being that is the source and substratum
of all that exists.’

questions.prompt: “Shuddha Advaitvad” was propounded by –
questions.explanation:
Shuddha Advaitavada is the “purely non-dual” philosophy
propounded by Shri Vallabhacharya, the founder and guru
of the Vallabha Sect. Vallabhacharya was the son of Telugu
Brahmin Shri Lakshmana Bhatta of Somyaji clan, who is said
to have developed the views of Vishnuswami into Shuddha
Advaita or pure non-dualism.

questions.prompt:
Which of the following statements regarding the Bhakti
Movement is not correct?

options.text: Nimbarka propounded the philosophy of Dvaitadvaita.

instead of Saguna Bhakti .

questions.explanation:
The renowned saint of the Bhakti Movement tradition,
Madhvacharya, was a proponent of Dvaita (Dualism)
philosophy. His central doctrine is "Dvaitavada", which states
that the individual soul (ātman), the material world, and the
Supreme Being (Paramatma) are distinct and fundamentally
different from each other. Madhvacharya followed the
Saguna Bhakti tradition, not the Nirguna Bhakti stream. He
considered Lord Vishnu as the supreme deity and strongly
advocated his worship. Thus, statement (c) is incorrect, while
other statements are correct.

questions.prompt:
How many Jyotirlingas are there devoted to Lord
Shiva?
questions.explanation:

India- Somnath is situated in Gujarat, Kedarnath is

was born on April 15, 1469 AD, in a Khatri family. He had
a strong faith in the worship of Nirakar Brahma. He passed
away in 1539 AD at Derababa Nanak (Kartarpur Pakistan).

Nanak used to believe in monotheism and emphasised the
worship of one formless God (Ik Onkar). He believed that
there was one and a shapeless God. He did not believe in
anthropomorphism.

questions.prompt: Mirabai was contemporary of :
questions.explanation:
Mirabai was the only daughter of Ratan Singh Rathore of
Merta. She was born into a royal family in the Kudaki village
of Merta, Rajasthan. Mira was married to Bhojraj, the eldest
son of the famous ruler of Mewar Rana Sanga. But, King
Bhojraj died after a few years. After the death of her husband,
Mirabai spent her whole life worshipping Lord Krishna. She
was the contemporary of Tulsidas (1532-1623 A.D.), Guru
Nanak (1469-1539 A.D.) and Chaitanya (1486-1533 A.D.), but
Ramakrishna (1836-1886 A.D.) was not contemporary of her.

questions.prompt:
Which one of the following leaders of the Bhakti
Movement was infl uenced by Islam?
questions.explanation:
Namdev played an important role in popularising Bhakti
Movement in Maharashtra. He was born in 1270 A.D. at
Narsi (Maharashtra). Vishoba Khechar was his teacher. He
was related to Varakari sect. He was a disciple of Vishoba
Khechar, who gave him education on mystic life and
introduced him to an omnipresent form of God. Namdev
was quite infl uenced by Islam among the Saints of Bhakti
Movement. He opposed idolatry, fasting, pilgrimage and
harsh physical practices. He said “One stone is lovingly
decorated, while another stone is walked upon. If one is a
God, then the other must also be a God”. Thus, option (c) is
the correct answer.

medieval period.

: The early Chishti Sufi s were fond of

into Persian, was possible due to the interest of rulers.
Mahmud of Ghazni took many books with him to Ghazni.
Firuz Tughluq and Sikandar Lodi got books from various
areas written especially in Sanskrit translated into Persian.
Later, Mughal emperors also translated various books of
Sanskrit in Persian. Therefore, it is clear that the statement
is correct. 'Sama' was the music assembly. Chishtis were the
supporter of music and considered music a medium to reach
God. Hence, it is clear that the reason is also true, but the
reason (R) is not the correct interpretation of the statement.

questions.prompt:
Which improvements among these were done by Sher
Shah Suri?
(1) Revenue reforms
(2) Administrative reforms
(3) Military reforms
(4) Currency system reforms
Select the right answer by using code given below –
questions.explanation:
Sher Shah Suri had a signifi cant role in medieval India. He
is considered the antecedent of Akbar as an administrative
imperialist.
(1) Revenue reforms: Sher Shah believed that for the
stability of the empire, it was essential to satisfy the
peasants and make them happy. He introduced numerous
reforms in land revenue administration. His land revenue
collection was based on Ryotwari and was settled directly
with cultivators. He adopted an improved and systematic
method of measuring the land and assessing its revenue.
(2) Administrative Reforms: Sher Shah managed his father’s
manor as manager and obtained the essential knowledge
of administration. He had a proper knowledge of military
composition, administration and fi nancial system of
Mughals. He was the head of the central government.
His administration was completely centralised before
victory over Bengal. He divided the whole kingdom
into 47 Sarkars (districts) (According to Dr. Kanungo).
He arranged a diff erent system for Bengal province.
He divided the province into 19 Sarkars (districts)
(According to Satish Chandra) and appointed a military
offi cial as Shiqdar to control.
A non-military offi cial Amir-i-Bengal was also appointed
for assistance. This arrangement was made for the
abolishment of revolt threat.
(3) Military Reforms: Sher Shah introduced many reforms
in military sector for empire consolidation. He was
inspired by reforms of Alauddin Khalji. He recruited and
paid the soldiers directly and every soldier had his chehra
(face) recorded and his horse branded with an imperial
sign, to stop fraud.
(4) Currency System Reforms: The reign of Sher Shah was
an era of experiment in the history of coins. V.A. Smith
rightly observes ‘’It is the basis of the existing British
currency’’. He introduced pure gold, silver and copper
coins in place of the beaten coins. His silver rupee coins
weighed 178 grains and coppers Daam weighed 308
grains (20 gm). Thus, credit of these reforms goes to Sher
Shah Suri.

questions.explanation:
Akbar was the fi rst among the monarchs of medieval India
to raise the policy of religious tolerance to the pinnacle of
secularism. The socio-political condition of the country
was such that Akbar thought it was advisable to adopt
independent views in religious matters. The non-Muslims
constituted the majority of his Indian subjects. Without
winning their confi dence and active support, Akbar could
not hope to establish and consolidate the Mughal rule in
India. Religion had played the role of a divisive force in
Indian society ever since the advent of Islam which most of
its people had refused to embrace. Akbar fully understood
the centrifugal tendencies of the complex Indian socio-
political order and made a serious attempt to eliminate these
by separating religion from politics. To win the goodwill of
Hindus, he abolished the pilgrimage tax and Jizya. Freedom
of worship, matrimonial alliances with Hindus, high civil and
military positions to Hindus, translation of Hindu scriptures,
establishment of Ibadatkhana, issue of infallibility decree,
freedom to construct temples, land grants, considerations
of Hindu sentiments, reforms in Hindu society were some
measures adopted by Akbar to establish religious harmony
but he had not forsaken Islam.

of each soldier maintained) and Dagh (branding of horses)
in 1573-74 A.D. After this action, he organised soldiers by
Mansabdari system in 1574-75 A.D. Mansab means rank
or position. Mansabdar means the offi cial who had a rank
or designation in the royal army. This was based on the
decimal system.

questions.prompt: In which measures Todarmal achieved fame ?

why it is known as Todarmal settlement. Under this system,
the average produce of diff erent crops, as well as the average
prices prevailing over the last ten years, was calculated. One-
third of the average produce was state Share (Maal), rest
two-third share was left to the cultivators (Kharaj).

horses in comparison to their ‘Sawar’ rank.
Sih-aspa : In this system, Mansabdars had to maintain a
triple number of horses in comparison to their ‘Sawar’ rank.

questions.prompt: Who re-imposed Jizya ?
questions.explanation:
Akbar had abolished Jizya during his reign but Aurangzeb
re-imposed it on non-Muslims in 1679 A.D. The Hindus were
categorised into three classes for the purpose of paying tax:
(i) Those with income less than 200 Dirham per annum,
had to pay 12 Dirham per annum as tax.
(ii ) Those with income 200 to 10,000 Dirham per annum,
had to pay 24 Dirham per annum as tax.
(iii) Those with income more than 10,000 Dirham per
annum, had to pay 48 Dirham per annum as tax.
Women, slaves, children under 14 years, beggars and
unemployed persons were exempted from it. The subordinate
Hindu kings and Brahmins were compelled to pay this tax.
About reviving Jizya, Europian traveller wrote that his motive
was to increase his treasure but it seems to be partially true.

questions.explanation:

and civil service of the empire which came to be known as
Mansabdari system. Very soon, this system became the main
basis of the military and civil administration of the Mughals.
The main intention to introduce Mansabdari was to provide

questions.prompt:
Who was responsible for the smooth functioning of
the Mughal Mansabdari system?
questions.explanation:
Mir Bakshi was responsible for the smooth functioning of the
Mughal Mansabdari system. The Mansabdari system was the
administrative system introduced by Akbar in Mughal Empire.
The word 'Mansab' is of Arabic origin meaning rank or position.
Hence Mansabdari was a system of ranking the government
offi cials and determining their civil & military duties, along
with their renumeration. The recruitment and promotion of the
Mansabdars was in the hands of the Emperor who could also
dismiss them at will. Mostly the recruitment of the Mansabdars
was done on the recommendation of Mir Bakshi.

questions.prompt:
Which one of the following is not true about the Mughal
Mansabdari System ?

options.text: They got conditional or Mashut rank.
Their ‘Sawar’ rank could exceed the ‘Zat’ rank.
All civil and military offi cers were given mansabs.

questions.explanation:
Mansab meant rank or status. Mansabdars or offi ceholders
were divided into 33 classes and were paid in cash according
to their respective grades. There were exceptions to this rule,
particularly when the mansabdar was serving in a diffi cult terrain
amidst the rebels. In such cases, the state often increased the
sawar rank without altering the zat rank. Obviously, the system
was not a static one. It changed to meet the circumstances. Thus,
reform was the use of conditional rank (Mashrut), which meant
an ‘increase of sawar rank for a temporary period. So, option
(c) is the correct answer.

questions.prompt:
With reference to Mughal India, what is/are the
diff erence/diff erences between Jagirdar and Zamindar?
1. Jagirdars were holders of land assignments in lieu
of judicial and police duties, whereas Zamindars
were holders of revenue rights without obligation
to perform any duty other than revenue collection.
2. Land assignments to Jagirdars were hereditary had
revenue rights of Zamindars were not hereditary.
Select the correct answer using code given below :
questions.explanation:
During Akbar's period, all the territory was broadly divided
into two : Khalisa & Jagir. The revenue from the fi rst went
to imperial treasury & that from jagir was assigned to
jagirdars in lieu of their salary in cash according to their
rank. Right to collect revenue was to utilize the same for
their salary & to meet their military obligation. The judicial
& police functions were performed locally by Zamindars.
An important feature of the Jagir System was shifting of
jagir-holders from one jagir to another for administrative
reasons. This system of transfers checked the jagirdars from
developing local roots. Thus, jagirs were transferable & could
be seized too. Zamindars, on the other hand, were hereditary.
The Zamindars were present in practically every part of the
Mughal Empire & held the most signifi cant position in the
agrarian structure of Mughal India. The word Zamindar is
derived from two Persian words -Zamin (land) & dar (holder).

Nasq/Muktai/Kankut

Gulbadan Begum was the daughter of Babur. She was born
in 1523 A.D. and died in 1603 A.D. She documented many
historical events in her book ‘Humayun Nama’. Akbar had
great respect for her. Gulbadan Begum wrote that she had
written the history of Babur and Humayun on the orders
of Akbar. She described the battle between Humayun and
Kamran in her book.

questions.prompt:

questions.explanation:
Hemu was also known as Hem Chandra Vikramaditya. Hemu
rose to become chief of the army and Prime Minister to
Adil Shah Suri of the Sur dynasty. He fought Afghan rebels
across North India from Punjab to Bengal and the Mughal
forces of Akbar and Humayun in Agra and Delhi, winning 22
consecutive battles. Hemu won the Battle against Targi Begh
and assumed the title of Vikramaditya that had been earlier
adopted by many Hindu kings since Vedic times. He was
defeated in the second battle of Panipat and was beheaded
by Bairam Khan, the commander of Akbar’s army.

questions.explanation:

questions.prompt:
With reference to the cultural history of India, consider
the following statements:
1. White marble was used in making Buland Darwaza
and Khankah at Fatehpur Sikri.
2. Red sandstone and marble were used in making
Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza at Lucknow.
Which of the following given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Buland Darwaza is constructed using red sandstone stone
along with white marble to decorate it. It is situated in Fatehpur
Sikri in Agra. However white marble was not used in the
construction of Salim Chisti's Khankah, instead it was used
in making his tomb. Bada Imambada and Rumi Darwaza are
both situated in Lucknow and were built by Asaf-ud-Daula.
Its roof is built using just bricks and without beams or garters.
Bricks and lime were used in its construction instead of stone
or marble. Rumi Darwaza which is main entrance gate was
built using lime plaster and lime moulding along with Lakhori
bricks. Hence neither statement 1 nor statement 2 is correct.

questions.prompt:
In the context of medieval India, the term "SARAIS"
refers to

options.text: A land given to religious places which was tax free
Type of tax imposed on peasants

A place meant to provide temporary accommodation
to Indian and Foreign travellers, pilgrims, merchants,
traders, etc.

questions.explanation:
A hugely interesting feature of medieval India was the 'Sarais'
which ringed cities and dotted the vast space of the Indian
sub-continent. Sarais were largely built on a simple square
or rectangular plain and were meant to provide temporary
accommodation to Indian and Foreign travellers, pilgrims,
merchants, traders, etc. In eff ect, sarais were public domains
which thronged with people of varied cultural backgrounds.
This led to cross-cultural interaction, infl uences and syncretic
tendencies in the cultural mores of the times and at the level
of the people.

questions.explanation:
Guru Arjan Dev and Guru Tegh Bahadur were awarded death
sentence by their contemporary rulers, Jahangir and Aurangzeb
respectively.
Guru Arjan Dev (1581-1606 A.D.)- He was the 5th Sikh Guru.
After the revolt against Jahangir, his rebellious son Prince
Khusrau fl ed from Agra to Afghanistan. During his escape
Khusrau met Guru Arjan Dev at Tarn Taran city. Guru gave
him support and shelter due to which Jahangir got angry
with Guru Arjan Dev. Jahangir accused him of conspiracy
and sentenced him to death sentence in 1606 AD. Guru
Arjan Dev established Taran Taran and Kartarpur towns.
His major work was a compilation of Guru Granth Sahib.
Guru Tegh Bahadur (1664-1675 A.D.): Revered as the
ninth Nanak, he was the ninth of ten Gurus of the Sikh
religion. According to the records written by his son Guru
Gobind Singh, the Guru had resisted persecution, adopted
and promised to protect Kashmiri Hindus. The Guru was
summoned to Delhi by Aurangzeb on the protest but when
he arrived, he was off ered “to abandon his faith and convert
to Islam.” Guru Tegh Bahadur refused, he and his associates
were arrested. He was executed on November, 1675 before
the public in Chandni Chowk, Delhi.

questions.explanation:
The other name of Banda Bahadur was Lachman Dev. This
name was given to him by Sikh Guru Gobind Singh.
Maratha State and
Confederacy
*Shivaji was born at the fort of Shivneri in 1627 or 1630 A.D.
He adopted the title of Chhatrapati after his coronation in 1674
A.D. He made Raigarh his capital. *Pandit Vishweshwar alias
‘Gagabhatta’, a great scholar of that era, declared Shivaji a
Kshatriya at his coronation. Shivaji died in 1680 A.D. at the
age of 53 or 50 years.
*The reason for the rise of Maratha power was its residents.
*The unity of the people on the grounds of regional/collective,
consciousness along with religious toleration and integration
of social groups, fl ourished the feeling of nationalism among
them. The geographical conditions of Maharashtra were helpful
in fl ourishing the Maratha power. *The high leadership quality
of Shivaji and other Maratha leaders contributed to the rise of
Maratha power.
*In 1659 A.D., the Sultan of Bijapur Adil Shah II sent
his experienced and trusted commander Afzal Khan for
suppression of Shivaji, but the diplomat and clever Shivaji
killed him.
*Treaty of Purandar was signed between Shivaji and Mughals
under Jai Singh in 1665 A.D. Shivaji was put under house
arrest by Aurangzeb in 1666 in Jaipur Bhawan at Agra when he
escaped from the custody of Mughals. Aurangzeb imprisoned
Shivaji in 1666 A.D. at Agra.
*‘Ashtapradhan’ was the Council of Eight Ministers (reaching
8 in no. by 1674) under Shivaji in Maratha administration.
The eight ministers were –
(i) Peshwa - Prime Minister of the King .
(ii) Amatya - Finance and Revenue Minister .
(iii) Waqianavis/Mantri - Interior Minister, managing
internal aff airs, especially intelligence and espionage .
(iv) Sachiv/Surnavis - Responsible for all correspondence.
(v) Sumant/Dabir - Foreign Minister .
(vi) Senapati/Sar-i-Naubat - Maintenance of appointments,
organization and food supply of military.
(vii) Pandit Rao - Appointed for religious aid.
(viii) Nyayadhish - Chief Justice.
*Rajaram led the Marathas as a representative of Shahu
from 1689 A.D. to 1700 A.D. After the death of Rajaram,
his widow Tarabai continued the struggle with the Mughals
placing his four year old son Shivaji-II on the throne. At the
time of Aurangzeb’s death, the Maratha leadership was in the
hands of Tarabai.
*Under Shahu, the power of Maratha kingdom came in the
hands of Balaji Vishwanath who made the administration easy
and convenient. *Maratha Chhatrapati Shahu appointed Balaji
to the post of Peshwa. November 1713 was an important day
not only for Balaji but also for the whole Marathas as the power
gradually shifted from Chhatrapati to the Peshwa.
*Balaji Vishwanath served as Peshwa from 1713 A.D. to 1720
A.D. *Shahu appointed the elder son of Balaji Vishwanath,
Bajirao - I as Peshwa whose tenure was from 1720 A.D. to
1740 A.D. *Balaji Bajirao served as Peshwa from 1740 A.D.
to 1761 A.D. after the death of Bajirao. Madhavrao’s tenure
was from 1761 A.D. to 1772 A.D.
*After the death of Madhavrao in 1772 A.D., his brother
Narayanrao became a victim of the conspiracy of his uncle
Raghunathrao, who himself wanted to become Peshwa.
*By the time of Balaji Bajirao, the Post of Peshwa became
hereditary. Previously the power was in the hands of the
Chhatrapati, but now the centre of power shifted into the hands
of Peshwas. By the treaty of Sangola in 1750 A.D., Peshwa
emerged as the real and eff ective head of Maratha confederacy.
*Saranzami system was related to Feudal-military land
grant system in Maratha period. The land given under
Saranzami system was provided for the livelihood of
Maratha Jagirdar (for maintenance of forts/troops for Public
Service) during the Maratha period.
*In January, 1757 A.D., Ahmad Shah Abdali entered Delhi
and looted up to Agra and Mathura. Before returning to his
motherland, he confi rmed Alamgir II as Emperor, Imadulmulk
as prime minister and Rohilla leader Najib-Ud-Daulah as his
chief agent and Mir Bakshi of the Empire.
*The third battle of Panipat was fought between Maratha
Sadashivrao Bhau and Afghan invader Ahmad Shah Abdali on
14th January 1761. Marathas were badly defeated by Afghans
in this battle. According to Kashiraj Pandit, a historian who
was eyewitness of this battle 'Third battle of Panipat proved
catastrophic for Marathas.' “Two pearls have been dissolved, 22
gold coins have been lost and of the silver and copper the total
cannot be cast up” that was the message which was sent to Balaji
Bajirao by a merchant after this agonising defeat of Marathas.
The immediate reason for the battle of Panipat was the Ahmad
Shah Abdali’s desire to avenge Marathas as they expelled his
Viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore. *Ahilyabai was a Maratha
ruler from Holkar dynasty. Holkars belong to Indore and under
Ahilyabai, the capital was moved to Maheshwar.

Disintegration of the
Mughal Empire
*After the death of Aurangzeb in 1707 A.D. his 63-year-old
son Muazzam (Shah Alam) ascended the throne adopting the
name of ‘Bahadur Shah I’. He ruled during the period from
1707-1712 A.D. *He was given the title of ‘Shah-e-Bekhabar’
by Khafi Khan. *Jahandar Shah was the fi rst emperor in the
Mughal dynasty, who proved to be weak and highly disqualifi ed
for governance. He ascended the throne with the help of
Zulfi qar Khan. He was defeated and later executed by his
nephew Farrukh Siyar in a battle in 1713 A.D. *Farrukh
Siyar issued a decree (farman) in which he granted duty - free
trading concessions to the British in Bengal in 1717 A.D. It
was mentioned in the contract that the East India Company
could trade without duty (charge) after paying the annual tax of
Rs. 3000 *Muhammad Shah (1719 - 1748 A.D.) was the last
Mughal emperor to sit on Peacock throne (built by Shah Jahan).
During his reign, Nadir Shah attacked India in 1739 A.D. and
defeated Mughals in the battle of Karnal. The contemporary
historian Anand Ram Mukhlis wrote, "Nadir Shah took sixty
thousand rupees, many thousands of gold coins, gold of one
crore rupees, jewels of fi fty crores, Kohinoor and peacock
throne with him to Iran." and remarked that "the accumulated
wealth of 348 years changed owners in a moment."
*Muhammad Shah (1719-1748 A.D.) spent most of his time
in watching animal fi ght. People called him Rangeela due to
his obsession towards wine and beauty and apathy towards
administration. A group of eunuchs and ladies dominated in
Mughal Darbar during the regime of Muhammad Shah.
*The tenure of Shah Alam-II was from 1759 to 1806 A.D. His
real name was Ali Gauhar. English captured Delhi in 1803
A.D. during his tenure.
*The last Mughal emperor was Bahadur Shah Zafar / Bahadur
Shah II (reigned 1837 -1857 A.D.). His father’s name was
Akbar -II (1806 -1837 A.D.). He was called as the "Emperor
without Empire".
*Ibrahim Zauq and Asad Ullah Khan Ghalib taught poetry to
Bahadur Shah Zafar. Hasan Askari was sufi saint and Pir to
Zafar. *Bahadur Shah Zafar got Rs 1 lakh per month from the
East India Company as pension, which consisted of Rs. 99000
given in Delhi and one thousand rupees for regular family
expenses in Lucknow. He died in 1862 A.D.
*Chin Qilich Khan aka Nizam-ul-Mulk founded the
independent Kingdom of Hyderabad in 1724. Nizam became
the real king after the death of the Mughal governor Mubariz
Khan in the battle of Sakhar - Kheda of Deccan, 1724 A.D..
*Sawai Jai Singh (Jai Singh II) (1688 - 1743 A.D.) of Amber
was a Rajput king of the 18th century. *He established ‘Jaipur’
city and made it the centre of science and art. *He built well-
equipped observatories in Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura and
Varanasi. He patronised the translation of ‘‘Euclid's Geometry”
in Sanskrit. *He organized two Ashvamedh sacrifi ces during
his reign.

questions.prompt: In which year Vasco-da-Gama arrived at Calicut ?
questions.explanation:
Vasco da Gama arrived at western coast port of Calicut on May
20, 1498 A.D. He discovered a new and alternative sea route
to India and he was welcomed by Zamorin (Zamorin was the
ancestral title of the rulers of Calicut), the then king of Calicut.
The voyage of Vasco da Gama opened the new trade dimensions
of the Indo-Portuguese (Europe) alliance. Vasco da Gama earned
60 times more profi t as compared to the cost of expeditions in
Europe from black pepper trade with India, which encouraged
other Portuguese traders. The Portuguese merchants established
their commercial fi rms in India at the ports of Calicut, Goa,
Daman, Diu and Hooghly. Francisco de Almeida came to India
in 1505 AD as the fi rst Portuguese Viceroy. The ‘Blue Water’
policy is attributed to Francisco de Almeida, the fi rst Viceroy of
Portuguese possessions in India. According to Blue water policy,
“The Portuguese should be the sole trade power in the Arabian
Sea and the Indian Ocean”. Portugese were the fi rst to build trade
relation with India, among the European nations, who came by
discovering new sea route to India. Albuquerque came to India
in 1509 A.D. after him, as a new Viceroy. He annexed Goa in
1510 A.D.from Bijapur Adilshahi Sultanate. The Portuguese
maintained Goa as the epicentre of their culture and entity.

questions.prompt:

questions.explanation:
The Portuguese were the fi rst Europeans, who came to
India during medieval period for trade. The fi rst Portuguese
and European voyager Vasco da Gama reached the coast
of Calicut in 1498 AD after a long voyage with the help of
a Gujarati route guide. The sequence of the arrival of the
European trade powers in India is as follows: Portuguese,
the Dutch, the English, the Danes and French. Portuguese
came to India in 1498 and returned in 1961 (longest period).

questions.prompt:

India?
questions.explanation:
The real founder of Portuguese power in India was
Albuquerque (1509-15 A.D.). He established Portuguese
State as a powerful regional power in India. The annexation
of Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur in November, 1510
was the fi rst signifi cant achievement of Albuquerque. The
victory at Goa consolidated the Portuguese monopoly on
the southern-western naval coast and established a regional
Portuguese State in India. He encouraged Portuguese men
to marry Indian women for enhancement of the Portuguese
presence in India and the formation of permanent colonies.

The fi rst Portuguese Viceroy Francisco de Almeida annexed

powerful in the Indian Ocean. During the battle of Diu
in 1509 A.D. Portugese defeated the combined forces of
Mamluk sultanate of Egypt, Gujarat sultanate (at western
coast) and Zamorin of Calicut. The Portuguese established
their monopoly over the Indian Ocean and levied a tax on
ships passing through their area.

questions.prompt:
Among the following factories in Bengal, the one
established by the Portuguese was :
questions.explanation:
In 1579 A.D., after receiving permission from the Mughal
Emperor Akbar, Portuguese in Bengal laid the foundation for
their settlements in Hooghly. They built forts and warehouses
along the banks of River Hooghly. This led to the town of
Hooghly, near Chuchchada, emerging as a major European
trading center. In 1599 A.D., as the Portuguese settlements in
Chuchesra Hooghly increased, the Portuguese arrived in the
area of Bandel (Presently located in Hooghly district of West
Bengal state), where they also established a Chruch named as
‘Bandel Church’ (also named as Basilica of Holy - Hojri). In
1535 A.D. Ghiyasuddin Mahmud Shah, the ruler of Bengal,
promised the portugese to establish the forts in Chittagong
and Satgaon, in return for their assistance of the ruler
during the Sher Shah Suri’s invasion of Bengal. After that,
Portuguese colonies were set up through Bengal. Chatgaon,
known as the great port of Portuguese maritime, was used
by them but in the 16th century Satgaon declined and was
replaced by Hooghly. Dutch built a fort named Fort Gustavus
in Chinsurah. Shrirampur was a major centre of Danes.
Therefore, Hooghly and Bandel, under the Hooghly itself,
both were the important major trade centre for Portuguese.

resistance from Portuguese, Hawkins arrived at the Mughal

of Mughal emperor’s favourable treatment for British traders.

an imperial embassy and a commercial endeavour. He was
sent by company, but with the credentials from the King,
which made him representative of both– the King and the
company, in the eyes of Mughal court. Hawkins was a good
speaker of Turkish language. Jahangir was impressed by his

a mansab of 400. Therefore, statement (I) is false and the
statement (II) is true.

questions.prompt:
What was the chief economic foundation of the
triangular commerce between India, China and
England?

options.text: More than one of the above

questions.explanation:
The triangular trade between India, China, and England
in the 18th and 19th centuries was centered on opium. The
British East India Company established their monopoly in
the cultivation of opium in the region of Bengal and Bihar
etc., they forced the farmers to cultivate opium and exported
it to China, where it was in high demand despite government
bans. Profi ts from the opium trade were used to purchase
Chinese goods like tea, silk, and porcelain for England,
while manufactured goods from England were exported to
India, completing the trade cycle. This exploitative system
had severe social and economic consequences, including the
Opium Wars between Britain and China. While commodities
like silk and black pepper were also traded, opium was the
chief economic foundation of this triangular commerce.

questions.explanation:
Plassey (present name - Palasi) battlefi eld is located on
the banks of the Bhagirathi River in Nadia district of West
Bengal. On 23 June 1757 AD, the troops of the British East
India Company led by Robert Clive defeated Nawab of

questions.chapter: East India Company and Nawab of Bengal
questions.prompt:
Which of the following shifted his capital from
Murshidabad to Munger?
questions.explanation:
Mir Qasim was the most effi cient successor among the
successors of Nawab Alivardi Khan. He demonstrated his
capability as Fauzdar of Poornia and Rangpur. He transferred
his capital from Murshidabad to Munger. The reason was
to secure himself from constant interference from Calcutta
and intrigues of Murshidabad. He organized his Army on
the European model. He managed the factory of arms and
ammunition at Munger for manufacturing of tanks and
matchlock guns. Besides, Mir Qasim had made efforts to
reform state’s fi nancial condition.

questions.chapter: East India Company and Nawab of Bengal
questions.prompt:
The most decisive battle that led to the establishment
of supremacy of the British in India was :
questions.explanation:
On 22/23 October, 1764 A.D. British Army defeated allied
forces of Mir Qasim, Nawab of Oudh Shuja-ud-Daula and
Mughal emperor Shah Alam II. British Army’s command was
in the hands of Major Hector Munro in the Battle of Buxar.
The battle of Buxar assured the result of Plassey battle and
established British supremacy on Banaras and Allahabad
(Prayagraj) across the Ganges. The battle of Buxar made way
for British and proved that there was no strong competitor
before the British. The battle of Buxar completed what Plassey
had begun. During the battle of Buxar Nawab of Bengal
was Mir Jafar. According to Sir James Stephen, ‘’The battle
of Buxar deserves more credit than the battle of Plassey as
the origin of British power in India”. If the results of both
signifi cant battles are analyzed, it can be said that the battle of
Plassey was won by treachery, but the battle of Buxar showed
the supremacy of English armies and military skills. Plassey
made the English the only controllers of Bengal while Buxar
raised the political prestige of the Company throughout India.

questions.chapter: East India Company and Nawab of Bengal
questions.prompt:
Which one of the following rulers had granted Diwani
to the East India Company?
questions.explanation:
As per the fi rst Treaty of Allahabad (August 1765 A.D.),
the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II was taken under the
Company’s protection and was to reside at Allahabad. The
Emperor issued an order dated 12th August, 1765 granting
Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. During this
time Robert Clive was Governor of East India Company in
Bengal. The emperor’s order legalized the political authority
of Company in Bengal and British rule expanded all over
India including Delhi. Successors of Shah Alam II i.e. Akbar
II (1806-37 A.D.) and Bahadurshah II (1837-57 A.D.) became
pensioners of East India Company.

questions.chapter: East India Company and Nawab of Bengal
questions.prompt:
Who was appointed Deputy Diwan of Murshidabad
by Robert Clive after the Allahabad Treaty?
questions.explanation:
According to the Treaty of Allahabad (August, 1765 A.D.),
Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II was taken under the Company’s
protection and had to reside at Allahabad. Shah Alam II
conferred Diwani (fi scal revenue collection authority) of
Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company by issuing ‘Farman’
on 12 August, 1765 A.D. Nazm-ud-duala (son of Mir Jafar)
was accepted as Nawab of Bengal. In return, the company
had to pay the emperor an annual sum of Rs 26 Lakhs as
pension. At that time, the Company was neither interested
in taking responsibility for tax revenue collection nor was it
capable of doing so. Therefore, the Company appointed two
Diwans- Mohammad Raza Khan for Bengal and Raja Shitab
Rai for Bihar. Thus, all business of Diwani and Nizamat was
conducted by Indians but authorized by the British Company.

Which one of the following is the correct chronological
order of the battles fought in India in the 18th Century?

options.text:

Ambur- Battle of Plassey

Wandiwash - Battle of Buxar

Ambur-Battle of Buxar.

Wandiwash-Battle of Plassey.

questions.explanation:
Battle of Ambur (August, 1749 A.D.):- The combined
armies of Muzaffar Jung, Chanda Sahib and the French
defeated and Killed Anwar-ud-din at the Battle of Ambur near
Bellore in August, 1749. Muzaffar Jung became the Subedar
of Deccan. Duplex was appointed Governor of all the Mughal
territories south of the river Krishna. The Nizam surrendered
some districts in the Northern Circars to the French. A French
army under Bussy was stationed in Hyderabad.
Battle of Plassey (June, 1757 A.D.):- Fought between
Nawab of Bengal Sirajuddaula and the British Army. Bengal
was in control of the British after Plassey. Mir Jafar was
placed on the throne by Robert Clive. In exchange, Mir Jafar
ceded an area of the south of Calcutta known as 24 Pargana
to the British for their services and gifted 2,34,000 pounds
to Clive as personal gift reward.
Battle of Wandiwash (January, 1760 A.D.) :- It occurred
between French and British. French were defeated by the
British. Sir Eyre Coote was the leader of the British Army
while French troops were led by Count de Lally.
Battle of Buxar (October, 1764 A.D.) :- Fought between
allied forces of Mir Qasim, Shujauddaula, Shah Alam II and
the British. British led by Hector Munro defeated the allied
forces badly. Thus, option (b) will be the correct answer.

questions.chapter: East India Company and Nawab of Bengal
questions.prompt:
Which of the following opposed British in India
vigorously?
questions.explanation:
Marathas opposed the British vigorously in India. Maratha were
suppressed after three Anglo-Maratha Wars. On the ruins of
Mughal Empire, Maratha laid down their foundation and British
also took advantage of these circumstances. British lost fi rst
Anglo-Maratha war badly and this war ended with the Treaty of
Salbai. Lord Wellesley trapped Peshwa in the cage of Subsidiary
Alliance in 1802. Lord Hastings established British supremacy
after the devastation of remnant strength of Marathas in 1818.
Regional States : Punjab
and Mysore
*Ranjit Singh was born to the chief of Sukerchakia Misl on
13
th November, 1780 A.D. Treaty of Amritsar was signed
between Maharaja Ranjit Singh and British East India Company
on 25
th April, 1809 A.D. Ranjit Singh captured Multan in
1818 A.D., Kashmir in 1819 and Peshawar and North-West
frontier (Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa) in 1834 A.D.. *In 1798 AD,
Zaman Shah attacked Punjab. While returning, his cannons
accidentally fell into the Jhelam River (some sources refer
for Chenab River but Jhelam River is authenticated by many
historians). These cannons were sent back to Jaman Shah by
Ranjit Singh. Happy with this gesture of Ranjit Singh, Jaman
Shah allowed Ranjit Singh to rule Lahore. As a result, in 1799
A.D., Ranjit Singh took control of Lahore and made it his
Capital. Zaman Shah gave him the title of Raja (in return of
his service and providing tanks and artileries) and appointed
him as the Subedar of Lahore. He also captured Amritsar from
Bhangi Misl in 1802. Now, both the political capital ‘Lahore’
and religious capital ‘Amritsar’ were under the control of
Ranjit Singh. *Ranjit Singh was an able ruler. He once said,
“God wants me to see all the religions as one, so he took the
light of my other eye”. *Shahshuja, descendant of Ahmed Shah
Abdali gifted Kohinoor diamond to Ranjit Singh. *His son
Kharak Singh succeeded Ranjit Singh after the laters death in
1839. He was an opium addict. During his reign two opposite
groups, one consisting of Dogra Brothers - Dhyan Singh,
Ghulab Singh and Suchet Singh other included Sandhawaliya
Sardar (an aid of Chait Singh) Atar Singh, Lahna Singh and his
nephew Ajeet Singh, and Dogras (Dhyan Singh, Gulab Singh
and Suchet Singh) were the main reason of growing chaos in
Punjab. *Battle of Chillianwala was fought on 13
th January
1849 A.D. between English forces led by Lord Gough and
Sikh forces led by Sher Singh. The war ended undecided. Lord
Dalhousie was the Governor-General of India during this war.
*Maharaja Duleep Singh was the last ruler of Sikh Empire.
He ruled from 1843 to 1849 AD. He converted to Christianity
and travelled to Russia. Later in 1886 A.D. he again accepted
Sikhism. He died in Paris in 1893 AD. His funeral took place
in England. In 1849 AD, after the Anglo-Sikh war, Punjab was
annexed by Britishers and Duleep Singh was sent to Britain on
a pension in 1854 A.D. After the annexation of Punjab, in 1849
A.D. Lord Dalhousie made a three-member body consisting of
Sir Henry Lawrence as Board’s President and, John Lawrence
and Charles Grenville Mansel as members to administer
Punjab. *The First Anglo-Mysore war in 1767-69 A.D. made
Haidar Ali victorious. The war ended in April, 1769 AD with
the Treaty of Madras. During this the Governor of Bengal was
Harry Verelst (1734-85). *The Second Anglo Mysore War
(1780-84 AD) - During this war, Haidar Ali made an alliance
with Nizam and Marathas against Britishers. In July 1780
A.D. Haidar attacked Carnatic and on 10 September 1780 AD,
colonel Baillie was defeated by the combined forces of Haidar
Ali and Tipu in the battle of Pollilur (other name Perambakam).
In 1781 A.D. Haidar Ali faced Sir Eyre Coote who defeated
Haidar Ali at Porto Novo (July, 1781 A.D.), Pollilur (In this
war, Haider Ali was out rightly defeated but his army faced
heavy loss during this) and Sholingur.
*Tipu Sultan made Srirangapattnam his Capital where he
established Jacobin Club and became its member. He planted
the tree of liberty in his capital as a sign of friendship between
Mysore and France.
*Tipu sent ambassadors to contemporary foreign states and also
established their embassies to maintain friendly relations and
to gather help from them against the Britishers. These foreign
states included - Iran, Istanbul, Afghanistan, France. *The
Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790-92 A.D.) ended with the
Treaty of Srirangapattna (March 1792 A.D.). The treaty fo
Seringapatam (Srirangapatna) was signed in March 1792 A.D.
between Tipu Sultan of Mysore and Lord Cornwallis on behalf
of British East India Company. The agreement also included
representatives of the Nizam of Hyderabad and Maratha
Empire, requiring Tipu to cede half of his Kingdom. Tipu Sultan
died fi ghting in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799 A.D.).
All the members of his family were imprisoned in Vellore.
British Commanders like Arthur Wellesley (brother of Governor
General of Bengal Lord Wellesley), Stuart and General Harris
led this war from the English side. In the happiness of this
victory, the Lord Society of Ireland conferred the title of
Marquess to Wellesley. After the war, a minor Krishnaraja
Wodeyar III (Mummadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar) from Wodeyar
dynasty was placed on the Mysore throne and the British took
possession of Kanara, Coimbatore, and Srirangapattnam.
*Begum Samru (1750-1836 A.D.) constructed a very famous
church at Sardhana near Meerut (Some sources mention the
birth year of Begum Samru is 1753 A.D.). Walter Reinhardt
Sombre, a European, was her husband who served many
kingdoms. Sombre was granted Jagir of Sardhana as a gift for
his service to the Mughal king Shah Alam II in defeating Zabita
Khan (induced by Najaf Khan). Begum Samru became ruler of
Sardhana after the death of her husband.

Governor/Governor General/
Viceroy
*Both Civilian and Military reforms took place during the
period of Robert Clive. Under the civilian reform, a ban was
imposed on the gift to offi cials and controlled private trade
(Clive imposed conditioned ban on accepting gifts; i.e. for
accepting gifts above Rs. 1000 of value, a pre-permission of
governor is necessary). Under the Military reforms, he ended
‘double batta’ for European offi cers and from January 1, 1766
AD this allowance was only granted to soldiers who served
outside the boundaries of Bengal and Bihar (except Allahabad).
*Under administrative reforms, Warren Hastings in 1772
A.D. ended the dual government system of Bengal by order
of the Court of Directors. He transferred the State’s treasury
from Murshidabad to Calcutta. Warren Hastings believed that
the whole land belonged to the ruler. To reform in Revenue
fi eld, he chose trial and error method. Warren Hastings in
1774 A.D. was made Governor-General of Bengal by the
Regulating Act 1773. The act provides for Governor-General
and four consellors (“Council of four”), total fi ve (including
Governor-general). The Governor General was head of the
government and had casting vote if equally divided. It was
established to look after the affairs of Bengal. The Chairman
of the Executive Council was called Governor-General. Several
types of reforms in Police, Judiciary, Taxation, Faujdari related
Acts etc. took place during the time of Cornwallis. *Asiatic
Society of Bengal was established on 15
th January, 1784 A.D.
in the tenure of Governor General Warren Hastings. *Warren
Hastings and Wellesley were related to the Ring-Fence theory.
*Impeachment proceedings were initiated on Hastings for
injustices and atrocities committed by him but in the light of
his service, proceedings which took place between the years
1788 A.D. and 1795 A.D. (until he was acquitted in April 1795)
The following were the policies of Britishers towards Indian
States (Princely States):-
1- Company’s struggle for equality with Indian provinces
(1740-1765 AD)
2- Policy of Ring Fence (1765-1813 AD)
3- Policy of Subordinate Isolation (1813-1857 AD)
4- Policy of Subordinate Union (1858-1935 AD)
5- Policy of Equal Federation (1935-1947 AD)
*Britishers developed a new system for justice delivery through
hierarchical institutions consisting of Diwani and Faujdari
Courts. This system was started by Warren Hastings but
Cornwallis made it more rigid. He concentrated all powers in
the hands of Collector. In 1787 A.D. the District Collector was
made the Diwani Judge of Diwani Courts and was granted some
Faujdari Powers to deliver Justice in some Faujdari cases too.*
In 1790-92 AD, District Faujdari Courts with Indian Judges
were abolished and in their place four Circuit Courts, three for
Bengal and one for Bihar, were appointed. These Courts were
headed by European offi cials and the Justice was delivered
with the help of Indian Kazis and Muftis. Cornwallis initiated
his rule of specifi cation of law, it was a set of regulations that
codifi ed administrative, revenue and judicial reforms of East
India Company in Bengal. *‘Cornwallis Code’ is the collection
of judicial reforms by Cornwallis in 1793 A.D. This reform
was based on the law of ‘Separation of Powers’. He separated
Revenue and Judicial administration. The judicial and faujdari
power of collector was taken back and he was entrusted with
powers related to taxation only. *A new hierarchy of offi cers
was created for jobs in the District Diwani Courts. District
Judges were given works of Faujdari and Police too. The modern
Indian Civil Services was reorganised and professionalised by
Cornwallis (1793). He forbade private trade and gifts, raised
salaries, separated functions and gave legal form to civil service
rules; he was regarded as the reformer of civil service. Lord
Cornwallis was the Governor General of Bengal from 1786 to
1793 and from 30
th July, 1805 A.D. to 5
th October, 1805 A.D. He
died at Ghazipur (Uttar Pradesh) on 5
th October 1805 A.D. His
grave is present in Ghazipur. *Treaty of Bassein (December,
1802) was made between Peshwa Bajirao II and Britishers.
Subsidiary Alliance of Lord Wellesley was accepted by the
Peshwa Bajirao II becoming the fi rst Maratha chief to do so.
According to subsidiary alliance, Peshwa accepted the offer of
protection of English. As per the treaty, Britishers provided 6
thousands soldiers to reinstate Peshwa at Poona and the Peshwa
promised lands are having revenues worth 26 lakhs annually
as a payback. *Lord Wellesley (1798-1805 A.D.) cleverly
used subsidiary alliance as a tool to make Indian provinces as
puppets of Britishers. He did not discover this method. This
method was in practice earlier also but it gradually evolved and
the fi nal shape was provided by Wellesley. Dupleix was the fi rst
European to give his Army to an Indian ruler on the promise of
a fi xed payment to the Company. Britishers used these tactics
too. First such instances can be traced as 1765 treaty in Oudh/
Awadh (can be marked as the precursor of subsidiary alliance)
where Company promised to protect the boundaries of Oudh
on a fi xed payment to the Company. *The evolved version of
the Subsidiary Alliance of Lord Wellesley was accepted by
the Princely States in the following Sequence- Hyderabad
(1798 A.D. and 1800 A.D.), Mysore (1799 A.D.), Tanjore
(October 1799 A.D.), Awadh (November 1801 A.D.), Peshwa
(December 1802 A.D.), Bhonsle of Nagpur/ Berar (December
1803 A.D.). Sindhiya Bharatpur (1803-05) (February 1804
A.D.), Some other alliances include Jodhpur (1818), Udaipur/
Mewar (1818), Bundi (Feb., 1818), Bikaner (March, 1818)
and Jaipur (April, 1818). *Lord William Bentinck in July 1828
A.D. assumed the offi ce of Governor-General of Bengal. He
took some bold steps to eliminate evil social practices such as
Sati system, Female Infanticide etc. On the will of Court of
Directors, he tried to adopt neutral policies towards the Princely
Indian States wherever possible. Mismanagement in Jaipur one
time grew so high that the British Resident was attacked there
but William Bentinck did not interfere. Similarly, he did not
interfere in the internal matters of Jodhpur, Bundi, Kota and
Bhopal when he had enough reasons to do so. Deviating from
this policy, he placed Mysore (in 1831 A.D.) and provinces of
Kurg (1834 A.D.) and Kachhar (in 1832 A.D.) under British
Empire because of extreme mismanagement prevailing there.
*During the seven- year rule of William Bentinck (1828-35
A.D.) the old policies of war and annexation were abandoned or
reduced. William Bentinck is remembered for his contributions
in the fi eld of Administrative and Social Reforms. *By the
Charter Act of 1833 an attempt was made towards totally
centralised Administration. Governor-General of Bengal
became Governor-General of India through this Act. Captain
Sleeman was appointed by the William Bentinck to tackle the
Thug Activities. He arrested 1562 thugs between 1826 to 1835
A.D. Many of them hanged and the rest of them were exiled.
By 1839 A.D., the organiZed nature of Thugi ended. *By the
declaration of 1789 A.D. the export of slaves from Bengal was
stopped. Acts related to slaves were formulated in 1811 A.D.
and 1823 A.D. The Charter Act of 1833 A.D. emphasized on
formulating law by the Governor to end slavery as soon as
possible. By 1843 A.D. slavery was declared illegal in most
part of British India (it removed the enforceability of slave
property in civil courts). In 1860 A.D., Indian Penal Code
declared slavery as a crime. (IPC was repealed and Bhartiya
Nyay Samhita came into force in 2024).
*Anglo-Nepal War (1814-16 A.D.) took place during the time
of Governor-General Lord Hastings (1813-23 A.D.) which
ended with Sugauli’s Treaty. *In 1854 James Outram was
made British resident of Oudh replacing Sleeman. He said
the administration of Oudh is very polluted and the condition
of the people was miserable. This report of Outram emerged
as the base for the annexation of Awadh. Lord Dalhousie
(1848-56 A.D.) blamed Nawab of Awadh Wajid Ali Shah for
maladministration and, in February 1856 A.D., Awadh was
annexed by Britishers. The States that were annexed through
the policy of Doctrine of Lapse are - Satara (1848), Jaitpur
and Sambalpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi
(1853), Nagpur (1854) etc. *Lord Dalhousie formulated the
fi rst comprehensive Railway Policy for India in 1853 and
strongly promoted railway expansion, though the earliest
railway proposals predated his tenure (like early plan of 1832
and Lord Hardinge 1844 plan etc.). The fi rst railway line was
laid between Bombay to Thane in 1853 A.D. The Great Indian
Peninsula Railway started the train travel in India. *Main
Reason for the development of railways was to export raw
materials from the inner parts of the country to different Ports
of India and also open Indian markets to British manufactured
goods. Its second objective was the swift movement of Army
in remote and distant areas to easily suppress any kind of revolt
taking place in any part of the country. *Railway expansion in
India accelerated particulary between 1880 and 1900, while
Lord Curzon’s contribution was mainly administrative such
as the establishment of the ‘Railway Board’ in 1905. *During
Dalhousie a separate Public Work Department was established
and a signifi cant amount was spent on public work through this
body. *With the efforts of Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar, Lord
Canning in 1856 A.D., passed Hindu Widow Remarriage Act.
According to Act XV (15) of 1856, widow remarriage and the
Child born to that marriage was legalized. Dhondo Keshav
Karve and Vishnu Shashtri were two propagators of widow
remarriage. Dhondo Keshav in 1896 A.D. established a widow
Ashram in Poona. On August 2, 1858 the British Parliament
passed the Government of India Act 1858, transferring British
power over India from East India Company. The act legally
abolished the company and created the secretary of State. This
act led to Queen’s Proclamation. *Queen’s Proclamation of
1858 was the most important result of the 1857 revolt. This
proclamation was announced on 1
st November, 1858 AD by
Lord Canning at a Court held in Allahabad. The 1858 Act
ended the Company rule and put the affairs of India under the
direct control of the British Crown. Lord Canning was made
fi rst Viceroy of India. Queen Victoria was made the ruler of
India in 1858 AD. A Grand Delhi Darbar organized in January
1877 AD. This Grand Durbar was organised by Lord Lytton,
following the ‘Royal Titles Act 1876. During this, Queen
Victoria was proclaimed ‘Empress/Sovereign of India’ &
conferred with the title Kaiser-e-Hind (Qaiser-i-Hind). *Under
Governor-General Auckland, fi rst Anglo-Afghan war took
place in 1839-1842 A.D. Lord Lytton was the Governor-General
when second Anglo-Afghan war broke in 1878-1880 A.D. By
Act-V of 1843 Slavery was abolished (removed legal enforce
ability) by Governor-General of India Lord Ellenborough.
During his tenure (1842-44 AD) in March 1843 AD Sindh
was fully merged into British Empire. The policy of Masterly
Inactivity in Anglo-Afghan relations was started during Lord
Ellenborough and continued till Lord North Brooke. This
period is called the Period of Masterly Inactivity. This policy
is often recognized with John Lawrence because during his
time at the offi ce, he got full chance to follow this policy and
evolution of this policy took place in his time only. Masterly
Inactivity word is taken from an Article published by J.W.S.
Wiley. *First Census took place in 1872 A.D. during Lord
Mayo (1869-72 A.D.). Proper census took place in 1881 A.D.
during Lord Rippon. Lord Mayo (1869-72 A.D.) was killed
during an excursion in Andaman and Nicobar Islands group by
a prisoner named Sher Ali Afridi. Mayo was the Viceroy who
was killed while holding the offi ce.
In 1876 A.D., Lytton became Viceroy and changed his policies
towards Afghanistan. *Vernacular Press Act of 1878 A.D. was
passed during Lord Lytton. This Act is also called the Gagging
Act. (some historians also called this as silencing act due to
its strict censorship). Sir Erskine Perry termed this act as a
dangerous step towards India’s right to expression. Sri S.N.
Banerjee termed this act as lightning from the sky. *Sir C.P.
Ilbert who was the law member of Viceroy executive council,
on 2
nd February, 1883 in Legislative council presented a bill
known as Ilbert Bill. This Bill was aimed at equalizing both
European and Indian Judges so that Indian judges can hereby
try a cases involving British subjects in various criminal cases
changing the decade-old provision of barring Indian civil
servants from doing so. This Bill was aimed at ending any
judicial disqualifi cation based on races. The Bill faced a severe
opposition by Britishers as they perceived this as an attack
on their privileges. *Lord Ripon is believed to be most pro-
Indian Viceroy of British India. He made some lenient laws
in favour of children employed in factories numbering 100 or
more, this was called as First Factory Act, 1881. According
to this act, a ban was imposed on the employment of children
below 7 years in factories and the working hours of children
aged 7 to 12 years were reduced to 9 hours daily and they got
4 holidays in a month. Second Factory Act, 1891 made week

questions.explanation:
Governor-General Lord Wellesley came to India in 1798
A.D. at a time when the British were locked in a life and
death struggle with France all over the world. The fear of
Napoleon haunted the Britishers everywhere. To achieve his
political aims, Wellesley relied on the system of Subsidiary
Alliance. While the practice of helping Indian rulers with
a paid British force was quite old, it was given shape by
Wellesley who used it to sub-ordinate the Indian states to the
paramountcy of the company. Under the subsidiary Alliance
system, the ruler of the allying state was compelled to accept
the permanent stationing of a British force within his territory
and to pay a subsidy for its maintenance. However, to secure
a fi xed income for the company was not under the agenda of
the Subsidiary Alliance.

questions.prompt:
First Maratha Sardar to accept the subsidiary
alliance of Lord Wellesley was-
questions.explanation:
The subsidiary alliance system was introduced in India by Lord
Wellesley. The main principles of a subsidiary alliance were –
1. An Indian ruler entering into a subsidiary alliance with
the British had to accept British forces within his territory
and also agree to pay for their maintenance.
2. The ruler would accept a British resident in his state.
3. An Indian ruler who entered into a subsidiary alliance
would not enter into any further alliance with any other
power.
4. The ruler would not employ any Europeans other than
the British.
5. In case of a confl ict with any other state, he would agree
to the resolution decided by the British.
6. The ruler would acknowledge East India Company as the
paramount power in India.
7. In return for the ruler accepting its conditions, the
company undertook the protection of the state from
external dangers and disorders.
8. If the Indian ruler failed to make the payments required
by the alliance, then part of its territory was to be taken
away as a penalty.
The Nizam of Hyderabad was the fi rst to enter into such an
alliance. Maratha ruler Bajirao II (1802 A.D.) also accepted
a subsidiary alliance. Several states like Hyderabad (1798
A.D.), Tanjore and Mysore (1799 A.D.), Awadh (1801 A.D.),
Bhonsle (1803), Sindhiya (1804 A.D.), Holkar (1818 A.D.)
etc. adopted this system.

infamous 'Famine Codes,' have been criticized for their
handling of the 1876-1878 famine in India, which resulted
in signifi cant loss of life.

Economic Impact of British
Rule on India
*The Indian administration was in British hands and was
conducted in a manner subserving the interests of England.
*Home charges refer to the expenditure incurred in England
by the Secretary of State for India on behalf of India. It includes
dividends to the shareholders of the East India Company,
interest on public debt raised abroad, Civil and Military charges,
store purchases in England etc.
*Interest and profi t on private foreign capital were another
important leakage from the National Income System.
*For banking, insurance and shipping services India had to
make huge payments.
*In British India, a term Imperial Preference was often used
for the empire-wide preferential tariff arrangement (Concession
given to British Imports in India). Under these arrangements,
Britain pledged to maintain free entry for most colonial goods
while imposing tariffs on foreign imports. This resulted in,
almost no charge levied on British Imports but Indian Exports
were charged heavily in Britain. *Strong preference to invest
in land property by the rich class of India during British Rule
proved detrimental for the development of Industries as they
were low on Capital Investments. *In 1793 A.D. Cornwallis
started Permanent Settlement of Land Revenue. Permanent
Settlement was called by different names such as Istimrari,
Malgujari and Bishwedari. This system was launched in
Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Varanasi of U.P. etc. Around 19% of
British India was under Permanent Settlement. A new section of
Zamindars was announced as landowners who were to provide
10/11 of the total revenue to Company and were paid the rest
1/11 of the total revenue for their duties. In the Permanent
Settlement, Zamindars were small capitalist.
*Ryotwari System was generated by Thomas Munro and
Alexander Read. Alexander Read fi rst implemented this land
system in Baramahal district of Tamil Nadu. Later on, this
system spread to Madras, some parts of Bombay, Assam and
Coorg (a part of modern Karnataka) etc.
*According to this system, the Ryots were given the ownership
and rights to occupy the lands and they were required to pay the
revenue directly to the government. By this system, the farmer
was the owner of his land. A total of around 51% British India
area was covered under this settlement. The rate of land taxes
in this system was very high and the recovery of agricultural
rent was handled very strictly.
*Under Mahalwari System the unit for revenue settlement
is the village or the mahal. The village land belongs to the
village community. The community was jointly responsible
for the payment of the land revenue. *This system prevailed in
around 30% of British India covering United Provinces, Central
Provinces and Punjab (with some changes).
*The constant fl ow of wealth from India to England for which
India did not receive any adequate economic, commercial or
material return has been described by national leaders and
economists as ‘drain’ of wealth from India. Before 1813 AD
company had a recurring surplus which accrued from (a) profi ts
from oppressive land revenue policy (b) profi ts from its trade
resulting from monopolistic control over Indian markets and
(c) exactions made by the company’s offi cials. The surplus
was used by the Company as an “investment”, i.e. for making
a purchase of exportable items in India and elsewhere. Against
the exports of goods made out of this investment, India did not
receive anything in return. This system was brought to an end
by the charter act of 1813. *From 1813 AD onwards economic
drain took the form of ‘unrequited’ exports. Dadabhai Naoroji
described the drain of wealth as the “evil of all evils” and the
main cause of Indian poverty. *Dadabhai Naoroji was one of
the earliest and most prominent propounder of the Drain of
Wealth theory. He with his articles and books ‘England’s Duties
to India’ (paper), ‘Poverty and Un-British Rule in India’, ‘The
wants and means of India’ and ‘On the commerce of India’
propounded his Drain of wealth theory.
*Romesh Chunder Dutt also emphasized the drain of wealth
theory. In his Article ‘The Economic History of India’
He proposed that half of the net revenues of India is being
outfl owed every year. *Indian National Congress in 1896 A.D.
accepted the Drain Theory in Calcutta session and announced
that the real cause for frequent famines and the poverty of Indian
nationals is the ongoing Drain of Wealth for the previous years.
*Syed Ahmad Khan was loyal towards British Rule and he
believed that the development of Muslim Community could
take place with British government only. *Dadabhai Naoroji
(1825-1917 A.D.) along with W.C. Bonnerjee established
London Indian Society in 1865 A.D. which popularized the
severe exploitation and the pain of Indian nationals. *Dadabhai
Naoroji was the fi rst Indian to be elected to the British House
of Commons on the ticket of the Liberal Party in 1892 A.D.

Given below are two statements, one is labelled as
Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R) :
Assertion (A) : The British Government introduced
different land revenue system in different
part of India.
Reason (R) : It led to create different classes in Indi-
an

questions.explanation:
British government followed different land revenue systems
in different parts of India. These systems were: Permanent
Settlement, Ryotwari & Mahalwari. Permanent Settlement
was introduced in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha & Varanasi of U.P.
Under this system around 19% area of entire British India
was included. Ryotwari (approx. 51% area) system was in

Province, Punjab. Hence, it is clear that because of this,

questions.chapter: Economic Impact of British Rule on India
questions.prompt:
With reference to revenue collection by Cornwallis,
consider the following statements:
1. Under the Ryotwari Settlement of revenue
collection, the peasants were exempted from
revenue payment in case of bad harvests or natural
calamities.
2. Under the Permanent Settlement in Bengal, if the
Zamindar failed to pay his revenues to the state,
on or before the fi xed date, he would be removed
from his Zamindari.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Under the Ryotwari Settlement of revenue collection,
individual peasants (ryots) were directly responsible for
paying land revenue to the government and peasants were
not exempted from revenue payment in case of bad harvests
or natural calamities. There were no explicit exemptions for
bad harvests or natural calamities rather sometimes few
remissions were provided and their rents were reduced.
Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.
Under the Permanent Settlement in Bengal, introduced by
Lord Cornwallis in 1793 A.D., 'Zamindars' were established
as the proprietors or owners of land. The state’s demand for
land revenue was permanently fixed, but under the ‘Sunset
clause’, if the Zamindar failed to pay tax due by sunset on
a certain date, his Zamindari (landholding rights) would be
taken over by the government and auctioned, and the rights
would be transferred to the new owner. Hence, statement 2
is correct.

grow cash crops that were imported to Great Britain as raw
materials for English factories. The period also saw a decline
in the urban population and destroyed domestic factories.

soldiers believed that this was an intentional act of the British
to besmirch their religion. This became the immediate cause
of the fi rst Independence Struggle of India in 1857 A.D.
