questions.prompt: What was the main cause of 1857 revolt?
questions.explanation:
The Indian Rebellion of 1857 had diverse political, economic,
military, religious and social causes.
The sepoys, a generic term used for native Indian soldiers of
the Bengal Army, had their own list of grievances against the
British East India Company administration. The spark that led
to the mutiny was the issue of new gunpowder cartridges for
Enfi eld rifl e in January 1857 A.D. There was a widespread
belief that the cartridges contained cow or pig fat. This insulted
both the Hindu and Muslim religious practices. Underlying
grievances like taxation and land annexations by East India
Company were ignited by the sepoy mutineers, and within
weeks dozens of units of Indian army joined the peasant army
in widespread rebellion. The old aristocracy, both Muslim and
Hindu, who were seeing their power being steadily eroded
by the East India Company also rebelled against British rule.

questions.prompt:
Which of the following was not a reason for making
the sepoys of the East India Company rebellious?

options.text:

Christianity
The order to the sepoys to travel on ships
The ineffi ciency of the offi cers
None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation:
The ineffi ciency of the offi cers was not a cause for the Sepoy
Mutiny. The Indian Rebellion of 1857 occurred as a result of
an accumulation of factors over time, rather than any single
event such as an effort by offi cers to spread Christianity
among the soldiers, which led to interference in the religious
matters of the people. The order of the Company to the
sepoys to travel on a ship was another reason as in Hinduism
it was believed that travelling by sea could deprive them of
their religious status of being a Hindu. A more immediate
cause of the sepoy’s dissatisfaction was the recent order
that they would not be given the foreign service allowance
(Bhatta/Batta) when serving in Sindh or Punjab along with
rumors of the use of animal fat in the cartridges of the New
Enfi eld Rifl e.

questions.prompt:
Which one of the following places did Kunwar Singh,
a prominent leader of the Revolt of 1857 belonged to?
questions.explanation:
Kunwar Singh was one of the most important freedom
fi ghters in the Sepoy Mutiny of 1857. Kunwar Singh was
born in Jagdishpur in Shahabad region of Bihar. He belonged
to Arrah in Bihar during the mutiny. When the people of all
parts of India rose against British authority in 1857 A.D.,
Babu Kunwar Singh was nearly eighty years old. At that age,
he fought against the English East India Company. Despite
his age and failing health, Kunwar Singh plunged into the
thick of it and battled against the British forces with grim
determination and undaunted courage. In Bihar, Kunwar
Singh was the Leader against the British. He assumed
command of the soldiers who had revolted at Danapur on
25th July 1857 A.D. Two days later he occupied Arrah, the
district headquarters. Major Vincent Eyre relieved the town
in August 1857, defeated Kunwar Singh’s force and destroyed
Jagdishpur. Kunwar Singh left his ancestral village and
reached Lucknow in December 1857 A.D. In March 1858
A.D., he occupied Azamgarh. However, he had to leave the
place soon. He was pursued by Brigadier Douglas, and he
retreated towards his home in Bihar. On 23 April 1858 A.D.,
Kunwar Singh had a victory near Jagdishpur over the force
led by Captain Le Grand, but on 26 April 1858 A.D., he
died in his village. The mantle of the old chief now fell on
his brother Amar Singh who, despite heavy odds, continued
the struggle and for a considerable time ran a parallel
government in the then district of Shahabad. In October
1859 Amar Singh joined the rebel leaders in the Nepal Terai.

questions.explanation:

zamindari of Jagdishpur in Bihar, led the rebellion. Thus,
Statement 1 is correct.
According to Lord Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse, if an
Indian ruler died without a biological heir, their kingdom
would be annexed by the British East India Company. In
1853 AD, Jhansi's ruler, Raja Gangadhar Rao, died without
a biological heir. Rani Lakshmibai adopted Damodar Rao
as her son. However, the British refused to recognize the
adopted son as the rightful heir and annexed Jhansi under
the Doctrine of Lapse in 1854 AD, making it a part of the
British Empire.

questions.explanation:
The major result of 1857 revolt was the Proclamation on
November 1st, 1858 by Queen Victoria. This was proclaimed
by Lord Canning during Durbar in Allahabad (Prayagraj). The
ruthless, exploitative era of the East India Company was ended
and a new era of British rule to be governed directly by British
Crown began. This proclamation included the abandonment

questions.prompt:

2. To place the Indian administration under the
British Crown
3. To regulate East India Company’s trade with India
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
British Government passed an Act in 1858, which is known
as ‘Act of Administrative Reforms in India’. Provisions of the
Act are mentioned below –
The company’s territories in India were to be governed by
Queen, the company ceased to exercise its power and control
over these territories. India was now to be governed in the
name of the Queen.
The Queen’s principal secretary of state for India received
the powers and duties of the company’s court of directors. A
council of fi fteen members was appointed to assist the secretary
of state for India. The Council became an advisory body for
Indian affairs. For all communications between Britain and
India, the secretary of the state became the real channel.
The Crown was empowered to appoint a Governor-General
and the Governors of the Presidencies.
An Indian Civil Service was to be created under the control
of the secretary of state.
All the property and other assets of the East India Company
were transferred to the crown. The crown also assumed the
responsibilities of the company along with their related
treaties, contracts and so forth.

immediately after the revolt of 1857. Sanyasi Rebellion
occurred in 1763-1800 A.D., Santhal Rebellion occurred
in 1855-56 A.D., and Pabna uprising took place in 1873-76
A.D. Indigo Revolt began in Govindpur village of Nadia
district in West Bengal led by two former employees of
indigo producers. Digambar Biswas and Bishnu Biswas
organized the peasants into a counterforce and refused
to sow indigo. This indigo revolt of Bengal was directed
against British planters who forced peasants to take advances
and sign fraudulent contracts which forced the peasants
to grow Indigo under terms that were least profi table to
them. In September, 1859 AD all the cultivators revolted
against the landlords. The agitation spread to regions like
Nadia, Pabana, Khulna, Dhaka, Malda, Dinajpur, etc.
All indigo factories were shut down due to this strike.
The intellectual class of Bengal expressed support for the
Movement through their articles and rallies. The editor
of “Hindu Patriot” Harishchandra Mukherjee played a
signifi cant role in this agitation. This revolt was vividly
portrayed by Dinbandhu Mitra in his play Neel Darpan.

movement was led by Syed Ahmad Barelavi, who was

and Shah Walliullah, the saint of Delhi. It was a revivalist

and Central Provincial regions. In 1830 A.D. Syed occupied

later in the following year Syed Ahmad lost his life in the
Battle of Balakot. Patna became the centre of the Wahabi
Movement after the death of Syed Ahmad.

questions.prompt: Ulgulan Revolt was related to –
questions.explanation:
Munda Rebellion was one of the most prominent 19th-Century
tribal rebellions in the subcontinent. Birsa Munda led this
movement in the region in 1899-1900 A.D. The Ulgulan,
meaning ‘Great Tumult,’ sought to establish an independent
Munda Raj. The Mundas traditionally enjoyed a preferential
rent rate as the Khuntkatti or the original clearer of the forest.
But in the course of the 19th century, they had seen this
Khuntkatti land system being eroded by the jaghirdars and
thikedars coming as merchants and moneylenders. In 1895
A.D., Birsa claiming to have seen a vision of God, proclaimed
himself a prophet with miraculous healing powers. Thousands
fl ocked to hear the ‘new word’ of Birsa with its prophecy of
an imminent deluge. The new prophet became a critic of the
traditional tribal customs, religious beliefs, and practices. He
called upon the Mundas to fi ght against superstition, give
up animal sacrifi ce, stop taking intoxicants, wear the sacred
thread and retain the tribal tradition of worship in the Sarna
or the sacred grove. It was essentially a revivalist movement,
which sought to purge Munda society of all foreign elements
and restore its pristine character. Christianity infl uenced the
movement as well and it used both Hindu-Christian idioms
to create the Munda ideology and worldview. On Christmas
Eve 1899 A.D., the Mundas shot arrows and tried to burn
down churches over an area covering six police stations in the
districts of Ranchi and Singhbhum. Next, in January 1900,
the police stations were targeted and there were rumours
that Birsa’s followers would attack Ranchi on 8th January,
leading to panic there. However, on 9th January, the rebels
were defeated. Birsa was captured and died in jail. Nearly
350 Mundas were put on trial, and three of them were hanged
and 44 transported for life.

* The Calcutta Madarsa was established by Warren Hastings
in 1780 A.D. for the study of Muslim law and related subjects.
Mulla Majduddin was the fi rst principal (Najin) of this Madarsa.
Farsi, Arabic and Muslim law were taught in this Madarsa
and the graduates from here worked as interpreters in the
British Raj. *The Sanskrit College was established in 1791
by Jonathan Duncan, (the resident at Benaras), for the study
of Hindu law, philosophy and literature. *Raja Rammohan
Roy was granted the membership in the Asiatic Society of
Paris (Societe Asiatique). * Halhed, in 1778, published Bengali
grammars namely – ‘A grammer of the Bengal Language’.
*Sir William Jones was appointed the Judge of the Supreme
Court in Calcutta during the tenure of Warren Hastings. On
his initiative, in 1784, Asiatic Society was established and
he himself became its fi rst President. This Society, through
publication named Asiatick Researches tried to shed light
on India’s past. In this order, in 1789, he translated Abhigyan
(Abhijnan) Shakuntalam of Kalidas into English. *To analyse
the educational development after 1854 in India, in 1882, W.W.
Hunter led Hunter Commission was established. The report
of this commission emphasized on reform and development
of the primary education in India. *On 8
th November, 1905,
Rangpur National School was established. It was the fi rst
milestone in the National Education Sector.* On 16
th November
1905, a session was organized in Calcutta and decision was
taken to establish National Council of Education, Bengal
to provide education related to Science, national literature
and technology. Satish Chandra Mukherjee and others
constituted the National Council of Education, Bengal on 11
March, 1906; the Bengal National College was inaugurated later
on 14 August, 1906. *By Charter Act of 1813 an arrangement
was made to spend not less than one lakh rupees per year on
Education. *Sadler Commission was related to education.
Government constituted a commission to study the possibilities
of Calcutta University in 1917. Dr. M.E. Sadler who was the
Vice-Chancellor of Leeds University, was appointed the chief of
the commission. Dr. Ashutosh Mukherjee and Dr. Ziauddin
Ahmad were two Indian members of the commission.
The commission was asked to inquire into the problems of
Calcutta University and to make wider recommendations
on secondary, intermediate and university education. The
commission suggested that if an improvement is desired in
the education system of the university, then the standards of
secondary education are required to be listed fi rst. *William
Bentinck appointed Macaulay (the law member of Governor-
General Executive Council) as head of Committee of Public
Instruction to present a description of the dispute regarding the
medium (language) of the Indian education system. Macaulay
advocated English as the language of Indian education.
*The theory of downward fi ltration is related to education
sector in colonial times. According to this theory, education
should be fi rstly granted to a higher section of society which
later on percolates slowly downward in the Society.* The
seed of the modern education system in India was sown by
the Lord Macaulay Minute (1835). Lord Macaulay held the
view that Indian learning was inferior to European learning, He
said. “A single shelf of a good European library was worth
the whole literature of India and Arabia”. The proposal

th
March, 1835. During the tenure of William Bentinck, on 7

March, 1835, English was offi cially accepted as the medium

questions.chapter: Development of Education in Modern India
questions.prompt:
The foundation of the modern educational system in
India was laid by:
questions.explanation:
The foundation of the modern educational system in India
was laid by Macaulay’s Minutes of 1835 A.D. (Issued on 2
February, 1835) In that minute, he commented on Sanskrit
or Arabic by saying that “a single shelf of a good European
library was worth the whole literature of India and Arabia.”.
Macaulay thus suggested making English the language
of higher education in India with Western literature as
the subject of study. Bentinck accepted his suggestion.
Accordingly, on 7th March, 1835 A.D., a resolution passed
by the Government declared: “His Lordship is of the opinion
that the great object of the British Government ought to be
the promotion of European literature and science amongst
the natives of India and that all the funds appropriated
for the purpose of education would be best employed on
English education alone.” Bentinck’s Resolution opened a
new chapter in the history of Indian education. It was at that
time that Western education began to spread rapidly in India.

questions.prompt:
Which of the following led to the introduction of
English Education in India?
1. Charter Act of 1813
2. General Committee of Public Instruction, 1823
3. Orientalist and Anglicist Controversy
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
In 1823 A.D. the governor-general in council appointed a
General Committee of Public Instructions, which had the
responsibility to grant one lakh rupees for education. The
committee consisted of 10 members, with Lord Macaulay
as the President. Interestingly, during that time, there was a
rapid change in attitude towards the composition of English
education mainly due to the missionaries and the political
infl uence of the English language. Thus, for the council of
East India Company, the decision to grant money faced a
greater problem. The controversy went on for 12 years. Even
the General Committee of Public Instruction was also not
able to decide the medium of instruction by vote, because
out of 10 members, fi ve were supporters of English language
or Anglicists as the medium of instruction and the rest were
supporters of the Classic language or Orientalists as a medium
of instruction. This is the famous Anglicist and Orientalist
controversy.
As the President of the General Committee of Public
Instruction, Lord Macaulay wrote a minute (detailed) where he
made the conclusion regarding the controversy. By introducing
the English language for the education of masses, Macaulay’s
opinion was that the public mind of India might expand under
the English system and through the English language it may
educate the people into a capacity for better government.

university. At present, this institute (Central Hindu School)
functions as a constituent institute of BHU.

Development of Press in Modern
India
*James Augustus Hicky in 1780 A.D. started the Bengal
Gazette, the fi rst newspaper in India. Lord Wellesley enacted
Censorship of Press Regulations, 1799. It imposed almost
wartime press restrictions including pre-censorship. In 1807
this Act included pamphlets, books and magazines too. *Lord
Hastings in 1818 abolished the strict pre-censorship of the press
in India and dispensed with their submitting their papers to an
offi cer of government previous to publications. Vernacular
Press Act, 1878 was passed during the tenure of Lord Lytton
(1876-1880 A.D.). The Act empowered the district magistrate
to call upon the printer and publisher of any vernacular
newspaper to enter into a bond with the government not to
cause disaffection against the government or antipathy between
persons of different religion, caste, race, through published
material. *The press and publisher could also be required to
deposit security which could be forfeited if the regulation were
violated, and press equipment could be seized if the offence
reoccurred. *Under this Act, proceedings were instituted against
Som Prakash, Bharat Mihir, Dacca Prakash and Samachar.
*B. G. Tilak was imprisoned for anti-British journalism in
1882. He was the fi rst Indian to be punished for the performance
of his duty in this fi eld. *Tilak was arrested after the murder
of W.C. Rand and offi cer Charles Ayerst on the grounds of the
publication of a poem, “Shivaji’s utterances” in Kesari, and a
speech that Tilak had delivered at the Shivaji festival, justifying
Afzal’s Khan murder by Shivaji. Tilak’s defence of Shivaji’s
killing of Afzal Khan was portrayed by the prosecution as an
incitement to kill British offi cials. In 1897, he was imprisoned
for 18 months for inciting Chapekar brothers for killing W.C.
Rand and Charles Ayerst through his articles published in
Kesari (he was charged for sedition for writing such articles). *
'The Free Hindustan' newspaper was started by Tarak Nath
Das in North America (Vancouver). *Raja Ram Mohan Roy
used the press as a medium to express and publish his views.
In 1821 he published ‘Sambad Kaumudi’ Bengali weekly
newspaper. After one year he published a newspaper ‘Mirat-
ul-Akhbar’ in the Persian language. ‘Indian Mirror’ was
published from Calcutta (Bengal). Credit for establishment
of Indian Mirror (1861) goes to Debendranath Tagore and
Manmohan Ghosh. * Lala Hardayal, Sohan Singh Bhakana
and Kartar Singh Sarabha, etc. founded Hindustan Ghadar
Party (Ghadar Party) in USA and Canada to free India from
British Rule. ‘Ghadar’ a weekly publication, was a manifesto
of the party which was fi rst published on 1st November, 1913
at San Francisco in Urdu. From 9th December, 1913 A.D.
its printing in Gurmukhi script also started. It was later on
published in Marathi, Hindi, English and Gujarati. Its one
edition was also published in Pashto language. *Amrit Bazar
Patrika, a Bengali (later English) weekly was launched February
20, 1868, in the village of Palua Magura in the Jessore district
of Present day Bangladesh, through the efforts of Sishir Kumar
and Motilal Ghosh. But later it started being published from
Kolkata (West Bengal), but to escape the Vernacular Press
Act, it got converted to English format overnight in 1878 A.D.
*Girish Chandra Ghosh started ‘The Bengalee’ in 1862 A.D.
which was transferred to S.N. Banerjee in 1879 A.D. Girish
Chandra Ghosh started the Hindoo Patriot. Later on, Harish
Chandra Mukherjee became its editor. *In 1881 A.D., Tilak
published two newspapers Kesari and Mahratta in Poona
(now Pune). Kesari in Marathi was the main newspaper of
Tilak’s Home Rule Movement. Earlier Gopal Ganesh Agarkar
was the fi rst editor of Kesari. The fi rst editor of the Maratta/
Maratha was Bal Gangadhar Tilak. Mahratta was published in
English. *Bangwasi, Kaal, Kesari etc. Newspaper supported
the revolutionary movements and criticized the moderate
policies of Congress. Sandhya, Yugantar and Kaal, advocated
revolutionary extremism during the freedom struggle. *Ishwar
Chandra Vidyasagar in 1858 started publishing ‘Som
Prakash’ newspaper, it supported the interests of the Indigo
revolutionaries. Vidyasagar mooted the original idea of the
newspaper, it was fi rst edited by Dwarkanath Vidyabhushan.
The Free Press Journal is an English-language daily newspaper
that was established by Swaminathan Sadanand. *Indian
opinion was started by Mahatma Gandhi in 1903 A.D. in
South Africa. Mansukh Lal Hiralal Nazar was its fi rst editor.
It was published in Gujarati, Hindi, Tamil and English.
*Young India was published bi-weekly from Bombay from
7 May 1919 A.D. under supervision of Gandhiji. Jamanadas
Dwarakadas and Shankarlal Banker were its foundational
member Shankar Lal Banker was its publisher. On 8th October,
1919 A.D. Mahatma Gandhi became the editor of Young
India and it was started publishing weekly from Ahmedabad.
Jamanadas Dwarakadas and Shankar lal Banker were members
of Home Rule Movement of Annie Besant. *Indigo Revolt of
Bengal was a direct fi ght against the exploitation of farmers.
Harishchandra Mukherjee editor of Hindoo Patriot put a
lot of effort in this respect. Girish Chandra Ghosh was the
editor of Hindoo Patriot in the fi rst two years (1853-55 A.D.).
In 1855 A.D., Harish Chandra Mukherjee became the editor
of Hindoo Patriot. He boldly spoke about the exploitation of
Indigo farmers by the plantation owners. He helped these
farmers in all possible ways. Kristodas Pal in 1861 became
the editor of Hindoo Patriot. *Aurobindo Ghosh was the
editor of English weekly Bande Matram. *In 1931 A.D.,
Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga started The Indian Nation.
It was published in Patna. *Ram Krishna Pillai was the editor
of Swadeshabhamini. *Gandhiji started Harijan in English,
Harijan Bandhu in Gujarati and Harijan Sewak in Hindi.
These were weekly newspapers. First edition of Harijan was
published on 11th February, 1933 A.D. from Pune, Maharashtra.
*On July 1924 A.D., B.R. Ambedkar in Bombay founded an
institute called ‘Bahiskrit Hitakarini Sabha’ whose aim was
to promote untouchables morally and physically. He started
a fortnightly bulletin Bahishkrit Bharat (fi rst published in
1927) *Abul Kalam Azad in 1912 A.D. started an Urdu weekly
called Al-Hilal. Al-Balagh was published in 1915 A.D. by him.
Al-Hilal was banned in 1914 A.D. by Press Act. *Lala Lajpat
Rai started the Vande Mataram (1905-06) an Urdu daily and
The People (1925, Lahore), a weekly in English. Before this,
he had already published Young India (1916) in America.
*George Allen published ‘The Pioneer’ newspaper in 1865
at Allahabad (Prayagraj). *Qaumi Awaz an Urdu newspaper
was started by Jawaharlal Nehru and Rafi Ahmed Kidwai in
1945 A.D. Its publication was stopped in 2008. *Rast Goftar
is a newspaper related to Dadabhai Naoroji. Motilal Nehru
demanding independence of India (or Home Rule for India)
started a newspaper called The Independent in February 1919
at Allahabad. * The Commonweal was an English newspaper
published in Madras by Annie Besant.

questions.chapter: Development of Press in Modern India
questions.prompt:
Who among the following repealed the Vernacular
Press Act of 1878?
questions.explanation:
Lord Lytton (1876-1880 A.D.) passed the Vernacular
Press Act in 1878 A.D. By this Act, the Magistrates of the
districts were empowered without the prior permission of
the Government to call upon a publisher of any kind to enter
into a bond, undertaking not to publish anything that might
“rouse” feelings of disaffection against the Government. The
magistrate was also authorized to deposit security, which
could be confi scated if the publisher violated the bond. If a
publisher repeated the violation, their press could be seized.
Thus, the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 gagged the native
language press. There was a popular protest against this Act.
This Act was later repealed by Lord Ripon in 1882.

questions.prompt:
Which newspaper wrote the following about the pos-
sible future role of the Indian National Congress: ‘...

options.text: More than one of the above

questions.explanation:
The article mentioned, regarding the potential future role of
the Indian National Congress, was written in the newspaper
The Indian Mirror in its January 1886 edition.
Socio-Religious Movements
*The dawn of the nineteenth century witnessed the birth of a
new vision, a modern vision, among some enlightened sections
of the Indian society. This enlightened vision was to shape
the course of events for decades to come and even beyond.
This process of reawakening, sometimes but not with full
justifi cation defi ned as ‘Renaissance’, did not always follow
the intended line and gave rise to some undesirable by-products
as well, which have become as much a part of daily existence
in the whole of the Indian subcontinent as the fruits of these
reform movements.
*Raja Ram Mohan Roy often called the Father of Indian
Renaissance is also known by names like ‘Prophet of Indian
Nationalism’, Father of Modern India, ‘First Modern Man’
and ‘Yugdoot’. In 1815 A.D. he set up the Atmiya Sabha in
Calcutta to propagate Monotheistic ideals of Hindu religion
among his youth followers (mostly rich and influential).
In 1828 A.D. he founded Brahmo Sabha, which was later
renamed Brahmo Samaj.* Devendranath Tagore founded
Tattvabodhini Sabha to propagate rational thinking, study
ancient texts (like Upanishad) and spread the ideals of Rajaram
Mohan Roy in 1839 A.D. Brahmo Samaj was the fi rst reform
movement in the Hindu religion which was infl uenced by
modern western liberal ideas and a new reading of ancient
Indian texts. *Mughal Emperor Akbar II gave Raja Ram Mohan
Roy the title of Raja and sent him to the court of British King
William IV as his ambassador in 1830. Roy was sent there to
discuss about the increment in the pension of Akbar II. On
27th September, 1833 Raja Ram Mohan Roy died at Bristol in
England. The mausoleum of Roy is present at Bristol.
*Raja Ram Mohan Roy advocated English Education in India.
According to him, a moderate Western education is necessary
to pull us out of the darkness and to provide Indians with
partnership in the administration of the country. He opposed
idol worship, Child marriage, practice of Sati etc. evil social
practices of India.
*Ramakrishna Paramahamsa emphasized that Hari, Ram,
Allah, and Christ are different names for the same God and
that there are many ways to God and salvation. *Swami
Vivekananda spread Ramakrishna’s message and tried to
reconcile it to needs of contemporary Indian Society. He
emerged as the preacher of Neo-Hinduism. At the Parliament
of the World's Religions held at Chicago in 1893, Swami
Vivekananda delivered his famous speech. Subhash Chandra
Bose said, “So far as Bengal is concerned Vivekananda may
be regarded as the spiritual father of Modern nationalist
movement.” Swami Vivekananda founded Ram Krishna
Mission in 1897 A.D. (it was registered offi cially in 1909
A.D. under Societies Registration Act 1860). Its headquarter
was opened at Belur in Howrah (West Bengal). The objective
of Ram Krishna Mission was non-political, non-sectarian
spiritual movement, engaged in various forms of humanitarian,
social and cultural service activity, but it was highly inspired
by the Ancient culture of India. The Theory of Pure Vedanta is
the ideal of this mission. Its main aim is the highest spiritual
upliftment of Human’s inner self. It also accepted traditional
practices of Hindu religion in their original form such as idol
worship, rituals, symbols, etc. The second feature of the mission
is : ‘Belief in the truth of all religions’. Swami Vivekananda
said that all religious beliefs are different ways to reach the
same destination that is one God.
*Mulshankar or Dayanand Saraswati was born in the old
Morvi Princely State, Kathiyawara in Gujarat in a Brahmin
family. From 1845-60 (for fifteen years) he wandered to
different places in search of knowledge. In 1860 he came
under swami Virajananda Saraswati at Mathura and started
preaching in 1864. In November, 1869, he engaged in a mighty
Shastrartha with leaders of Hindu orthodoxy at Kashi. In 1867
A.D., he hoisted “Pakhand Khandini Pataka”. In 1875 A.D.,
he founded ‘Arya Samaj’ in Bombay. His views are inscribed
in his famous book Satyartha Prakash. Rigvedadibhashya-
bhumika, Rigveda Bhashya, Advaitmat Khandan, Panch
Mahayajya Vidhi and Ved-Viruddh-mat-Khandanam were
important works of Dayanand Saraswati. The Arya Samaj was
spreading rapidly as a reaction against the western infl uences. In
1877 A.D., its headquarter was shifted to Lahore which helped
in accelerating the spread of this movement. Dayananda’s
slogan of “Go Back to Vedas” was a call for a revival of
Vedic learning and purity of religion. He rejected the religious
practices like idol worship, incarnations, tantra-mantra, etc. His
aim was the oneness of all religions, society, and of the nation
itself. He is also called as “The (Martin) Luther of India” for
his efforts in religious reforms. Arya Samaj got divided into two
groups, one supported western education and other one opposed
western education. Swami Sraddhanand (Mahatma Munshi Ram
Vij), Lekhraj etc. were opposed to western education. They
established ‘Gurukul’ in 1902. Lala Lajpat Rai and Hansraj were
supporters of western education. They established Dayanand
Anglo Vedic College. Dayanand Saraswati was the fi rst to use
word Swaraj and advocated Hindi as the offi cial language of
India. He was the fi rst to suggest renunciation of foreign goods
and the adoption of country-made indigenous goods.
*After being inspired by Keshab Chandra Sen, Atmaram
Pandurang founded Prarthana Samaj in 1867 A.D.
*Mahadev Govind Ranade in 1869 A.D. joined this
organization. The main aim of this organization was to oppose
the caste system, increment in the age of men and women
for marriage, promotion of widow remarriage and women
education. Ranade is also called as “Precursor of cultural
Renaissance of Western India”.
*Shiv Narayan Agnihotri at Lahore in 1887 A.D. founded ‘Dev
Samaj’. The Preaching of this Samaj is mentioned in a book,
Dev Shastra. *Jyotirao Phule in 1873 A.D. founded Satya
Shodhak Samaj. He was born to a gardener family in 1827
A.D. With his book Gulamgiri and his Samaj, he criticised the
opportunistic Vedas of the Brahmans and called for the need
for protection of lower castes from exploitation. *Radhakant
Deb opposed Socio-Religious reforms and supported orthodox
elements by founding Dharma Sabha in 1830 A.D. at Culcutta
(Bengal). *Radhasoami (Radhaswami) Satsang movement
began in Agra in 1861. The fi rst and founding member of this
movement was Shiv Dayal Singh (Soamiji) or Swamiji Maharaj
originally he was ‘Persian Language translator’ later joined
his father’s moneylending business. His followers believed in
one god, the greatness of teacher, Satsang and ordinary social
life.* Social reformer of Maharashtra Gopal Hari Deshmukh
(1823-92 A.D.) was famous as Lokahitwadi. He was also
a member of Governor-General Council in 1880. *Vishnu
Shastri Pandit was a social reformer and advocate of widow
remarriage during 19th century. (specifi cally in Maharashtra).
In 1850’s he founded ‘Punarvivahottejak Mandali to promote
the practice of widow remarriages. Vishnu Shastri published
a Marathi translation of Vidyasagar’s book in Indu Prakash in
1868. *Behramji M. Malabari, a Parsi social reformer, was
born in 1853 A.D. at Baroda. The Age of Consent Act, 1891
was passed through his efforts. *M.G. Ranade and Raghunath
Rao in 1887 A.D. founded Indian National Social Conference.
The main aim of the Conference was to abolish social evils like
Polygamy, Child marriage, and Patriarchy.
The widow remarriage got legal backing By Hindu Widows
Remarriage Act of 1856. The Bengal Sati Regulation, 1829
was passed by then Governor General Lord William Bentinck,
making the practice of Sati illegal. *Ishwar Chandra
Vidyasagar, principal of Sanskrit College, struggled a lot
for the Widow Remarriage. He tried to prove the affi liation
of widow remarriage through spiritual sactions by Hindu
Shastras/Dharmashastras. By his efforts, The Hindu Widows
Remarriage Act (Act XV of 1856) was passed on 25 July,
1856. *Raja Ram Mohan Roy opposed Sati Practice strongly.
Sati Practice was abolished (by Regulation XVII (1829) passed
by the Governor-General in Council) by his efforts in 1829
A.D. Slavery became illegal in 1843 A.D. by an Act passed
by Lord Ellenborough. *Keshab Chandra Sen in 1872 played
an important role in the passing of Native Marriage Act (Act
III of 1872 commonly referenced as the Special Marriage Act,
1872) according to which the minimum age of girls and boys
for marriage was fi xed at 14 years and 18 years respectively.
This is also called as Brahmo Marriage Act of 1872. The Child
Marriage Restraint Act 1929 was enacted through the efforts of
Indian Judge Dr. Har Bilas Sharda. On his name, it was called
Sharda Act. By this Act, the minimum legal age of girls for
marriage was 14 years and for boys, it was 18 years. This act was
amended in 1978 and later repealed substituted by ‘Prohibition
of Child Marriage Act’, 2006. At present marriage age is 18
years for girls and 21 years for boys. *Theosophical Society
was founded by Madame H.P. Blavatsky, Colonel H.S. Olcott
(American army offi cer) and others in 1875 A.D. It was founded
in New York. They shifted their Headquarters from New York
to Adyar in 1882 on the outskirts of Madras which later on
became its International Offi ce. In 1889 A.D. Annie Besant
became a member of the Society and in 1893 A.D. she arrived
in India and played the most active role for the Society. She
believed Hinduism as the most spiritual and esoteric religion.
*Gopal Krishna Gokhale, in 1905, founded Servants of India
Society. He chaired the 21
st Session of Congress in 1905 A.D.
He was the political guru of Gandhi. *In 1910 A.D., Mukund
Rao Patil and Shankar Rao Jadhav in the infl uence of Jyotiba
Phule founded Bahujan Samaj. *The demand of rights to
enter the temple by Nadars led to several riots in Tirunelvelli.
In a conference organized on the abolition of untouchability,
Tilak said, “If God tolerates the untouchability then I do not
believe in God”. Tilak is often called as Lokmanya or Betaj
Badshah. *The founding members of Darul Uloom Deoband,
was Muhammad Qasim Nanautawi, Haji Syed Muhammad
Abid Deobandi, Mahtab Ali Deobandi, Zulfi qar Ali Deobandi,
Fazlur Rahman Usmani Deobandi, Haji Fazle Haq Deobandi,
Shaikh Nihal Deobandi and others; and the foundation was
laid on 31 May 1866.

questions.prompt: The founder of ‘Bhartiya Brahmo Samaj’ was :
questions.explanation:
The founder of ‘Brahmo Samaj of India’ (Bhartiya Brahmo
Samaj) was Keshab Chandra Sen. Devendra Nath stripped
the title of ‘Acharya’ from Keshab Chandra in 1865. Hence
Keshav Chandra Sen came out from original Brahmo Samaj
and group under the infl uence of Devendra Nath Tagore
called themselves as ‘Adi Brahmo Samaj.’ The group under
the leadership of Keshab Chandra Sen called themselves as
‘Bhartiya Brahmo Samaj’ or ‘Neo Brahmo Samaj.’ Again
in 1878 A.D., ‘ Navin Brahmo Samaj’ was further divided
when Keshab Chandra Sen got married his under 14 year-
old daughter with the king of Coonch Behar. To oppose his
action, Anand Mohan Bose and Shivnath Shastri formed
‘Sadharan Brahmo Samaj.’
Note : On 20 August, 1828 A.D. Raja Rammohan Roy
rented a house from Feringhee Kamal Bose, where he
formed Brahmo Samaj. Tarachand Chakroborty was its
fi rst secretary. Devendra Nath Tagore joined this society
in 1843 and Keshab Chandra Sen in 1857 A.D. Due to the
difference of opinion between Devendra Nath and Keshav
Chandra, on 11 November, 1866, Keshav Chandra formally
formed ‘Bhartiya Brahmo Samaj’ whereas earlier established
Brahmo Samaj was known as ‘Adi Brahmo Samaj.’ All these
details are available on the website www.thebramhmosamaj.
net, Gazetteer of India (vol-IInd : History and Culture) and
Macmillan published ‘social, cultural and economic history
of India’ (writers – Puri, Das, and Chopra). Later famous
historians Prof. B. L. Grover and Prof. R. L. Shukla etc. in
their book unknowingly described Keshav Chandra’s ‘Neo
Brahmo Samaj’ as ‘Adi Brahmo Samaj.’ As described by
famous historians, other books, and examination institutions
termed Keshab Chandra Sen as the founder of ‘Adi Brahmo
Samaj’ whereas the fact is entirely opposite. Therefore
Keshav’s ‘Neo Brahmo Samaj’ was ‘Bhartiya Brahmo Samaj’
and basic Brahmo Samaj under the leadership of Devendra
Nath was ‘Adi Brahmo Samaj’.

questions.prompt: Who was the founder of ‘Prarthana Samaj’?
questions.explanation:
Prarthana Samaj was founded by Aatma Ram Pandurang on
the inspiration of Keshab Chandra Sen in 1867 in Bombay.
Mahadev Govind Ranade joined the society in 1869. The
movement was started for religious and social reform in
Maharashtra and was much more like Brahmo Samaj.
The main objectives of this society were disapproval of
caste system, raising the age of marriage for both males
and females, widow remarriage and women’s education.
The socio-reform movement of Ranade was continued
successfully until the end of the 19th century. Dhondo Keshav
Karve and Vishnu Shastri were two other followers of his in
social reform programmes. Ranade and Karve started widow
remarriage movement and also founded ‘Hindu Widows
Home’ to provide education to widows. Ranade is mentioned
as the “Father of cultural renaissance in Western India.”

reformer and intellectual thinker from Maharashtra, India.
He was born in Pune. At the age of 25, Deshmukh started
writing articles aimed at social reform in Maharashtra in the
weekly ’Prabhakar’ under the pen name ’Lokahitvadi.’ In the
fi rst two years, he penned 108 articles on social reform. That
group of articles has come to be known in Marathi literature
as ’Lokahitawadinchi Shatapatre.’ He became a member of
the Council of Governor-General in 1880 A.D. He appeared
in the court of Delhi wearing hand-woven Khadi clothes, as
a supporter of the national self-reliance.

obtain a share in Government for educated Indians, to create

to Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay. The fi rst
session of Indian National Union was held on 28-30 December,
1885 A.D.. In this session on the advice of Dadabhai Naoroji,
the organization was renamed as ‘Indian National Congress.’

questions.prompt:
The last session of Indian National Congress attended
by Bal Gangadhar Tilak was :
questions.explanation:
The last session of Indian National Congress attended
by Bal Gangadhar Tilak was Amritsar Session,1919. He
had mellowed sufficiently to oppose Gandhi’s policy
of boycotting the elections to the legislative councils
established as part of the reforms that followed from
the Montagu-Chelmsford Report to Parliament in 1918.
Instead, Tilak advised the delegates to follow his policy
of ‘responsive cooperation’ in carrying out the reforms,
which introduced a certain degree of Indian participation
in regional Government. He died on 1
st August, 1920.
Moderates and Extremists
in Congress
*The fi rst two decades of INC are often described in history
as a moderate era. Some of the prominent moderate leaders
were Dadabhai Naoroji, Surendra Nath Banerjee,
Mahadev Govind Ranade, Pherozeshah Mehta, Gopal
Krishna Gokhale and Anand Mohan Bose. They had a
sense of confi dence in British justice and their generosity.
They never aimed at aggressive nationalism for attaining
independence. Leaders like Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala
Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, raised extremist ideology.
*Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Dinshaw Wacha,
Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee and Surendra Nath Banerjee were
leaders of Moderate group. They all belonged to urban areas,
in fact most of the Moderate leaders who believed in moderate
politics belonged to Urban areas. The Congress during moderate
phase was dominated by people having professions like
Advocates, Doctors, Engineers, Journalists and Person related
to Literature works. the Connection to common masses was
missing in Congress during Moderate domination. *Pherozeshah
Mehta once said, that the voice of Congress is not of Masses,
but it is the responsibility of citizens in contact with Congress
to understand these emotions and propagate these to the Nation.
*Gopal Krishna Gokhale was a moderate leader. He believed in the
purity of Means and Ends. He was the political mentor (Guru) of
Mahatma Gandhi. For the fi rst time, he took part in politics in 1889.
*In 1897 A.D., Gokhale and Dinshaw Wacha were asked
to present proofs of Indian expenditure in front of ‘Welby
Commission’. In 1899 A.D., Gokhale was elected to Bombay
legislative council and in 1901 A.D. was elected to Imperial
council of the Governor general of India. *In early 1900s
Extremist leaders of Congress emerged in Indian Political
Scenario. Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin
Chandra Pal and Aurobindo Ghose were four important
extremist leaders. Their main objective was ‘Swaraj’. They
didn’t believe in the agitation through constitutional means
of the Moderates. They blamed the Congress for politics of
Petition, Prayers and Protest. Under their leadership, the policy
of petition and prayers was criticised/challenged. *Moderates
believed in constitutional agitation, annual sessions, speeches,
sending petitions to British Parliament, etc. but extremists
believed in self-sacrifice, mass movement, aggressive
resistance and strong determination. *Extremists wanted
‘Swaraj’; as Congress presidential address, Calcutta, 1906
defi nes Swaraj as – self government like that of the United
Kingdom or the Colonies on the other hand moderates believed
in “Self rule under the colonial empire”. *Lala Lajpat Rai also
known as Sher-e-Panjab, was the representative from Punjab
and an extremist leader. He is also known as Punjab Kesari.
*Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal and Bal Gangadhar Tilak
are together called Lal-Bal-Pal. During a protest against Simon
Commission Lala Lajpat Rai was injured in lathi charge due
to which he died on 17 November, 1928 A.D. After reading
the Biography of Mazzini Lala Lajpat Rai accepted him as his
political mentor. *He translated a work of Mazzini ‘The Duties
of Man’ into Urdu.
*During the Partition of Bengal, Aurobindo Ghosh was one
of the prominent leader of the Swadeshi Movement. Other
important leaders of this movement were Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal
Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal. Tilak believed in
sacrifi ce and had courage to challenge British establishment.
He was called the “Father of Indian unrest” by Sir Valentine
Chirol. After Bal Gangadhar Tilak’s 1897 sedition conviction
and the rejection of his Privy Council appeal, Professor Max
Muller and Sir William Hunter led an infl uential petition to the
Queen, asking mercy for Tilak on the ground that he was a great
Sanskrit scholar. *Later in 1908 A.D., Tilak was jailed for 6
Years in Mandalay (Myanmar then Burma) on the charges of
sedition initiated against him for printing an anti-British Article
in his Newspaper ‘Kesari’. *Tilak wrote ‘Gita Rahasya’ from
‘Mandalay’ prison. Starting Shivaji Mahotsav and Ganpati
festival, he tried to grow the feeling of Nationalism amongst
the masses. He died on 1st August, 1920 A.D., and his funeral
bier was lifted by Mahatma Gandhi, Maulana Shaukat Ali and
Saiffudin Kichlew. Maulana Hasrat Mohani read the eulogy
after his death.

culture of modern Europe.
2. Strongly criticized the economic aspects of British
imperialism.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
questions.explanation:
During the Moderate Phase (1885-1905 AD) of the Indian
National Movement, there was support for the rich democratic
and scientifi c culture of modern Europe. The moderate leaders
advocated for constitutional reforms, political participation
and the expansion of modern education. They supported
English education, as they believed it would help develop
a modern outlook and social progress in India. However,
the growing masses viewed British colonial policies with
increasing resentment. Notably, Dadabhai Naoroji strongly
criticized the economic aspects of British colonialism. His
book, "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India," highlighted
issues related to the economic drain, heavy taxation, and
the decline of Indian industries. The moderates attempted to
address such concerns through constitutional means rather
than direct confrontation.

questions.prompt:
The protest method of moderate leaders of the Con-
gress was ?
questions.explanation:
The methods employed by the two groups (Moderates and
Extremists) of Congress were different in their tempo and
approach. Congress split into two different groups at Surat
Session of Congress in 1907 A.D. While the moderates had
infi nite faith in the effi cacy of constitutional agitation and
in appealing to the British sense of justice and fair play, in
holding an annual conference, making speeches, passing
elaborate resolutions and sending deputations to England.
The extremists had no faith in the benevolence of British
public or Parliament, nor were they convinced of the effi cacy
of merely holding conferences. Extremists had faith in the
concept of passive resistance.

questions.prompt:
Which one of the following movements has contributed

questions.explanation:

party into two groups : ‘Moderates’ and ‘Extremists.’ Moder-
ates believed in the policy of settlement of minor issues with
Government by deliberation, strikes, and boycotts to force
their demands. The moderates opposed the resolutions on
Swaraj (self-governance), Swadeshi National Education and
boycott of foreign goods but extremists were not in favour of
these. Hence, the difference of opinion between moderates
and extremists fi nally reached to split in the Congress at the
Surat Session (1907).

questions.prompt:
Who was the founder of ‘Hindustan Socialist
Democratic Union’?

options.text:
Gopen Chakravarti, Fanindra Banerjee, Dharni
Goswami

Vyomesh Chandra, Gopen Chakravartee, Sachindra
Sanyal

Vyomesh Chandra Banerjee, Ajay Ghosh, Sachindra
Sanyal

questions.explanation:
No Organisation by the name of Hindustan Socialist
Democratic Union has existed in history. In Srikrishan
Saral book Indian Revolutionaries 1757-1961,
Vol-3, the name of the organisation formed by Bhagat Singh,
Chandrashekhar Azad, Sachindra Sanyal etc. in year 1928
has been given as Hindustan Socialist Democratic Union
but in contemporary documents, authentic books of history,
the name of the organisations has been given as 'Hindustan
Socialist Republican Association' (HSRA). Therefore in the
question asked, one error is in the name of the organisation
and the other is that considering the names of founders given
in options of question, Yatindranath was martyred in the year
1915 itself. Gopen Chakravarti and Dharani Goswami were
members of the Calcutta Anushilan Samiti associated with
the communist movement and accused in Meerut conspiracy.
However both of them were not members of HSRA. Womesh
Chandra Banerjee was a moderate leader and the first
president of Indian National Congress. None of the options
are correct from this point of view. UPPSC has considered
option (b) as correct in initial answer key.

name of ‘’Master Da’’ The Indian Republican Army (IRA)
was established by Surya Sen in Bengal and on 18th April,

members of IRA namely Ganesh Ghosh, Lokenath, Nirmal
Sen, Ambika Chakrobarty, Naresh Roy, Kalpana Dutt, Anand
Gupta, Tegrabal etc. including Surya Sen. Struggle took
place on 22nd April, 1930 A.D. between members of Govern-
ment forces and members of IRA in which 80 soldiers and
12 revolutionaries were killed. On 16 February, 1933 A.D.,
Surya Sen was arrested and put through legal proceedings
and ultimately hanged on 12th January, 1934 A.D.

Revolutionary Activities
Outside India
*In February 1905 AD, Shyamji Krishna Verma established
the Indian Home Rule Society (IHRS) at London . IHRS
established nationalist student hosted, named as 'India House'
(1905-10) to foster radical Indian nationalist thoughts. The
aim of this society was to establish self-rule by promoting
nationalistic ideas/propaganda among Indians in Britain. From
here a monthly journal ‘The Indian Sociologist’ was started
in Jan 1905.
*The Ghadar Party was founded on 21st April, 1913 (at
Oregon) with its headquarters at San Francisco (USA) with
an objective to free India from British rule. Indians residing
in Canada and the USA founded this party. * In 1913,
Sohan Singh Bhakna founded a society named ‘Hindustan
Association of the Pacifi c Coast’. This society published a
newspaper named Ghadar, that is why this party became famous
as Ghadar Party. Lala Hardayal was the torchbearer of this
party. *Barakatullah, Rash Behari Bose, Raja Mahendra Pratap,
Abdul Rahman, Madam Bhikaji Cama, Bhai Parmanand, Kartar
Singh Sarabha and Pt. Kashiram were prominent members of
the party. *Raja Mahendra Pratap with Barakatullah Khan
founded the fi rst provincial government of India in Afghanistan
(Kabul) during the fi rst world war on December 1, 1915. Raja
Mahendra Pratap himself became President and Baraktullah
Khan was the Prime Minister. *Madam Cama was born on
24th September, 1861. Her parents were Parsi. She served as the
personal secretary of Dadabhai Naoroji in Indian Nationalist
Movements. She was married to Rustomji who was an advocate
and a social worker.
*Bhikaiji Rustom Cama was a supporter of Revolutionary
Nationalism. She operated revolutionary activities from
Europe and America. She participated in International Socialist
Congress held at Stuttgart (Germany) where she was the
fi rst person to hoist Indian Flag on foreign land, which
was designed jointly by V.D. Savarkar, Shyamji Krishna
Verma and Bhikaiji Rustom. She is famous as the ‘Mother
of the Indian Revolution’. * Madanlal Dhingra and Udham
Singh were hanged for the assassination of British offi cials in
England. Madanlal Dhingra on 1st July, 1909 A.D., shot and
killed Curzon Wyllie who was the political aide-de-camp to
the Secretary of State for India and Cowasji Lalkaka during a
meeting of National Indian Association. Udham Singh killed
Michael O' Dwyer (Former Lieutenant Governor of Punjab) in
London in March 1940 who was responsible for endorsing and
upholding the actions taken during Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.
The Kamagata Maru was a Japanese steamliner chartered by
an affl uent Punjabi businessman, Gurdit Singh to bring Indian
immigrants to Canada. The ship departed in 1914, taking
376 Indians for Canada’s Vancouver port, but the Canadian
authorities refused their entry in Canada. A Shore Committee
was constituted to protect the rights of Indian travellers under
the leadership of Hussain Rahim, Balwant Singh, and Sohan
Lal Pathak. Indian, Bhagwan Singh, Baraktullah, Ramchand
and Sohan Singh also carried out a movement in favour of
Indian emigrants. When Kamagatamaru reached Budge Budge
port at Calcutta, a clash occurred between angered passengers
and British Police. In fi ring by the Police, 20 of the passenger
were killed, one drowned and 202 passengers were sent to Jail.
*Rash Bihari Bose was an Indian National living in Japan.
He organized a conference in Tokyo on 28th-30th March 1942
A.D. to discuss political problems of India. *This conference
was given an organized form in June, 1942 A.D. and Subhas
Chandra Bose was invited. Ras Bihari Bose founded Indian
Independence league in this conference and unanimously
elected as President of the league.

Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi
Movement
*British Government announced the partition of Bengal on
20 July, 1905 A.D. (Resolution date was July 19, 1905) On 7
August 1905 A.D., a historic meeting took place at the town
hall of Calcutta and the Swadeshi movement was started. The
historic Boycott resolution was passed here. After this anti-
partition movements started in various parts of Bengal. *On 16
October 1905 AD, the partition formally came into force and
Bengal was divided. The day was observed as the 'Mourning
day' in the whole Bengal. On the suggestion of Rabindranath
Tagore the day was celebrated as ‘Rakhi Diwas’ amongst the
people of Bengal. *After its partition, the Bengal was divided
into East and West Bengal. East Bengal was merged into Assam,
and a new province was formed (named as Eastern Bengal
and Assam) which included Rajshahi, Chatgaon (Chittagong),
Dhaka etc. Decca (now Dhaka) was the capital of this province.
*Its second part included Bengal province, Orissa and Bihar.
*Bengal was divided during the tenure of Lord Curzon (1899-
1905 A.D.). *Sir Andrew Henderson Leith Fraser was an offi cer
of Indian Civil Service. He served as the lieutenant governor
of Bengal from 1903-1908 A.D. He played an important role in
the planning of Bengal Partition. *Rabindranath Tagore was a
critic of certain aspects of Swadeshi movements like aggressive
and exclusive nationalism and reliance solely on boycotts etc.,
and he emphasised on better relation between the East and West
cultures. He believed that the West had committed some mistake
in understanding the East, this doesn't mean East do the same
with the West. *Krishna Kumar Mitra the editor of ‘Sanjivani’,
published a special edition on 13 July 1905 A.D., and for the
fi rst time suggested that people should boycott British goods,
and mourn against the partition and should break all linkages
from British offi cers and offi ces. All of this should be done as
a protest against the partition of Bengal.
*A public gathering on 16 July 1905 A.D., at Bagerhat (then
in Khulna district, Bengal Presidency, British India) supported
the suggestion of Krishna Kumar Mitra. *British Government
called partition a necessity for the administrative purposes but
the real reason was to weaken the growth of nationalism in
Bengal. According to then viceroy Lord Curzon, “Calcutta is
the centre from which the Congress Party is manipulated
throughout the whole of Bengal and indeed the whole
of India .... . The whole of their activity is directed to
creating an agency so powerful that they may one day be
able to force a weak government to give them what they
desire.” *The announcement of Partition of Bengal was the
immediate cause of Swadeshi movement. Bal Gangadhar
Tilak, Aurobindo Ghosh, Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat
Rai were the prominent leaders of this idea. They wanted a
country wide Swadeshi movement but the moderates wanted to
keep movement limited to Bengal & preferring constitutional
methods. *The Swadeshi Movement that started in Bengal
was spread to throughout the country and Tilak was prominent
leader in Maharashtra region. Ajit Singh and Lala Lajpat Rai
led the movement in Punjab and U.P., Syed Haider Raja led
this movement at Delhi and V.O. Chidambaram Pillai led
the Swadeshi movement in Madras Presidency. *To organise
masses for this movement Ashwini Kumar Dutt founded
“Swadesh Bandhav Samiti”. Women played an active role in
this movement. However, farmers and Muslims showed limited
participation in Swadeshi and Boycott movements. *Vande
Mataram became the anthem/ralley cry song of Indian National
movement during the Swadeshi movement.
* British journalist H.W. Nevinson was related to Swadeshi
Movement. He travelled for four months across India and he
reported for Manchester Guardian, Glasgow Herald and Daily
Chronicle. Later on, he compiled his reports in a Book titled
‘The New Spirit in India’. *In the atmosphere of increasing
National Movement Abnindranath Tagore and his brother
Gaganendranath Tagore founded Indian Society of Oriental
Art in 1907 AD (which was initiated by E.B. Havell) to
reconstruct the precious Indian Arts and Culture and to develop
new consciousness among the masses.

questions.prompt:
Which of the following classes was mainly unaffected
by the Swadeshi Movement of 1905?
(i) Women
(ii) Farmers
(iii) Muslim
(iv) Intellectuals
Select your answer from the following codes –
questions.explanation:
On 20 July, 1905 A.D., Curzon issued an order for partitioning
of Bengal. On 7 August, 1905 A.D., one of the fi rst mass
protests was organized in Calcutta’s Town Hall, which was
known as ‘Swadeshi Movement’. From this Movement,
people started opposing the British offi ce, institute, and
boycott foreign goods. A remarkable aspect of the Swadeshi
Movement was seen in the active participation of women. To
collect the public support, Aswani Kumar Dutt organized the
committee which is known as (Swadesh Bandhav Society).
Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai and Aurobindo Ghosh played leading
role in the fabrication of the Movement's character. In this
Movement, women actively participated but farmers and
Muslims were very limited involved in this Movement. They
separated themselves from this Movement. Thus, option (c)
is the correct answer.

questions.chapter: Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi Movement
questions.prompt:
Vande Mataram became the theme song of the Indian
National Movement during –
questions.explanation:
During Swadeshi Movement, the actual day of partition,
October 16, 1905 A.D., was declared a day of mourning
throughout Bengal and the hearths in the houses were kept
unlit. People tied rakhis on each other wrists as a symbol
of brotherhood. In Calcutta, most of the offi ces were kept
closed, and a strike was observed in some jute mills and
railway workshops. The streets reverberated with Vande
Mataram which became the overnight National Song of
Bengal and later, the Theme ralley cry or anthem of the
National Movement.

Glasgow Herald, and Daily Chronicle. He re-edited these
pieces into a book. 'The New Spirit in India'.

In 1905, Lord Minto was appointed as Viceroy of India in
place of Lord Curzon and John Morley was appointed as
Secretary of State for India. The reforms introduced by them
are known as Morley-Minto Reforms. The Indian Councils
Act, 1909, commonly known as the Morley-Minto Reforms
was an Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom that
brought about a limited increase in the involvement of Indians
in the governance of British India. The major dispute regarding
this act was separate electorate for Muslims in India.

(a) Dyarchy
(b) Communal representation
(c) Federation
(d) Provincial autonomy
U.P.P.C.S. (Pre) 1996
Ans. (b)
The main fault of the Indian Council Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto)
was a system of communal representation for Muslims by
accepting the concept of “separate electorate.” According
to this system, Muslim members were to be elected only by
Muslim electorates, not by general electorates in Councils.
Indeed it meant that the Muslim community was considered
as an absolutely separate class from India. Antiquated National
integrity vanished in only one storm. Gandhi Stated:- "The
Morley – Minto Reforms have been our undoing. Had it not
been for the separate electorates then established then we
should have settled our differences by now."

Lucknow Session of Congress
(The Lucknow Pact)
*In December 1916 AD, both Indian National Congress and
Muslim League held their sessions at Lucknow.
*Both parties passed separate resolutions on demands for
constitutional reforms and agreed on a pact to work together
in the political fi eld on a common programme. This is known
as Lucknow Pact or Congress-League Scheme. *Ambika
Charan Majumdar was president of Congress in this session.
As a result, they together released 19 bulletins to give a positive
direction to the contemporary political scenario. *Lucknow
session was very signifi cant due to two reasons, fi rst, the
Extremists who were separated from Congress nine years ago
(in 1907 A.D.) were again merged to Congress and, secondly
there was a pact between Congress and League. Annie Besant
and Tilak played a signifi cant role in the return of Extremists
to Congress. On the other hand, the efforts of Jinnah and Tilak
were responsible for Congress-League Pact. The period from
1916 A.D. to 1922 A.D. was the time of consensus between
Congress and League (although the rupture in their relation
stated in 1920, as Jinnah resigned from Congress in 1920 due to
his disagreements with Mahatma Gandhi's approach). Lucknow
Pact was just a temporary arrangement. Muslim League, besides
this pact had its own identity and it advocated for the interests of
Muslims where ever possible. Both League and Congress were
together until 1922 A.D.

questions.chapter: Lucknow Session of Congress (The Lucknow Pact)
questions.prompt:
In December, 1916 both Indian National Congress and
Indian Muslim League held their session at:
questions.explanation:
An important step towards achieving Hindu-Muslim unity
was the Lucknow Pact, 1916 A.D. Anti-British feelings were
generated among the Muslims following a war between
Britain and Turkey, which opened the way for Congress and
Muslim League unity. Both the Congress and the Muslim
League held sessions at Lucknow in 1916 A.D. This meeting
settled the details of an agreement on the composition of the
legislatures and the quantum of representation to be allowed
to the two communities. The agreement was confi rmed by
the annual sessions of the Congress, and the League held at
Lucknow on 29 and 31 December, 1916 A.D. respectively.
The Congress accepted the separate electorates and both
organizations jointly demanded dominion status for the
country. Hindu-Muslim unity weakened the British attitude.
In 1916 A.D., the British Government announced a policy
whereby the involvement of Indians in the Government was
to be increased, and there was to be a gradual development of
local self-Government institutions. Sarojini Naidu described
Jinnah, the chief architect of the Lucknow Pact, with the title
of the ‘Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity.’

Home Rule League
Movement
*Tilak started Home Rule League in April, 1916 A.D. Annie
Besant started the Home Rule League in September, 1916
A.D. *Besant through The Commonweal (weekly) and New
India and Tilak through Mahratta and Kesari promoted their
league to masses.
*Joseph Baptista was the fi rst president of Tilak’s Home Rule
League and N.C. Kelkar was its secretary. *George Arundale
was the organizing secretary of Annie’s Home Rule League.
*Tilak and Annie Besant divided their areas of work. Tilak got
Karnataka, Maharashtra (except Bombay), Central Provinces
and Berar. Rest of India was part of Annie’s Area of work. Both
leagues never merged because in Annie Besant's words, “Some
of Tilak’s supporters dislike me and some of mine dislike him.
We however, had no quarrel with each other". *In Home Rule
League movement both Tilak and Annie Besant had same
meaning of ‘Swaraj’ i.e. to get a responsible government and
administration at central and provincial levels under the British
Empire and to have treatment like white ruled states like Canada
and Australia which were dominion states of British. Annie
Besant described Home Rule Movement in her newspaper
'The Common Weal' on 2nd January, 1914 A.D. Under this
a programme was made for Religious freedom, National
Education, Social and Political reforms keeping in mind the
objective of Self government under the British Commonwealth.
*The movement was very famous in India during the fi rst
World War. Lucknow session of 1916 A.D. was an excellent
occasion for Home Rule League’s members to show their might.
*A train was reserved to transport the supporters of Tilak to
Lucknow, some people named that train as ‘Congress Special’
and some people named it as Home Rule Special. George
Arundale, organizing secretary of Besant’s League asked
their supporters to show their presence at Lucknow in huge
numbers. *Theosophical society was established in 1875 by
Colonel Henery Steel Olcott and Madame Helena Petrovna
Blavatsky and William Quan Judge. Annie Besant became
its member in 1889.
1.
Who launched the fi rst Home Rule League Movement?
(a) Annie Besant
(b) Sarojini Naidu
(c) Surendranath Banerjee (d) Tilak
U.P P.C.S. (Pre) 1993
U.P P.C.S. (Pre) 1991
Ans. (a)
During the fi rst World War, Mrs. Annie Besant and Tilak
decided to put new life in the National Movement in the
country. Tilak decided to use the term ‘Home Rule’ in place of
Swaraj as the goal of his Movement. Tilak started Home Rule
League in April, 1916 A.D. with its headquarters at Poona.
A similar Home Rule League was founded by Annie Besant
in September, 1916 A.D. with its headquarters at Adyar near
Madras. However, the movement itself was fi rst talked about
by Annie Besant in his newspaper The Common Weal in 1914.
2. Two Home Rule Leagues were started in 1915-16 under
the leadership of:
(a) Tilak and Annie Besant
(b) Tilak and Aurobindo Ghosh
(c) Tilak and Lala Lajpat Rai
(d) Tilak and Vipin Chandra Pal
U.P. U.D.A./L.D.A. (Pre) 2001
Ans. (a)
See the explanation of above question.
3.
Annie Besant is mostly associated with :
(a) Civil Disobedience Movement
(b) Home Rule Movement
(c) Khilafat Movement
(d) Non-Cooperation Movement
U.P.P.C.S. (Mains) 2010
Ans. (b)
Annie Besant, a theosophist, settled in India and worked
for its liberation. She was inspired by the Irish Home
Rule Movement and formed the Home Rule League in
India in September, 1916 A.D., at Adyar in Madras. She
already explained her views about this Movement in The
Commonweal (a weekly newspaper) in 1914 A.D. Annie
Besant started this Movement to demand self-governance at
all levels of administration. Her Home Rule League became
active throughout India. She was arrested along with her co-
workers and released after widespread agitation against the
action of Government.

(b) Annie Besant

40th B.P.S.C. (Pre) 1995

H.S. Olcott was not associated with Home Rule League but

Annie Besant started Home Rule League in September,1916.
S.Subramania Iyer was also associated with the Home Rule

7. In which conference could the Home-Rule supporters
demonstrate their political power successfully?
(a) Lucknow Conference of Congress in 1916
(b) All India Trade Union Conference held at Bombay in
1920
(c) First U.P. Farmers Association held in 1918.
(d) Joint A.I.T.U.C and N.T.U. Sabha at Nagpur in 1938.
39th B.P.S.C. (Pre) 1994
Ans. (a)
The Lucknow Session of Congress in December 1916 A.D.
presented the Home Rule Leagues with the long-awaited
opportunity for demonstrating their strength. Tilak’s Home
Rule League established a tradition to which Congress was
pinned for many years.
8. Home Rule Movement was symbol of starting a new
phase of freedom movement in India because :
(a) It put a perfect project for the self-Government before
the nation
(b) Leadership of the movement came into the hands of
Gandhiji
(c) Hindus and Muslims started to struggle jointly
(d) It established co-ordination between extremists and
moderates
41st B.P.S.C. (Pre) 1996
Ans. (a)
It is true that Home Rule Movement was a symbol of starting
a new phase of Freedom Movement in India because it put
a perfect picture of the self-governance before the Nation.
The object of this Home Rule League was to attain Home-
Rule or Self-Governance within the British Empire by all
Constitutional means and to educate and organize public
opinion in the Country towards the attainment of the same.
Both Tilak and Besant toured all over the country and carried
out the message of the Home Rule among the masses. Thus,
the Home Rule Movement became a powerful Movement
during the First World War. The Movement aimed at
self-Government to be granted to India within the British
dominions during the war. It was within Constitutional limits.
9. Which of the following is not correct about the Home
Rule League:
(a) The plan was fi rst presented in 1914-15 by Annie
Besant
(b) The Home Rule League of Tilak was confi ned to
Maharashtra, Karnataka, Central Provinces and Berar
(c) The Home Rule League founded by Tilak was much
stronger
(d) Despite the differences between Tilak and Besant,
both the Leagues continued to exist
U.P.P.C.S. (Pre) 2004
Ans. (*)
The concept for the foundation of Home Rule League was
fi rst introduced by Mrs. Annie Besant. Self-Governance
Movement began with the publication of the weekly review
newspaper The Commonweal on January 2, 1914 A.D. The
Movement was started by B.G. Tilak in Poona in April, 1916
A.D.and Annie Besant and S. Subramania Iyer at Adyar near
Madras in September, 1916 A.D. Tilak’s League worked in
Maharashtra (except Bombay), Karnataka, Central Province
and Berar. It was the most organized League and Annie
Besant’s League was in the rest of India. The objective of
the Movement was self-governance for India in the British
Empire. Tilak linked up the question of Swaraj with the
demand for the formation of linguistic states and education
in the vernacular languages. He gave the slogan ‘Swaraj is
my birthright, and I shall have it’. The Mahratta and Kesari of
Tilak and Annie Besant’s The Commonweal and New India
became the organs of the Home Rule movement. Both Home
Rule League were complementary with each other, so there
was no dispute between Tilak and Annie Besant and both
Leagues continued to exist. Therefore, all options are correct.

13. Which Congress leader visited Bihar in 1918 in order
to strengthen the activities of Home Rule League?
(a) B.G. Tilak
(b) Annie Besant
(c) Mahatma Gandhi
