71st B.P.S.C. (Pre) 2025
Ans. (b)
Annie Besant visited Bihar (Patna) twice in 1918; on 18 April,
1918 to strengthen the activities of the Home Rule League,
and on 25 July, 1918 to understand the views of the Home
Rulers. During these visits, she held meetings, increased
contact with local workers, and strengthened the League’s
organisational base.
14. In 1920, which of the following changed its name to
"Swarajya Sabha"?
(a) All India Home Rule League
(b) Hindu Mahasabha
(c) South Indian Liberal Federation
(d) The Servants of India Society
I.A.S. (Pre) 2018
Ans. (a)
The Home Rule Movement, the All India Home Rule League,
was a national political organization founded in September
1916 by Annie Besant. Tilak's Indian Home Rule League in
Karnataka, Maharashtra (except Bombay), Central Provinces
and Berar. The rest of the country fell under the care of Annie
Besant's League. The aim of the League was to achieve self-
government in a constitutional manner within the British
Empire. In 1920, the All India Home Rule League elected
Mahatma Gandhi as its President and Mahatma Gandhi
changed its name to 'Swarajya Sabha' (Assembly).
Gandhi and His Early
Movements
*Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born on 2nd October,
1869 AD at Porbandar, Gujarat. Gandhiji's education started
in a Pathshala in Porbandar but at the age of seven he moved
to Rajkot due to his father's transfer and he studied in Rajkot
till high school. Mahatma Gandhi was married to Kasturba
Gandhi at the age of 13. He took training as Barrister from
‘Inner Temple’, London. Karamchand Gandhi was Diwan
of Porbandar, Wankaner and Rajkot. He is also known as
‘Kaba Gandhi’.
*Gandhi, in 1894 A.D., founded Natal Indian Congress
in South Africa. *He along with his colleagues established
a new colony named as Tolstoy Farm in 1910 and started
living there. *He started a newspaper there named Indian
Opinion (Published in English, Gujarati, Hindi and Tamil).
The fi rst issue of this newspaper was released in June 1903.
*He established an Ashram at Phoenix (Durban, South
Africa) in 1904 A.D. It was reopened on 27th February, 2000
A.D. Phoenix Ashram was the fi rst Ashram established by
Gandhiji. *In his thoughts Gandhiji emphasized more on
practical idealism than idealism. Like Marx he also believed
in the removal of State and had no problem on being called
as Philosophical Anarchist. *Truth and Non-Violence
were the two principles of Ram Rajya of Gandhiji. He made
these two as the base of Modern society of his dreams. He
was a true socialist. He took care of both private and social
interests. He wanted to bring functionality to the noble ideals
of Social Justice. Gandhiji himself said to Louis Fischer, “I
am a true socialist and the aim of my socialism is progress
of all”. Socialism of Gandhiji has some glimpses of Marxism.
Gandhiji gave extraordinary importance to labours. *He
wanted to bring into action the principle that everyone is
given work according to their capacity and everyone to be
paid remuneration according to their needs. *Gandhiji said, “I
am engaged in solving the same problem that faces scientifi c
socialists. It is true, however that my approach is always and
only through unalterated non-violence”. Gandhiji is called an
Individualist and Marxist among the socialists. *Strike was
the last option in the Satyagraha strategy whereas fasting
was his fi rst weapon. According to Gandhiji Satyagraha was
‘Agni-Baan’. The objective of Satyagraha of Gandhiji was
to change the heart of enemy according to the demand of
protestor instead of defeating the enemy. This was to be done
by the suffering that Satyagrahi took upon himself. Gandhiji
termed self- control as the best solution for Family Planning.
*Mahatma Gandhi used to say that “Ahimsa and Truth are so
intertwined that it is practically impossible to disentangle and
separate them. They are like the two sides of a coin, or rather
of a smooth unstamped metallic disc. Who can say, which is
the obverse, and which is the reverse? Nevertheless, Ahimsa
is the means; Truth is the end. Means to be means must always
be within our reach, and so Ahimsa is our supreme duty. If we
take care of the means, we are bound to reach the end sooner
or later. When once we have grasped this point, fi nal victory is
beyond question. Whatever diffi culties we encounter, whatever
apparent reverses we sustain, we may not give up the quest for
Truth which alone is, being God Himself”. Mahatma Gandhi
was convinced that if we take care of our means, the end will
be taken care of itself.
*In 1893 (24 May), at the age of 23, Gandhiji went to Durban
(South Africa) to fi ght a case of Gujarati trader Dada Abdullah.
He stayed in Africa for 21 years and returned to India in 1915
A.D. The public welcomed him with enthusiasm, his struggle
and victories in South Africa made him popular here too. *After
coming to India, he met Gopal Krishna Gokhale. He was
his political mentor. Gandhiji, for the fi rst time, participated
in a Congress session at Calcutta in 1901 A.D. In this session
resolution of Gandhiji on Africa was passed. This session
was chaired by Dinshaw Wacha. During his stay in South
Africa, Gandhiji came to India in 1901 A.D. and established
his offi ce of law at Bombay in 1902 A.D. Gandhiji, in 1915
A.D., established Satyagraha Ashram at Ahmedabad. The
Ashram was moved to the banks of Sabarmati River on 17th
June, 1917 A.D. considering various economic activities.
*Gandhiji believed that active politics was an important tool
for social upliftment and public welfare. In this context the
decentralization of power was the most important suggestion
of Gandhiji. With the decentralization of power Gandhiji meant
the power to Gram Panchayats to manage and administer
their villages. The political system shown by Gandhiji was
the inclusion of Morality, Religion and Humanity but the
complete ideal political system of Gandhiji had no place for
State power. He wanted the establishment of stateless society.
Gandhiji named the ongoing struggle in Africa as passive
resistance, but later on, it was replaced by Satyagraha. It was
widely used in India’s struggle for Independence. But both
the terms were not the same for Gandhiji. According to him,
passive resistance is a political weapon whereas Satyagraha
is moral power. *During India’s freedom struggle, Gandhiji,
in 1917 A.D., started Champaran Satyagraha at Bihar. This
was his fi rst successful Satyagraha in India. *Gandhiji linked
the boycott of foreign clothes with Nation’s Respect. Boycott
of foreign clothes by Gandhiji’s Movement was effective as
India was believed to be the market for foreign manufactured
goods. With Gandhiji’s formula of Boycott of foreign goods the
production and sale of Indian goods were promoted. *Gandhiji
read the book ‘Unto This Last’ written by John Ruskin during
his stay in Africa. Gandhiji wrote in his biography that this
book changed his life. According to Gandhiji, the Message of
this book was - “The good of the individual is contained in
the good of all”. On this basis, Gandhiji rendered his ideology
of the welfare of all. Among the western thinkers ‘Thoreau,
Ruskin and Tolstoy’ highly infl uenced the Gandhian ideology.
From ‘Thoreau’ he learnt civil disobedience and benefi ts of
refusal to pay takes. Ruskin taught him to respect the physical
labour. Gandhiji was highly infl uenced by the statement of
Tolstoy- "The Kingdom of God is within you" and this
became the base of his non-violence and non-cooperation.
*Gandhiji worked very hard for the improvement in the
conditions of untouchables in India. Gandhiji said, “Service
of Harijan is the breath of my life without which I won’t
survive one single minute”. Champaran and Kheda were
Farmers’ Movement. Champaran movement in Bihar was
the fi rst Satyagraha of Gandhiji in India. In the beginning of
19th century white owners of plantations made an obligation
with the farmer to cultivate Indigo on 3/20th part of their
land. This was called as Teen Kathiya System. Plantation
owners imposed Tawan (a lump-sum compensation or illegal
levy charges) and other charges/cesses to exploit farmers
and make it impossible to get out of the contract. Against
this exploitation of the farmers Gandhiji started Champaran
Satyagraha. To investigate the matter, the Government
constituted a committee and Gandhiji was also one of the
members. Plantation owners agreed to return the 25% of
illegally collected money. In this way the fi rst Satyagraha of
Gandhiji was successful. *Pt. Rajkumar Shukla persuaded
Gandhiji to look into the matters of the exploitation of
farmers in Champaran. The people that accompanied Gandhiji
to Champaran for investigation included - Acharya J.B.
Kriplani, Dr. Rajendra Prasad, Mahadev Desai, C.F.
Andrews, Dr. Anugrah Narayan Sinha, Braj Kishor
Prasad, etc. N.G. Ranga opposed Gandhiji’s support to
Champaran movement, whereas Rabindranath Tagore gave
him the title of 'Mahatma'. *After Champaran Movment, the
next experiment of Gandhiji was the dispute between cotton
mill owners and labours of Ahmedabad on the issue of
plague bonus. Gandhiji convinced workers and owners to
hand over this issue to a tribunal. To encourage and motivate
the labourers, he himself sat on fasting. This protest showed
some result and the owners handed over all these matters to
the tribunal. Later on tribunal pronounced a 35% increase
in dearness allowance (wage increment). *In 1918 A.D., at
Kheda, after the failure of crops. The Government didn’t
give any concession in revenue, nor did they stopped the
collection of land revenue. On this matter, Gandhiji constituted
a Satyagraha in favour of farmers. *Subhash Chandra Bose, for
the fi rst time called Gandhiji as the Father of Nation. In July,
1944, speaking on Azad Hind radio, Subhash Chandra Bose
addressed Gandhiji and said, “India's last war of independence
has begun. Father of Nation we need your blessings and good
wishes on this expedition.” *Pyarelal Nayyar was the secretary
of Gandhiji (since 1942) during Noakhali communal riots. His
sister Sushila Nayyar was the personal Doctor of Gandhiji.
Pyarelal played an important role in Gandhiji’s Dandi March.
Jamnalal Bajaj (Cloth trader, Banker, Congress Social Worker)
was a close associate of Mahatama Gandhi. Jamnalal Bajaj was
born at Sikar District (Rajasthan). He was adopted by a rich
businessman of Wardha. He got in touch with Gandhiji in 1915
A.D. and remained his follower for life. He took part in the
Indian National Congress at the age of 30. He renounced the
title of Rai Bahadur protesting the policies of British towards
India. He was treasurer of Congress and founder of Gandhi
Seva Sangh. He took a deep interest in village industry and
handloom clothes. He was jailed in 1923 A.D. for taking part
in Nagpur Flag Satyagraha and again in 1930 A.D. during
Civil Disobedience Movement.
*Charles Andrews (Dinbandhu Andrews) began teaching at
Saint Stephen's College, Delhi. He was deeply attached with
Indians and wanted to be an Indian in all forms. He had strong
relations with Rabindranath Tagore, Gopal Krishna Gokhale
and Mahatma Gandhi. *He stayed too at Phoenix Settlements
(Ashram) with Gandhiji. Gandhiji, after seeing him completely
devoted towards upliftments of poor, gave him the title of
Dinbandhu. *Andrews was the president of All India Trade
Union Congress in 1925 A.D. and 1927 A.D. He accompanied
Gandhiji when he went to London to take part in Round Table
Conference. *Gandhiji was not a member of Congress during
India’s Independence. In the year 1934 A.D., he resigned from
Congress. Afterwards, he never became a member of Congress
offi cially but his ideologies played a very signifi cant role in the
then political scenario.
*In 1903, Gandhiji founded a law fi rm in Johannesburg and
stayed there till 1910 (before transit to Tolstoy farm). Gandhiji
applied the principles of Trusteeship. Gandhiji believed that the
economy of each country should be determined after keeping
into consideration the climate, land, nature of residents of that
country. This economics is totally opposed to exploitation,
whether done by one group to the other group of a country or
exploitation of a country by another country. Gandhiji wanted to
establish such a system in which a person with his fundamental
efforts in a free environment can choose to work and perform
labour. For this, he wanted the revival of Indian goods industries
so that there is enough food to feed all and no one suffers from
hunger. Gandhiji emphasized on the importance of cottage
industries like - making jaggery, thrashing grass, extracting oil,
paper making, leather works etc. with this Gandhiji believed
that the poor and exploited will have Social and Economic
improvement. On 30th January, 1948, Nathuram Godse shot
Gandhiji. On his death, Nehruji said, “The light has gone out
of our lives and there is darkness everywhere. I do not know
what to tell you and how to say it. Our beloved leader, Bapu
as we called him, the Father of The Nation, is no more."

He said ‘Ahimsa’ or ‘Non-violence’ is the means; Truth

questions.prompt: Which of the following may be true regarding Gandhi?

options.text:
An Individualist among Socialists and a Marxist
among Socialists

questions.explanation:
Gandhi’s thought has been linked to philosophical anarchism
and can be compared with strands of Marxist thought. But
during present circumstances, he was not in the favour to
abolish the state. Human being are not capable enough to
manage their collective affairs on their own. Hence, State
and law are required in the society. In addition to this, he also
believed that the jurisdiction of the State should be minimum.
Gandhi told Louis Fischer "I am a true socialist. The meaning
of my socialism is Sarvodaya." There is a great similarity
between Gandhi and Marx, the fi nal aim of both of them was
to establish a stateless and classless society, but their means of
achieving this aim were different. For Gandhi, it was through
non-violence, but for Marx, it was through violent means.

In January, 1915 A.D. Mahatma Gandhi returned from South
Africa and people warmly welcomed him. The struggles and
successes in South Africa made him very popular in India. In
India, he came in contact with Gopal Krishna Gokhale and
accepted him as his political mentor. He linked himself to
India’s active politics under the infl uence of Gopal Krishna
Gokhale.

questions.prompt:
In which of the following railway stations in South
Africa, Mahatma Gandhi was thrown out of the train?
questions.explanation:
Gandhi arrived in Durban, South Africa in 1893 to serve as legal
counsel to the businessman Dada Abdullah. In June, he was
asked by Dada Abdullah to undertake a trip to Pretoria in the
Transvaal, a journey which fi rst took Gandhi to Pietermaritzburg.
There Gandhi was seated in the fi rst-class compartment since
he had purchased a fi rst-class ticket. A European who entered
the compartment hastened to summon railway offi cials, who
ordered Gandhi to shift himself to the van compartment since
‘coolies’ and non-whites were apparently not permitted in
fi rst-class compartments. Gandhi protested and produced his
ticket, but was warned that he would be forcibly removed if
he did not make a gracious exit. As Gandhi refused to comply
with the order, he was summarily pushed out of the train, and
his luggage was tossed out on to the platform.

questions.prompt:
Sabarmati Ashram, established by Mahatma Gandhi
during India’s Independence movement, is located on
the outskirts of :
questions.explanation:
Gandhi’s Satyagraha Ashram was originally established at
the Kocharab Bungalow of Jivanlal Desai, a barrister, and
friend of Gandhi. At that time, the Ashram was called the
Satyagraha Ashram. But Gandhi wanted to carry out various
activities such as farming and animal husbandry, in addition
to other pursuits which required a much larger area of usable
land. So two years later, on 17 June 1917 A.D., the Ashram
was relocated to an area of thirty-six acres on the banks of the
River Sabarmati, in Ahmedabad and later came to be known
as the Sabarmati Ashram.

questions.prompt:
Who among the following was the ‘Political Guru’ of
Mahatma Gandhi?
questions.explanation:
Gopal Krishna Gokhale was one of the early social and
political leaders during the Indian Independence Movement
against the British Empire in India. Gokhale was famously a
mentor of Mahatma Gandhi in his formative years. In 1912,
Gokhale visited South Africa at Gandhi’s invitation. As a
young barrister, Gandhi returned from his struggles against
the Empire in South Africa and received personal guidance
from Gokhale, including knowledge and understanding of
India and the issues confronting common Indians. By 1920,
Gandhi emerged as the leader of the Indian Independence
Movement. In his autobiography, Gandhi calls Gokhale as
his mentor and guide.

questions.prompt: As per Mahatma Gandhi politics meant –
questions.explanation:
For Gandhi, politics meant social welfare and public welfare.
The most important suggestion about politics from Gandhiji
was ‘decentralization of power’. For him, the decentralization
meant to encourage the village Panchayats and control their
local administration.

questions.prompt:
Which of the following is not a feature of politics of the
Gandhian model?
questions.explanation:
The paradigm of politics presented by Gandhiji is the
combination of three elements – morality, religion and
humanity. But in Gandhian political model, there is no place
for authority. He wanted to establish a Stateless Society.

questions.prompt:
The cook from Bihar who saved Mahatma Gandhi's
life from a murder attempt by food poisoning in 1917
was
questions.explanation:
Batak Mian was a cook for a British manager of an Indigo
plantation in Bihar known as Erwin in popular memory.
During Champaran Satyagrah he invited Gandhiji for dinner
and coerced Batak Mian to poison Gandhi through milk. But
Batak Mian while serving milk to Gandhiji, broke down and
told Gandhiji about the poison and Gandhiji escaped unhurt.
This story was corroborated by Dr. Rajendra Prasad in one of
his speeches given in 1950s at Motihari which is mentioned
in Delhi University Professor Dr. Girish Mishra's article
"Gandhi's Champaran Struggle".

questions.prompt:
Who amongst the following coined the word
‘Satyagraha’?
questions.explanation:
The nephew of Mahatma Gandhi, Magan Lal Gandhi fi rst
used the term ‘Sada Graha’ during a competition for which
he was rewarded. Satyagraha means truth and rigidity. Later
on, Gandhi improvised the word as ‘Satyagraha.’ Hence, it is
clear that the word ‘Satyagraha’ was used fi rstly by Gandhi.

questions.prompt:
During the India’s struggle for Independence who was
the fi rst to start ‘Satyagraha’?
questions.explanation:
Satyagraha is a term comprising two words; Satya or
truth, and Agrah or insistence. Hence, in its loose English
interpretation, Satyagraha means 'insistence on truth'. The
Champaran Satyagraha of 1917 A.D. was Mahatma Gandhi’s
fi rst successful Satyagraha in India.

questions.prompt:
Which of the following was Gandhiji's fi rst Satyagraha
Movement in India in which he used Civil Disobedi-
ence?

options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation:
Champaran Satyagrah of 1917 A.D. was the first Civil
Disobedience Movement led by Gandhiji in India.
In 1917 A.D., in the Champaran of Bihar, farmers were
protesting against having to grow indigo with barely any
payment for it from British.
On the invitation of Raj Kumar Shukla, Gandhiji went there
and started non-violent protest against this, which eventually
led to acceptance of the demands of farmers. This was the
fi rst victory of Satyagraha in India.

questions.prompt:
During the Champaran Satyagraha, the cultivation of
Indigo was known as _________.
questions.explanation:
During the Champaran Satyagrah, the cultivation of Indigo
was known as Tinkathia system. Tinkathia was the most
prevalent system in Champaran. According to it, the factory
owners convinced the tenant to grow indigo in a specifi c area
of his holding for which a fi xed price was paid. In this, the
ryot was under an obligation to cultivate three kathas per
beegha of his land with indigo i.e. 3/20th of his land holding.

questions.prompt:

which of the following?

options.text: Use of passive resistance to achieve Indian Independence.
Desire to establish an Islamic nation.
Opposition to Hindus holding political offi ce.
Encouragement of violence to end British rule.

questions.explanation:
Struggle done by Gandhi in South Africa was termed
as ‘Inactive resistance ‘but later Gandhi chose the word
‘Satyagraha’ in place of inactive resistance. Satyagraha was
the term, which was used most during the freedom struggle.
But Gandhi differentiated between Satyagraha and inactive
resistance. As per him, inactive resistance is a political
tool, whereas Satyagraha is moral power. He differentiated
Inactive Resistance and Satyagraha by comparing it with the
north and the south pole.

questions.prompt: Whose work has infl uenced the Gandhian concept?

influenced Gandhian Ideology. One person that greatly
influenced Gandhi and his tactics for achieving Indian
Independence was Henry David Thoreau. Primarily his essay
on Civil Disobedience. From Ruskin, Gandhiji learned to
respect physical labour. Tolstoy famous quote 'the kingdom
of God is within you,' inspired Gandhiji and it became the
basis of his Non-Violence Movement.

questions.explanation:
Jamnalal Bajaj was an industrialist, a philanthropist, as
well as a freedom fi ghter. He was also a close associate and
follower of Mahatma Gandhi. Gandhiji used to call Jamnalal
his ‘fifth son.’ A loyal member of the Indian National

was decided to organize tricolour fl ag procession in Nagpur
and the Government banned it. Later, Jamnalal Bajaj took
the challenge and organized the Flag Satyagraha and was
sentenced to jail for 18 months and Rs. 3,000/- as fi ne. The
leadership qualities he showed as the commander of Flag
Satyagraha made him a real hero and a National leader.

questions.prompt:
According to M.K. Gandhi socio-economic improvement
of untouchables can be brought about :

options.text:
By earmarking funds for their socio-economic
development
By establishing cottage industry for them

questions.explanation:
Gandhi’s socio-economic policy opposes all forms of
exploitation. India lives in its villages. Naturally, the
development of the country depends on the development of
villages. That is why Gandhi stressed on the growth of rural
industries such as khadi, handlooms, sericulture, handicrafts,
etc. Rural industries are based on family labour and require
less amount of capital. Raw materials are available in local
and surrounding areas and the goods thus produced are
sold in local markets. Therefore, there is no problem with
production and market. Gandhi has strongly advocated the
development of cottage industries in villages, which would
reduce the burden on agriculture. Cottage industry can
also work as a good support system for villagers. Thus, all
villagers can get employment in their respective villages,
which will check the migration to urban areas. According to
Gandhi, socio-economic improvement of untouchables can
be brought about by establishing cottage industry for them.

Peasant Movement and
Kisan Sabha
*Workers of Home Rule League were very active in Awadh.
They started to organize Peasants. Organization was named as
'Kisan Sabha'. * U.P. Kisan Sabha was formed in February
1918 A.D. by Indra Narayan Dwivedi, Gauri Shankar
Mishra with the support of Madan Mohan Malaviya. The
organizations organized peasants on a large scale. *These
organizations spread awareness amongst the farmers on such
a large scale that in 1918 A.D. Delhi Session of Congress a
huge number of farmers participated from U.P. *In Pratapgarh
District of Oudh ‘Nai-Dhobi bandh’ social boycott movement
was started against the exploiting landlords. *Jhinguri Singh
and Durgapal played an important role in this movement, but
later on, a new face, Baba Ramchandra emerged who operated
the movement wisely and made it strong and combative.
In mid 1920 A.D., he emerged as a peasant’s leader and
started organizing peasants in Oudh. He had extraordinary
organizational capability. In 1920 A.D., with his efforts,
Oudh Kisan Sabha was established. *Swami Sahajanand
Saraswati was the founder of Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha
(BPKS) in 1929. In his Agricultural Reform programme, the
main aim was the eradication of Zamindari system and to bring
ownership rights to the farmers. For his devoted services to
farmers he is also called as ‘Kisan-Pran’. *On April 11, 1936.
All India Kisan Congress was formed in Lucknow. Swami
Sahajanand became its fi rst President and N.G. Ranga became
fi rst General Secretary. *The Kisan Congress was later renamed
as 'All India Kisan Sabha' (AIKS) held its session at the same
time of the Congress session in Faizpur which was chaired by
N.G. Ranga. *Eka Movement (1921-22 A.D.) was led by
Madari Pasi of a lower class family. The main centres of this
movement were Hardoi, Barabanki, Bahraich and Sitapur. Main
complains of farmers included the increment in rent and the
system of collection of rent in produce. Rent was 50% higher
than the recorded rent generally. In this movement, people
didn’t refuse to pay rent and insisted on collecting the revenue
in cash because of high infl ation. *Vallabh Bhai Patel led the
peasant movements in 1928 A.D. from Bardoli which later on
became popular as Bardoli Satyagraha. With the success of
this movement, the women of Bardoli gave the title of ‘Sardar’
to Vallabh Bhai Patel.
* When the kisan leaders found that large sections of Bargadars
were eagerly awaiting a call for struggle for their ‘Tebhaga
demand’ and that their mass militancy was at a high pitch, the
Bengal Provincial Kisan Council decided, in September 1946,
to a launch the ‘Tebhaga Movement’ in the ensuing harvesting
season in November 1946. In this movement share-croppers
demanded that the share of the Zamindars to be reduced to
one-third from the present half of the produce. Rest of the
produce i.e. two-third should go to the Share Cropper. The
districts of North Bengal and beyond were most affected by this
movement. *Acharya Vinoba Bhave visited Nalgonda district;
Phochampally/Bhudhan Pochampally, is now in Yadadri
Bhuvanagiri district (which is carved out of Nalgonda district)
of Telangana on 18 April 1951 A.D., in relation to Sarvodaya
conference. This district was then the centre of communist
activities. Vinoba ji stayed at Bhudan Pochampalli village.
Ramchandra Reddy, a landlord of that village donated 100
acres of land to 40 Harijan families to solve their problems of
the land. *Bhoodan movement began on 18th April 1951, and
in October 1951, Vinoba set the target of 50 million acres by
1957; though the movement continued beyond 1957 but later
it began to wane.
1.
The fi rst peasant movement of India was:
(a) Champaran
(b) Bardoli
(c) Begu
(d) Bijolia
R.A.S./R.T.S. (Pre) 1992
Ans. (d)
Feudal exploitation of the peasantry was common in Mewar
(Modern Rajasthan) in the latter half of the nineteenth
century. This led to Bijolia Movement. It was the fi rst Peasant
Movement of India. The leadership of the Movement was
initially provided by Sadhu Sitaram Das in 1913 A.D. and
later in 1915 A.D. by Vijay Singh Pathik.
2. Consider the following statements related to Bijolia
Peasant Movement:
1. Vijay Singh Pathik went to meet Mahatma
Gandhiji to give information regarding the Bijolia
Peasant Movement.
2. Prayag’s Abhyudaya and Calcutta’s Bharat Mitra
newspaper regularly published news related to the
Bijolia Peasant Movement.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
(a) Only 1 is true.
(b) Only 2 is true.
(c) Both 1 and 2 are true. (d) Neither 1 nor 2 is true.
(e) Question not attempted.
Rajasthan P.C.S. (Pre) 2024
Ans. (b)
The Bijolia Peasant Movement began in 1897 A.D. in the
Mewar state of Rajasthan, led by the local farmers. This
movement is considered one of the longest peasant movements
in India, lasting approximately 44 years. The fi rst phase of the
movement was led by Sadhu Sitaram Das, while the second
phase was led by Vijay Singh Pathik. Vijay Singh Pathik was a
renowned freedom fi ghter and peasant leader. He organized the
farmers of Mewar against the excessive taxes imposed by the
rulers and raised his voice against these injustices. However,
it is not true that Vijay Singh Pathik went to Mahatma Gandhi

10. What was the aim of Eka Movement in Oudh?
(a) To stop to give rent to the Government
(b) To protect the rights of landlords
(c) End of Satyagraha
(d) Transformation of rent into cash.
39th B.P.S.C. (Pre) 1994
Ans. (d)
The grassroot leadership of the Eka Movement was Madari
Pasi and other low-caste leaders and many small Zamindars.
Towards the end of 1921 A.D., peasant discontent resurfaced
in some northern districts of the United Provinces—Hardoi,
Bahraich, Sitapur etc. The issues involved were:
(i) High rents—50 per cent higher than the recorded rates;
(ii) Oppression by Thikedars in charge of revenue collection;
and
(iii) The practice of share-rents.
The meetings of the Eka or the Unity Movement involved
a symbolic religious ritual in which the assembled peasants
vowed that they would:
i. Pay only the recorded rent but would pay it on time;
ii. Not leave when evicted;
iii. Refuse to do forced labour;
iv. No help to the criminals;
v. Abide by Panchayat decisions.
By March 1922 A.D., however, severe repression on the part
of the authorities succeeded in bringing the Eka Movement
to its end.

*Madras Labour Union was formed in 1918 A.D. under
the leadership of B.P. Wadia and V. Kalyanasundaram and
it became the First modern labour Union. Buckingham and
Carnatic Clothe Mills labourers were part of this union. Soon,
two Labour Unions in Bombay, one at Calcutta (The Indian
Seamen's Union) and four Labour Unions at Madras were
established.
*The Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association was established
on February 25, 1920, by Anasuya Sarabhai (she became
president of the association) and Mahatma Gandhi. It emerged
following the 1918 Ahmedabad mill strike. *All India Trade
Union Congress was founded by N.M. Joshi on 31st October,
1920 A.D. at Bombay. *Lala Lajpat Rai was the fi rst President
of All India Trade Union Congress and Joseph Baptista was the
Vice President. Dewan Chaman Lal was its General Secretary
(they all were among the founding members) The motive behind
its formation was the establishment of International Labour
Organization in 1919 A.D. So Indian labourers decided to
organize themselves as labour unions. This organization was
divided for the fi rst time in 1929 A.D. at Nagpur, Jawaharlal
Nehru was president at that time. *Communist International
was founded in March 1919 A.D. by Vladimir Lenin and
Bolshevik Party of Russia. *M.N. Roy visited Russia on
the invitation of Lenin and joined communist International
becoming the fi rst Indian to do so. To stop the growing power
and influence of Communist activities, some communist
members were arrested on the grounds of a conspiracy
held in Kanpur. This case is popularly known as Kanpur
Conspiracy. *British government in 1924 A.D. started cases
against M.N. Roy, Shripad Amrit Dange, Ghulam Hussain,
Ramcharan Lal Sharma, Muzaffar Ahmed, Shaukat Usmani,
Singaravelu Chettiar, Nalini Gupta, Shamuddin Hassan, M.R.S.
Velayndhun, Dr. Manilal, Sampurnanand and Satyabhakta in
Kanpur conspiracy. The government charged them with the
conspiracy of establishing a revolutionary organisation in India.
*Revolutionary period of trade union is believed to be 1926-
1939 A.D.. During this M.N. Roy, Muzaffar Ahmed, Shripad
A. Dange, Shauqat Usmani etc. were the main leader of the
Trade Union Movement. * In 1940 AD, M.N. Roy established
Radical Democratic Party. *Saumendra nath Tagore in
1934 established Revolutionary Communist Party of India.

Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala
Bagh Massacre (1919)
Government constituted a committee under the Chairmanship
of Justice Sidney Rowlatt, in 1917 A.D. with the objective to
investigate and report on the nature and extent of the criminal
conspiracies connected with revolutionary movements in India
and recommending legislative/legal changes. Based on the
recommendations made by this committee, an Act was passed
in March 1919 A.D. which empowered to arrest/search/detain
persons suspected of sedition/revolutionary activity (including
without warrant/trial as per provisions). This Act was also called
as an act of No Dalil, No Vakil, No Appeal. Rowlatt Act was
passed during the tenure of Lord Chelmsford (1916-1921 A.D.)
in 1919 A.D. In his struggle against Rowlatt act, Gandhiji used
different stages of movements-Rowlatt Satyagraha-hartals/civil
disobedience (1919), non-cooperation and Khilafat movement
(began in January 1921).
*First bold step of Gandhiji in All India politics was the Rowlatt
Satyagraha. *On 13th, April 1919 A.D., a meeting was called
to protest against the arrest of two popular leaders of Punjab,
Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal. The meeting
was organized in Jallianwala Bagh Amritsar on the day of
Baisakhi. Brigadier General Reginald Edward Harry Dyer
ordered to open fi re on unarmed peaceful gathering killing nearly
estimates 379 individuals and wounding hundreds more (cited
by UK Parliament). After the Massacre at Jallianwala Bagh,
Rabindranath Tagore renounced the title of Knighthood granted
by the British Government. *Shankaran Nair resigned from
the Viceroy's Executive Council in protest against the massacre.
*Hunter Commission was constituted by the Government of
India to inquire into the incident of Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.
C.H. Sitalwad, Pt. Jagat Narayan and Sultan Ahmad Khan
were Indian member in this commission. The commission in
its report presented in 1920 didn't fi nd government guilty in
this incident. It was said that disorder sometimes becomes
revolt. That is why Martial law was compulsory and it is
fully justifi able to open fi re at that huge gathering. Also, this
commission said that incident was just as an error in judgement
of Dyer. *General Dyer was directed to resign his appointment
as Brigade commander in India after this incident but British
newspaper presented him as the protector of British Empire and
British Lords of assembly praised him as the Lion of British
Empire. For his services to Britain, he was given the Sword
of Honour. In March 1940 A.D., a Revolutionary from Punjab
Udham Singh killed the Lieutenant governor (of Punjab at
the time of Massacre) Sir Michael O' Dwyer in London to
avenge the Jallianwala Bagh killings. Gandhiji was given the
task of writing the draft of the report of Congress Investigation
Committee on Jallianwala Bagh Massacre. *Montagu termed
the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre as Preventive Killing.

questions.prompt:
Consider the following statements about The Rowlatt

(2) The Rowlatt Act curbed fundamental rights such as
the freedom of expression and strengthened police
powers.

options.text: Both the statements (1) and (2) are correct

questions.explanation:
Rowlatt Act was passed by the Imperial legislative council
in 1919 A.D. The act was an effective plan to suppress the
increasing revolutionary activities in country. It curbed
fundamental rights such as the freedom of expression and put
severe restrictions on press. The act strengthened police powers
so much that anybody could be arrested without any trial
against them. In response Gandhiji started Rowlatt Satyagrah
(1919 A.D.) which was although restricted to cities but turned
to be the fi rst all-India struggle against the British government.

questions.chapter: Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (1919)
questions.prompt: The fi rst venture of Gandhi in all-India politics was the:
questions.explanation:
Every movement started by Gandhiji helped Indian Nationalism
to attain an unprecedented height. The Movements conceived
by Gandhiji like Champaran Peasant Movement (1917 A.D.),
Ahmedabad Mill Workers Movement (1918 A.D.), Kheda
Peasant Movement(1918 A.D.) were limited to the specifi c
issue of a particular section of the society. The scope of the
area was also very limited. But Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919
A.D.) against the censure of freedom of press and detention
without trial was proactively joined by all the sections of the
society. Sentiments of the aggrieved common people were
addressed. Knitting of people from all religions, all castes, all
age groups, and both the genders in the Nationalist Movement
had a distinguished characteristic of the Rowlatt Satyagraha.
National newspapers, political journals, etc. made Gandhi a
popular fi gure. This was the fi rst all India level Movement
launched by Mahatma Gandhi.

The massacre of the crowd at Jallianwala Bag at

questions.explanation:
Jallianwala Bagh Massacre or Amritsar massacre was
an important incident in the history of Indian Freedom
Movement during the British rule. On April 13, 1919 the
infamous Jallianwalla Bagh incident took place. On that day
a large crowd gathered in the enclosed ground of Jallianwalla
Bagh to protest against the Government’s new repressive
measures and to protest against the arrest of two famous
leaders of Punjab Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal.

outside from the city, many villagers were unaware of the
martial law that had been imposed. Dyer entered the area,
blocked the exit points, and opened fi re on the crowd, killing
thousands of people.

questions.chapter: Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (1919)
questions.prompt: The Hunter Committee was appointed after the:
questions.explanation:
The Government established a Disorders Inquiry Committee
headed by Lord William Hunter, a Senator of College of
Justice of Scotland. The Committee had 7 members 4 British
and 3 Indians. It was set up to investigate the Jallianwala
Bagh Tragedy. Before the Committee could publish its report,
Congress put forward its view. This view criticized Dyer’s act
as inhuman and also said that there was no justifi cation for
the introduction of the martial law in Punjab. But the Hunter
Report, as expected, saw the things differently. Although it
condemned most of the decisions taken by Brigadier General
Dyer, it agreed with the imposition of martial law in Punjab.
It also criticized the method of Satyagraha adopted by Gandhi
and held Gandhi partially responsible for “deteriorated” law
and order situation. As a result, Dyer was sent to England
relieved of his command. The British Government called
Brigadier General Dyer ‘Lion of British Empire’ and gave
‘Sword of Honour’ for his service.

questions.chapter: Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (1919)
questions.prompt:
Which one of the following aroused a wave of popular
indignation that led to the massacre by the British a
Jallianwala Bagh?
questions.explanation:
The Government appointed a commission headed by Justice
Sidney Rowlatt to investigate the nature of discontent and the
cause of revolutionary activities. On the recommendation of
the commission, Rowlatt Act was passed in March, 1919. The
Act empowered the Government to arrest any person without
assigning any reason or ground for the arrest; search any place
without a warrant and imprison any person without a trial.
The Rowlatt Act raised a storm of protests and a wave of
popular indignation throughout the country. The Press and
the Congress called it the ‘Black Act.’ There were strikes
and public meetings at various places throughout the country.
At Amritsar, the arrest of Gandhiji and two prominent local
leaders Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal aroused a
wave of protests. On April 13, 1919 a peaceful and unarmed
protest rally was held in the open, but enclosed ground called
Jallianwala Bagh. While the meeting was in progress, a
British offi cer Brigadier General Dyer along with his troops
entered the park. Without any warning or asking the people to
disperse, Brigadier General Dyer and his troops started fi ring
at them. The park had a small exit gate; it too, was closed.
In just ten minutes, about a thousand persons were killed,
and many thousands wounded. The fi ring stopped only after
ammunition had been exhausted.

• During the years 1919-1922 A.D., two mass movements
emerged in India as a means to oppose British rule: the
Khilafat movement and the Non-Cooperation Movement.
The non-cooperation Movement marked the beginning of
the Gandhian Movement against British colonialism.
• The movement saw significant participation from
students, who left government-established schools and
colleges in large numbers to join the cause. However, as
the movement progressed, some of them began to harbour
reservations about Gandhi's program. Hence statement 3
is correct.

Swadeshi (indigenous production and boycott of foreign
goods) by the nationalists, supported the economic
boycott called for during the movement.
• Peasants also actively participated in the movement, but
it did lead to confrontations between different castes,
particularly between the lower and upper castes.

the middle classes, but as time passed, many of them
expressed reservations about Gandhi's approach. Hence
statement 1 is incorrect.
• The Non-Cooperation Movement provided an opportunity
for the oppressed masses to express their grievances
against both the British and their Indian oppressors.
• Women played a crucial role in the movement, participating
in large numbers, giving up purdah (seclusion) and
contributing their ornaments to the Tilak Fund.
• The movement faced violent reprisals from the police,
resulting in the loss of many lives.

political system and preferred continued British presence.

his praise for Brahminism. Hence statement 2 is incorrect.

widespread participation from various sections of society,
but as it progressed, some segments showed reservations,
and it also faced opposition from political groups like the
Justice Party.

questions.explanation:
Montagu-Chelmsford reform (Government of India act, 1919)
provided for a Constitutional Commission to review its working
and operations. The Government of India Act, 1919 was
passed on the basis of recommendations of Lord Chelmsford
and Samuel Montagu to introduce self-governing institutions
gradually to India. For this purpose, Simon Commission was
appointed in November, 1927 AD by the British Conservative
Government under Stanley Baldwin to report on the working
of the Indian Constitution established by the Government
of India Act of 1919. The Commission consisted of seven
members under the chairmanship of Sir John Simon.
None of the members of this Commission was Indian thus
Indian leaders opposed the Commission saying it ‘White
Commission.’ Simon Commission advocated reconstitution
of Central legislature with a federal character instead of a
unitary character and its members should be elected from
provincial legislature indirectly. Simon Commission reached
Bombay on February 3, 1928 A.D. on that day Countrywide
strike was held.

Empire in India. The march took place in April 1930 A.D.

organized by Mahatma Gandhi, both in the framework

sea, the marchers broke the Salt Law.

Communal Award and Poona
Pact (1932)
*A consensus among several parties for the separate electorate
for Dalits was not reached in Second Round Table Conference.
The His Majesty Government's declared position (endorsed by
Parliament) that if communities failed to agree the government
would devise and apply a scheme. As a result British P.M.
Ramsay MacDonald fi nd a solution (although Europeans,
Anglo-Indians, Indian Christians got separate electorates
in 1919). * On 16th August 1932 A.D. Ramsay MacDonald
announced Communal Award. In this award, each minority
group was given some reserved seats in Legislative Assemblies
and elections to those seats were to be held by a separate
electorate. Members of the depressed classes qualifi ed to vote,
will vote in a general constituency and they one also entitled
to vote in a general constituency.
*Earlier Muslims and Sikhs were considered minorities but
with this award the Dalit section of Hindu constituencies
also got separated from it and now considered as a minority.
Now Muslims, Indian Christians, Sikhs, Anglo-Indians
and others including depressed classes were given separate
electorates which were available in elections at Provincial
Legislatures only. * Gandhiji started his fi rst fast unto death
on 20th September, 1932 A.D. from Yerwada jail against the
Communal Award which ended with the Poona Pact between
B.R. Ambedkar and Gandhiji. Gandhiji didn’t sign this
Pact. On 24th September, 1932 A.D. Poona Pact was signed
between Dr. Ambedkar from Dalit section and Madan Mohan
Malaviya from Hindu community. *M.R. Jayakar, Devdas
Gandhi, P. Baloo, Gavai, Thakkar, Solanki, T.B. Sapru, G.D.
Birla, Rajagopalachari, Dr. Rajendra Prasad, Rao Bahadur
Srinivas, M.C. Rajah, C.V. Mehta, Bakhale and Kamat signed
this Pact too. *71 seats were reserved for Depressed classes in
Communal Award which was increased to 148 by Poona Pact
(Madras-30, Sindh with Bombay - 15, Punjab - 8, Bihar and
Orissa - 18, Central Provinces - 20, Assam - 7, Bengal -30 and
United Provinces 20). (This number is however 147 in some
books). Also, 18% of General seats were reserved for the Dalits
in central legislature. After the Poona Pact, Gandhiji didn't
show more interest in the Civil Disobedience Movement and
shifted his focus towards the fi ght against untouchability. He
founded All India Anti-Untouchability League which was
later renamed ‘Harijan Sevak Sangh’. Ghanshyam Das Birla
was its fi rst President.
All India Depressed Classes League was founded by Babu
Jagjivan Ram. All India Scheduled Castes Federation was
founded by B.R. Ambedkar in 1942 A.D., while All India
Depressed Classes Association was founded in 1926 A.D.
by M.C. Rajah. On 14th August, 1931 A.D., B.R. Ambedkar
in a conversation with Gandhiji said that "History tells that
Mahatmas, like fl eeting phantoms, raise dust, but raise no level".

Congress Socialist Party
(1934)
*In May 1934, the All India Congress Committee met at Patna
to set up a Congress Parliamentary Board to fi ght elections
under the aegis of Congress itself. However, some of the
members of All India Congress Committee held separate
meetings and founded All India Congress Socialist Party, and
this party was offi cially inaugurated in October 1934 A.D. The
policies and working methods were to be decided in a meeting
that was to be held in Bombay.
*Jaya Prakash Narayan was the convener of All India Congress
Socialist Party in Patna, 1934. He was the general secretary of
party and Acharya Narendra Dev was the President. The
objective of the was to push the Indian National Congress
towards a clear socialist agenda, focusing on full independence,
abolition of landlordism and nationalisation of key industries.
Its members were :- Ashok Mehta, Achyut Patwardhan, Minoo
Masani, Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia, Purushottam Trikam
Das, Yusuf Meherally, Ganga Sharan Sinha and Kamla Devi
Chattopadhyay, etc. Bihar Socialist Party was founded by
Ganga Sharan Sinha, Rambriksha Benipuri and Ramanand
Mishra (in 1991). Sri Narsingh Narayan Azad was a socialist
and was an important member of Bihar Socialist Party. *J.P.
Narayan belonged to Bihar Socialist Party. *J.P. Narayan also
known as Loknayak secretly organized Indian masses during
Quit India movement with the help of Dr. Ram Manohar
Lohia and Aruna Asaf Ali. On 5th June, 1974, he called for
total revolution (Sampoorna Kranti) from Gandhi Maidan. He
was awarded Bharat Ratna posthumously in 1999. In April,
1946 A.D., ‘Jaya Prakash Day’ was celebrated for the release of
Jaya Prakash from prison. A rally was conducted in Bankipur
Maidan of Patna where the release of Jaya Prakash Narayan
was demanded and criticism of government policy regarding
the arrest of political persons was made.*In May, 1936 A.D.,
21 businessmen of Bombay signed Bombay Manifesto. The
manifesto was against propagating the principles of socialism
as conveyed by Nehru in Lucknow Session.

the following statements:

evasion of taxes.

socialist caucus within the INC. Its members rejected what
they saw as the anti-rational mysticism of Gandhi as well
as the sectarian attitude of the Communist Party of India
towards the Congress party. Infl uenced by Fabianism as
well as Marxism, the CSP advocated armed struggle as well
as non-violent resistance. The CSP advocated decentralized
socialism in which cooperation, trade unions, independent
farmers and local authorities would hold a substantial share
of economic power. As secularists, they hoped to transcend
communal divisions through class solidarity. Hence, option

Provincial Election and
Formation of Cabinet (1937)
*On the basis of Government of India Act, 1935, in February
1937, election results were announced of provincial legislatures
in which Congress by defeating its opponents secured majority
in fi ve provinces.
1. Madras (159 seats out of total 215 seats) - Congress
2. Bihar (98 seats out of total 152 seats) - Congress
3. Central Provinces and Berar (70 out of 112) - Congress
4. United Provinces (134 seats out of 228) - Congress
5. Orissa (36 out of 60 seats) - Congress
* Congress emerged as the single largest party in Bombay (86
seats out of 175), Assam and North-West Frontier Province.
Only in Bengal, Punjab and Sindh did Congress not secure
enough support from masses to form the government on its
own. The cabinets formed by Congress after 1936-37 A.D.
elections only lasted for 28 months. In July 1937 A.D.,
Congress formed cabinets in 6 provinces - Madras, Bombay,
Central Province, Orissa, Bihar, and United Province and
with the support of other parties Congress formed a coalition
government in Assam (a coalition government was formed
by Muhammad Saadulla in 1937, but later resigned and
Congress government led by Gopinath Bordoloi took offi ce in
September 1938) and North-West Frontier Provinces. Based
on 1937 results, Sir Sahibzada Abdul Qayyum Khan, formed
a coalition government although Indian National Congress was
the single largest party, the Congress formed the government
there by moving no-confi dence motion against Qayyum Khan.
The inclusion of Indians into the Second World War without
consultation led to the resignation of all Congress cabinets.
On 22nd October, 1939 A.D. Congress cabinet of all provinces
resigned as an act of protest. Congress coalition government
in Assam under Gopinath Bordoloi was resigned from the
government in November, 1939 and the NWFP government
was also resigned in November, 1939. On the resignation of the
Congress cabinets, Jinnah called Indian Muslims to celebrate
22nd December, 1939 A.D. as a Day of Deliverance. *Working
Committee of Indian National Congress decided for abolition of
feudal intermediaries/peasants proprietorship in 1937 A.D. as a
result of which Congress governments in U.P. and Bihar passed
tenancy bills. Congress secured 134 seats out of 228 seats in
United Provinces and formed government on its own. *Govind
Ballabh Pant was the Prime Minister (Premier) while Kailash
Nath Katju was Law and Justice Minister and Revenue/Home/
Jail Ministry was given to Rafi Ahmed Kidwai. * In Congress-
ruled states the reports related to Muslims grievances were in
the following chronological order.
•
- Pirpur Report - 1938
- Sharif Report - March, 1939
- Fazlul Haq Report (Muslims Sufferings Under Congress
Rule Report) - December, 1939

questions.prompt:
Who among the following first coined the word
'Pakistan'?
questions.explanation:
The term "Pakistan" or Pakstan (later became Pakistan) was
fi rst coined by Chaudhary Rahmat Ali, a Pakistani nationalist
in a pamphlet published in 1933 A.D. The word was formed
by combining the names of the regions that were to constitute
the proposed nation: Punjab, Afghan Province (North-West
Frontier Province), Kashmir, Sindh and Balochistan. The idea
of Pakistan gained further momentum, leading to the creation
of the independent state of Pakistan in 1947.

considered as the originator of the idea of a separate Muslim
nation. Inspired by the spirit of Pan-Islam in All India
Muslim League at Allahabad Session in 1930. Muhammad
Iqbal said “ I would like to see Punjab, the North-West
Frontier Province, Sindh and Balochistan amalgamated into
a single state. Self-government within the British Empire,
or without the British Empire, formation of a consolidated
North-West Indian Muslim state appears to me to be the fi nal
destiny of the Muslims, at least of North-West India.

questions.prompt:

1. Gyani Pritam Singh
2. Mohan Singh
3. Subhash Chandra Bose

Select correct answer by using codes given below:
questions.explanation:
The Indian National Army (INA) was the brainchild of
Giani Pritam Singh Dhillon along with Mohan Singh Major
Fujiwara and on 15 July, 1942 The Indian National Army was
formed under the leadership of Mohan Singh. Giani Pritam
Singh became actively involved in the Indian Independence
Movement and Gadar Party. He met with Iwaichi Fujiwara,
who had even before the declaration of war by Japan, reached
an agreement of collaboration with the Japanese at Bangkok
in December, 1941. It was Giani Pritam Singh’s idea working
with Iwaichi Fujiwara who released Indian soldiers who
were asked to join an Indian National Army to fi ght for
Indian independence. These plans were started long before
the war broke out, among a group of revolutionaries based
in Bangkok. Thus, Capt. Mohan Singh was not the founder
of INA, but was only the fi rst operational Commander of the
INA. He accepted the position at the insistence of Giani Ji
and Iwaichi Fujiwara. The brains behind INA were Iwaichi
Fujiwara and Giani Pritam Singh Dhillon.

questions.explanation:

announced the establishment of the Provisional Government
of Free India and took charge of INA.

developed into violent confrontations with authority and
pressure from the political parties from India; Commander-

let the defendants go free.

questions.explanation:
The Cabinet Mission of 1946 AD came to India to discuss
the transfer of power from the British Government to the
Indian Leadership, with the aim of preserving India's unity
and granting it independence formulated at the initiative of
Clement Attlee, the Prime Minister of United Kingdom, the
mission included Lord Pethick-Lawrence, the secretary of
state for India, Sir Stafford Cripps, President of the Board
of Trade and A.V. Alexander, the fi rst Lord of the Admiralty.
Lord Wavell, the Viceroy of India, did not participate in
every step but was present. The Mission arrived on March
24, 1946 AD.
According to the Mission, the representation of the Provincial
Legislatures were to be broken up into 3 sections
(a) Section A : Madras, United Provinces, Central Province
and Berar, Bombay, Bihar & Orissa.
(b) Section B : Punjab, Sindh, NWFP
(c) Section C : Assam and Bengal.
Apart from this, the Provinces of Chief Commissioners,
Delhi, Ajmer-Marvar and Coorg will be included in category
(A) and Baluchistan will be included in category (B).
The Congress accepted the proposals related to the constitu-
ent assembly. But since, the Muslim league had been given
disproportionate representation; it rejected the idea of the
interim government.
The Muslim League fi rst approved the Plan. But when
congress, declared that it could change the scheme through
majority in the Constituent Assembly they rejected the plan.
Muslim League on repeated request by Lord Wavell joined
the Interim Government on 13 October, 1946 AD.

questions.explanation:
Under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946, elections were held
for the fi rst time for Constituent Assembly. The elections
for the 296 seats assigned to the British Indian provinces
were completed by July, 1946 AD. Congress won 208 seats
and Muslim League won 73 seats and other independent
candidates won 15 seats. M .A. Jinnah was not a member of the
Constituent Assembly of India. The Constituent Assembly was
the fi rst Parliament of Independent India. Dr. Sachchidananda
Sinha was the fi rst President (Temporary Chairman of the
Assembly) of the Constituent Assembly when it met on
December 9, 1946 AD. Dr. Rajendra Prasad then became the
permanent Chairman of the Constituent Assembly, and later
became the fi rst President of India. The Constitution of India
was adopted on 26th November, 1949 AD.

questions.prompt:
Which political party's National Executive called for
the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly and its re-
election by adult suffrage?
questions.explanation:
The National Executive of the Indian Socialist Party in 1946
A.D. demanded the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly
and its re-election through universal adult suffrage. Socialist
leaders such as Jayaprakash Narayan and Ram Manohar
Lohia argued that the Constituent Assembly, which was
indirectly elected by the Provincial Legislatures, did not
adequately represent the common Indian people. Therefore,
these leaders advocated for a more democratic process and
called for the reconstitution of the Constituent Assembly
based on universal adult suffrage.

Formation of Interim
Government (1946)
*On 12th August, 1946 AD Lord Wavell invited Congress
President Jawahar Lal Nehru to form the Interim Government. On
24th August, 1946 AD under the leadership of Jawaharlal Nehru,
Congress announced a communique of fi rst Interim Government
of India. On 2nd September, 1946 AD First Interim Government
of India was formed in which Muslim League didn’t participate
in the beginning.
*Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the Minister of Agriculture and
Food in the Interim Government. Baldev Singh was Defence
Minister. External affairs and Commonwealth Affairs were
looked after by Jawahar Lal Nehru in this interim government.
Asaf Ali held Communication (Rail and Transport) Ministry
in the interim government of 1946 AD. *Muslim League
after repeated requests by Lord Wavell joined the Interim
Government in 1946 AD. In October, 1946 AD fi ve members
of League joined the Interim Government. *Liaqat Ali Khan
was given Finance Ministry, who in his Budget presentation
imposed several taxes on businessmen and industrialists. *Abul
Kalam Azad was not a member of this Interim Government.
*This Interim Government had twelve (out of planned 14)
Ministers- Jawahar Lal Nehru, Sardar Vallabh Bhai Patel, Dr.
Rajendra Prasad, Asaf Ali, C. Rajagopalachari, Sharat Chandra
Bose, Dr. John Mathai, Sardar Baldev Singh, Sir Shafat Ahmed
Khan, Jagjivan Ram, Syed Ali Zaheer and C.H. Bhabha. Three
of these twelve were to be removed when Muslim League
joined the Interim Government, they were - Syed Ali Zaheer,
Sharat Chandra Bose and Sir Safat Ahmed. *Krishak Praja
Party in the leadership of A.K. Fazlul Haq joined hands with
Muslim League and formed coalition government after the
election in Bengal and Cabinet of the Muslim League was
formed in Bengal which ruled till 14th August 1947 AD. * H.S.
Suhrawardy was its Prime Minister. *16th August, 1946 AD
was decided as Direct Action day by Muslim League. On the
Direct Action Day rioting activities were prevalent. It was
shown through violence that Hindu and Muslim couldn't live
together in one country. ‘Calcutta’ was the main centre of
these activities Noakhali riots began later (in October 1946).
The All India Muslim League formally demanded a separate
state for muslims, known as the Pakistan Resolution (or Lahore
Resolution) on March 23, 1940 as its general session in Lahore.
The League offi cially decided to join the interim Government
on October 13, 1946 (after the direct action day). Initially they
boycotted the government established on September 2, 1946.

will best ensure the future happiness and prosperity of India

depart from India with honour and with minimal damage.
*Mountbatten during the talks on the transfer of power reached
a conclusion that partition of India and formation of Pakistan is
a must. He prepared a plan, keeping in mind the instructions by
Attlee. The plan was prepared for the partition of India, this plan
is known as the Mountbatten Plan (3rd June, 1947 AD). *As
per the plan on July 1947 AD, Indian Independence Act was
passed by the British Parliament in which two nations India and
Pakistan were given dominion status and the deadline for the
formation of Pakistan and India as two nations were fi xed to 15th
August, 1947 AD. *Indian Independence Bill was presented
by Attlee on 4th July, 1947 AD in the House of Commons in
British Parliament. House of Commons passed this Bill on 15th
July, 1947 AD and was passed by House of Lords the next day.
The Bill got Royal Assent of his Majesty on 18th July, 1947 AD.
*Between 24 March and 6 May 1947 AD, in series of 133 full
records of talks with Indian politicians Mountbatten reached on
a conclusion that Cabinet Mission Plan had been impractical.
So he prepared another substitute plan for this and termed it as
“Plan Balkan”. *Punjab Boundary Commission and Bengal
Boundary Commission were formed by Mountbatten on 30th
June, 1947 AD to determine the division of land between India
and Pakistan along with Punjab and Bengal. Cyril Radcliffe
was the chairman of both the Councils. The councils was given
the task to demarcate the boundaries of Punjab and Bengal on

Muslim majority population. For this task, he had to take in

supporter of partition till my last breath. If I were to choose I

existing central Legislature ceased to exist and its place was
taken by Constituent Assembly which, primarily a constitution
making body, was to function as the Dominion Legislature as

Constitutional Development
of India
*British Parliament passed Regulating Act, 1773 to curb
rampant corruption and misgovernance. According to this act,
Madras and Bombay Presidencies came under the Calcutta
Presidency. Governor of Bengal became Governor-General
of Bengal (under Governor General and Council of Fort
William in Bengal in specifi ed matters). Warren Hastings
was appointed the fi rst Governor-General of Bengal. The
aim of the Regulating Act was to put the activities of East
India Company in India under the supervision of the British
Government.
*By the Regulating Act of 1773 a Supreme Court was
established at Calcutta with a Chief Justice and three other
judges. The Supreme Court was established in 1774 AD with
Elijah Impey as its Chief Justice, and Robert Chambers,
Le Maistre and John Hyde as its other justices. *In the year
1786 AD, a bill was presented and passed before the British
Parliament for amending measures, enabling the Governor-
General to act against/overrule the council. According to the
new rule, the Governor-General was given power to overrule
the decision of its council in some special cases. Cornwallis
didn’t want the District Magistrate to be very powerful so
he adopted the principle of separation of power (separating
fi nancial/revenues from judicial functions). *Monopoly of
trade of East India Company (except trade in tea and trade
with China) came to an end by 1813 Charter Act. With this
Act of 1813 for the next 20 years the Company was granted
the control of revenue of the British territorial acquisitions in
India under company government. *By the Charter Act of
1833, the company's monopoly of trade/commercial privileges
were abolished; it ceased to be a mercantile corporation and
the company was given only political works. By this Act, the
Governor-General of Bengal became the Governor General of
India. By this act a law member was added as the 4th member
to the Governor-General's executive council this law member
should not belongs to company itself, Also, he was not entitled
to sit or vote in executive meetings. The Law member will be
of English origin. *Macaulay became the fi rst law member of
the Governor-General's executive council. *By the Charter Act
of 1853, the salaries of Members of Board of Control started
to be decided by the Crown (His majesty) by Warrant but was
paid by the East India Company. The number of directors were
decreased 18 out of 24, and 6 out of those were to be nominated
by crown. There was a provision in this act that recruitment
to the service would be done by competitive exams set to
regulations/qualifi cations without any discrimination as per
the non-discrimination clause mentioned in 1833 Act. *British
Government by the Government of India Act, 1858, took away
the control of Administration of India from the Company. Now
all the powers of the Board of Control and Court of directors
was handed over to Secretary of State for India. *Governor
General of India was granted right to issue ordinance in
Emergency Period by the Indian Councils Act, 1861. These
ordinances had a maximum life of 6 months. By this Act, the
executive council of viceroy was given law-making powers.
*Lord Canning started Portfolio system, Lord Canning
gave departments to other members of his council this way he
prepared the base of Ministerial government system in India. By
this system, each department of administration was assigned to
one member. On the recommendation of Montagu Chelmsford
reforms, Civil Services exam started to be held together in India
and England from the year 1922 AD.
*Aitchison Commission in its report in 1887 stated that the
Indian Civil Services Exam should not be held in India and
England together. *The reforms announced on 20 August 1917
AD are also known as Montagu declaration on the name of
the then Secretary of State for India Montagu. *The report of
then Viceroy Lord Chelmsford and Secretary of State for India
Montagu became the base of Government of India Act, 1919.
* The Dyarchy at provinces was introduced by Mont-ford
reforms, 1919. It is also called as Government of India Act
1919. By this Act, the subjects of provinces were divided into
two categories reserved and transferred subjects. Transferred
subjects were given to the governor acting with ministers
appointed under the act; whereas the reserved subjects were
looked on by the Governor in Council. * In 1926 AD, India’s
Public Service Commission was constituted. By the Indian
Councils Act 1861, the council of viceroy was expanded and
additional members minimum 6 and maximum 12 were added
to this council, for lawmaking processes. They were nominated
by Viceroy and had a tenure of two years. In this council, at least
half of the persons so nominated were to be non-offi cials. *By
this act the Madras and Bombay Presidencies were restored of
their lawmaking power and were allowed to make amendments
to the existing law. But the laws made by these Presidencies
would be valid only after the assent of the Governor-General.
*High Courts at Bombay, Madras and Calcutta were established
by Indian High Courts Act, 1861. *By the Indian Councils
Act, 1892, the rights of the Members of Legislative Councils
were increased in two aspects -
(i) They were given the right to discuss the budget without the
right to vote or to move any amendment to the budget.
(ii) After giving the advance notice of 6 days, they were allowed
to asks questions on Public interests.
*Indian Councils Act, 1909 was of the shortest duration
amongst the constitutional experiments of Britain in India. In
words of Ramsay MacDonald, “This reform is incomplete
and momentarily deal between democracy and bureaucracy”.
*Montagu-Chelmsford reforms in its report in 1918 stated
that the Indians participation in administration should be
increased. It was also proposed in the report that the exam of
Indian Civil Services should be held simultaneously in India
and Britain and one-third of the posts (at least) should be held
by Indians. *By the 1935 Act, the Public Service Commission
became the Federal Public Service Commission (it was set
up on April 1, 1937). *From 1937 AD, Federal Public Service
Commission and The Civil Service Commission (UK) started
conducting their exams separately. In 1950, after the enactment
of constitution, the Federal Public Service Commission was
renamed as Union Public Service Commission. *By this
Act Dyarchy at Provinces were abolished and Dyarchy was
introduced at the centre. Provinces were given autonomy and
the dual governance came to an end. With this the distinction
between the reserved and transferred was abolished. The
reserved seats under a joint electorate was expanded and now it
included Scheduled Castes, Muslims, Sikh, Europeans, Anglo-
Indians, Indian Christians etc. The present Constitution of India
is very similar to the 1935 Act.
The Main Provisions of 1935 Act are-
(1) Provision for establishment of a federation.
(2) Dyarchy at Centre
(3) Autonomy of provinces was restored and Dyarchy at
provinces abolished.
(4) Bicameral central legislative
(5) System of Provincial government
(6) Provincial Legislative Assembly
(7) Division of Power between centre and provinces
(8) Establishment of federal court, etc.
*Jawaharlal Nehru said, "1935 Act is a Machine (Car) with
strong brakes but no Engine". He was the Prime Minister of
India from 1947 to 1964 AD. He was the proponent and architect
of 'Five Principle of Peaceful Coexistence' (Panchsheel) and a
believer of Non-aligned Movement. Nehru in his address to
Congress in Lucknow Session, 1936 AD rejected Government
of India Act 1935, he termed this Act as Charter of slavery and
offered some severe criticism. Lucknow Session (1936) was
chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru. *Act of 1935 was the lengthiest
enactment in the history of laws made by Britain for British
India. It included 14 parts, 321 sections and 10 schedules. *The
“Instrument of Instructions” of the Government of India
Act,1935 was included as Directive Principles of State Policy
in India’s Constitution in 1950.

By a Regulation in 1793, the District Collector was
deprived of his judicial powers and made the collecting
agent only. What was the reason for such regulation?

options.text:

effi ciency of revenue collection would enormously
increase without the burden of other work.

Lord Cornwallis felt that judicial power should
compulsorily be in the hands of Europeans. While
Indians could be given the job of revenue collection
in the districts.

Lord Cornwallis was alarmed at the extent of power
concentrated in the District Collector and felt that such
absolute power was undesirable in one person.

India and a good training in law and Lord Cornwallis
felt that District Collector should be only a revenue
collector.

questions.explanation:
Cornwallis judicial reforms took their fi nal shape in 1793
AD and were embodied in the famous Cornwallis Code.
The new reforms were based on the principle of Separation
of Powers. Under the infl uence of the eighteenth-century
French philosophers Cornwallis sought to separate the
revenue administration from the administration of justice. The
Collector was the head of the revenue department in a district
and also enjoyed extensive judicial and magisterial powers.
Cornwallis believed that concentration of all powers in the
hands of the Collector in the District retards the improvement
as a judge of the Diwani Adalat redress the wrongs done by
him as collector or assessor of revenue? Thus, neither the
landlords nor the cultivators could regard the Collector as
an impartial Judge in revenue cases. The Cornwallis Code
divested the Collector of all judicial and magisterial powers
and left him with the duty of administration of revenue. A
new class of offi cer called the District Judge was created to
preside over the District Civil Court. The District Judge was
empowered with magisterial and police functions.

questions.prompt:
The real intention of the British to include the Princely
States in the Federal Union proposed by the India Act
of 1935 was to –

options.text:
Exercise more direct political and administrative
control.

Involve the princes actively in the administration of
the colony.

Finally effect the complete political and administrative
take-over of all the princely States by the British

Use the princes to counter-balance the anti-imperialist
doctrines of the nationalist leaders.

questions.explanation:
The real intention of the British to include the Princely
States in the Federal Union proposed by the India Act of
1935 was to use the princes to counter balance the anti-
imperialist doctrines of the nationalist leaders. Princely States
represented approx 25% of the population of India while
under the Government of India Act, 1935 out of 260 members
156 were to represent the provinces and 104 to the Princely
States in the Upper House and the Lower House consisted
of 375 members out of whom 250 were to represent the
provinces and 125 to represent the Princely States. In both
Houses of the Federal Legislature, the states were given their
quota of representation. But the members from the State were
not to be elected. Despite such a wide range of provisions, the
princely states however refused to join the Federation. They
were alarmed by the changing situation in the country caused
by the rapid spread of the National Movement. The British
Government miserably failed to overcome the opposition of
the Indian National Congress, the Muslim League and the
princes against the Federal Scheme. So the Federal Scheme
was withheld except the establishment of the Federal Court
and the Provincial scheme was introduced on 1st April, 1937
causing a drastic change in the pattern of provincial politics.

questions.explanation:
First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82 AD) - The internal
problems of the Marathas and the growing ambition of
the English brought the beginning of the Anglo-Maratha
struggle. The primary cause of the fi rst Maratha war was the
interference of the English Government at Bombay in the
internal affairs of the Marathas. The First Anglo-Maratha War
ended with the Treaty of Salbai signed between the Mahadaji
Scindia and the Warren Hastings in 1782 AD. In the Treaty
of Salbai, status quo was maintained which gave the British
20 years of peace with the Marathas.
Third Anglo- Mysore War (1790-92 AD)– It was
fought between British and Tipu Sultan. British attacked
Srirangapatnam with the help of Nizam and Marathas. Under
the leadership of William Medows, British defeated Tipu
Sultan and they had a treaty in Srirangapatnam in March,
1792 AD. According to this treaty, Tipu Sultan was to give
away half of his kingdom and he had to pay 3 crores to British
for damages done in the war.
The First Anglo-Burmese War (1824-26 AD) – The
fi rst of three wars fought between the British and Burmese
Empires in the 19th century. The war which began primarily
over the control of northeastern India, ended in a decisive
British victory, giving the total British control of Assam,
Manipur, Cachar and Jaintia as well as Arakan Province
and Tenasserim. The Burmese were also forced to pay an
indemnity of one million pounds, and sign a commercial
treaty ‘Treaty of Yandabo’.
Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848-49 AD)-The Second Anglo-
Sikh War took place in 1848 and 1849 between the Sikh
Empire and the British East India Company.

Rammohan Roy. Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar initiated the
concept of Widow Remarriage and he also opened the doors
of colleges and other educational institutions to lower caste
students, which were earlier reserved only for Brahmins. For
his immense generosity and kind-heartedness, people started
addressing him as “Daya Sagar” (ocean of kindness). Major-

the Pindaris from all sides - on the north and east from Bengal,

massive army of 113,000 men and 300 cannons was divided
into two parts - on the northern side under Hastings’ command
and the southern under the control of Thomas Hislop. By the

1818 the Pindaris were practically exterminated.

Indian society. However, their criticism was limited to the

people, the Indian National Congress was declared
illegal by the colonial rulers.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Indentured labourers were those who were taken out of India
as labourers for fi xed periods in the British colonies. Their
condition was like that of bonded labourers. Gandhiji fi rst
raised his voice in favour of indentured labourers in South
Africa in 1894 AD. In the year 1914 AD, by the Gandhi's-
Smuts Agreement, the tax of 3 pounds on these labourers
ended. After coming back to India, Gandhi negotiated with
Viceroy Lord Chelmsford to end the indentured system and
fi nally in July 1917 AD the indentured system was banned.
Thus statement (1) is correct. After Gandhiji's Dandi March
and his breaking of salt law on April 6, 1930 AD, Indians
across the country started violating the salt law. In response to
this, many Congress leaders and Satyagrahis like Jawaharlal
Nehru, Mahadev Desai etc. were sent to prison and Indian
National Congress was declared illegal by British rule. Thus
statement (3) is correct.

role in setting the national agenda. He introduced the concept
of Non-Alignment to establish peace and cooperation among
people. The three major objectives of Nehru’s foreign
policy were to preserve the hard-earned sovereignty, protect
territorial integrity and promote rapid economic development.

(NAM) goes back to the friendship between three leaders –
Yugoslavia’s Josip Broz Tito, India’s Jawaharlal Nehru, and
Egypt’s leader Gamal Abdel Nasser. Indonesia’s Sukarno and
Ghana’s Kwame Nkrumah strongly supported them. These
fi ve leaders came to be known as the fi ve founders of NAM.
The fi rst non-aligned summit was held in Belgrade in 1961.

announced in the year :
questions.explanation:

propounded on April 6, 1948 AD in the proposal of industrial

questions.explanation:

questions.explanation:

inclusion of India in the war without Indian consent, Congress
ministers resigned in October 1939 AD. Subsequently, the
53rd session of the Congress was held in March 1940 AD at
Ramgarh (present-day Jharkhand), presided over by Maulana

to India. This mission proposed limited self-governance
for India and was part of a series of efforts to secure Indian
cooperation in the war effort.

questions.prompt:
The objective of the Butler Committee of 1927 was
to :

options.text:
Defi ne the jurisdiction of the Central and Provincial
Governments.
Defi ne the powers of the Secretary of State for India.
Impose censorship of the national press.

Improve the relationship between the Government of
India and the Indian States.

questions.explanation:
The Indian State Committee constituted a committee in the
year 1927 under the Chairmanship of Sir Harcourt Butler,
also known as the Butler Committee. The formation of this
Committee was about the investigation and classifi cation
of relationship between the Supreme power and the Native
kings. The Committee visited 16 states and submitted its
report in the year 1929. After examining the existing relations
of Supreme (British) power in Indian and princely states the
Committee presented its recommendations regarding the
fi nancial and economic relation of these two.

questions.prompt:
When was the special rights and privy purse enjoyed
by the Indian Princely States abolished?
questions.explanation:
Privy purse was a payment made to erstwhile Indian princely
states' ruling families by central government of India as part
of their agreement to merge their states with the Republic of
India in 1949 thereby ending their ruling rights. However all
the special rights and privy purse enjoyed by Indian Princely
States were abolished by 26th Constitutional Amendment Act,
1971 in the year of 1971.

Panchayat (HMP, estd 1948), unions of Forward Block and
